P22 (S3 file store) code slice landed — bucket names de-hardcoded, Minio client made region-aware, EnsureBucketAsync tolerant of a least-privilege denial, CSP media-src added, nginx recordings proxy made cloud-safe. DEF-015 was under-scoped: it named three recording handlers, but Topics/AttachFileToTopic.cs carried a FOURTH const ('acmp-topics'), a bucket no AWS environment provisions and which the app IAM cannot create — topic attachment would have failed outright in cloud. All four now read StorageOptions (Storage:RecordingsBucket / Storage:AttachmentsBucket); defaults reproduce the on-prem MinIO split so nothing moves, and both cloud services point at the single per-env bucket. U1's offline half is answered and PINNED BY TEST rather than by a spike run: Minio 6.0.3 recognises any Amazon host and substitutes its own region map (AWSS3Endpoints), so us-east-1 is addressed as s3.amazonaws.com path-style regardless of the configured ACMP_S3_ENDPOINT — the CSP media-src origin therefore had to be s3.amazonaws.com, and getting that wrong would have blocked playback silently with nothing in the API logs. Reading the SDK also showed PutObjectPartAsync issues an AbortMultipartUpload on a part-count mismatch for known-size streams (every upload we make) while 03-iam.sh granted no s3:AbortMultipartUpload — added to both policy documents before P20 is ever run, so it is a script edit rather than a live IAM change. DEVIATION from the slice text, recorded not silent: the nginx /acmp-recordings/ proxy is neutralized (variable upstream + resolver, so nginx stops resolving 'minio' at config load and the cloud web container boots) rather than deleted, because deleting it would regress the on-prem/ngrok dev playback path that deploy/.env actually uses and force a second nginx template ahead of P25. NOT DONE, and not claimed: AC-078 and AC-083 both need a live bucket and stay Pending; no AWS call was made; the AWSSDK.S3 fallback was not built. Evidence: full backend suite green (dotnet test exit 0), coverage gate 99.64% global (>=95% target) exit 0, dotnet format clean.

P22 code slice: StorageOptions across four handlers, region-aware Minio client, denied-create tolerance, CSP media-src, cloud-safe nginx recordings location, s3:AbortMultipartUpload in 03-iam.sh. P22 follow-up: the nginx leg was asserted before it was verified, and verifying it found a real break. Rendering the template in the pinned nginx-unprivileged image proved BOTH halves of the recordings-proxy deviation mechanically — with keycloak/api resolvable and NO minio host the committed template passes `nginx -t`, while restoring the literal `proxy_pass http://minio:9000;` fails with `[emerg] host not found in upstream "minio"`, so the variable+resolver form is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. The first verification run was itself wrong, though: it mounted the template into the BASE image, which substitutes every defined env var, whereas Dockerfile.web pins NGINX_ENVSUBST_FILTER to KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN alone. CI caught it (acmp-web-1 exited 1 on the e2e stack). A template variable missing from that filter is not left harmlessly alone: the surviving ${ACMP_MEDIA_ORIGIN} is then read by nginx as one of its OWN runtime variables and the config dies at load with `unknown "acmp_media_origin" variable`. Fixed by listing it in the filter regex with an empty default in the image, and re-verified as UID 101 in all three combinations (old filter reproduces the CI failure; new filter renders `media-src 'self' ;` when empty and `media-src 'self' https://s3.amazonaws.com` when set). Lesson for any future CSP source added to the template: the envsubst filter must be extended in the same edit.

P23 (backup / restore / DR) code slice landed, and the drill earned its keep. backup.sh now backs up BOTH stateful databases (Acmp + keycloak, which ADR-0036 put on the same instance), WITHOUT the WITH COMPRESSION clause that SQL Server Express rejects outright, and copies the .bak files to S3 as a hard requirement rather than a best-effort leg. The pg_dump and mc-mirror legs are gone — Keycloak has no Postgres, and mirroring an S3 bucket onto a 4 GiB instance would be copying AWS's own durability into the thing you are protecting against. restore.sh's Keycloak leg piped a gzipped pg_dump into psql inside a container ADR-0036 DELETED, written to fail non-fatally: it could only ever have reported a successful restore of a system nobody can log into. It now restores keycloak as a SQL database, resolves every .bak before touching any of them, and stops only the dependents actually running (SINGLE_USER alone is a race — the api reconnects and takes the single-user slot). THREE FAILED DRILL RUNS, each worth the time: (1) MSYS rewrote the in-container /opt/mssql-tools18 path to C:/Program Files/Git/opt/... — a Windows harness artifact, not a script bug; (2) the same again because the gate suppressed its own output, so the gate was changed to print the failure — a gate that cannot say why it failed is not a gate; (3) the real one, DEF-017: SQL Server writes the .bak ITSELF as uid 10001 while Docker had created the bind mount root-owned 0755, so BACKUP died with 'Operating system error 5(Access is denied.)'. That would have failed identically on the EC2 host, at 02:00, in a cron log, while the deployment looked backed up. backup.sh now preflights the mount and names the fix. Also added: 02-s3.sh expires CURRENT versions on the backups bucket ONLY (recordings never expire) — uncompressed nightly backups for two databases would otherwise grow without bound on an account whose budget actions cut access at 100% and stop instances at 120%. Evidence: U4 gate PASSES unattended — 3 -> 0 -> 3 on keycloak, Express, no COMPRESSION, Keycloak healthy after its database was restored (16 passed / 1 failed overall). NOT DONE and not claimed: the S3 upload leg and the Acmp-database half of AC-080 need a live environment; AC-080 stays Pending. UNRESOLVED and not mine: U3's Arabic CONTAINS() gate failed in all four of today's runs after passing in the previous session — nothing in this slice touches full-text search, and it is a populate-crawl timeout on a machine that has been running Docker all session, but it has NOT been diagnosed and should not be assumed flaky.

P23: both databases backed up without COMPRESSION (Express), S3 off-instance copy as a hard requirement, restore.sh rewritten for SQL-Server Keycloak, DEF-017 backup-mount preflight, backups-bucket lifecycle expiry, cloud DR runbook. AC-080's local half proved by the new U4 drill gate; the AC stays Pending until a live environment covers the S3 leg and the Acmp database.

P20 landing zone EXECUTED against the live account 565393059398 (us-east-1) by the operator on 2026-08-03 — the first time these scripts touched AWS. Created: IAM admin user acmp-admin (+access key), SNS topic acmp-budget-alerts with an email subscription AWAITING CONFIRMATION, security groups acmp-uat-web (sg-0b6d2e67df7af657b) and acmp-prod-web (sg-0524ce0a87443b8fd) with 443 only — no 22, no 80; four S3 buckets (acmp-{uat,prod}-{recordings,backups}) all public-access-blocked + SSE-S3 + versioned; two per-env app IAM users and two instance roles/profiles; four ECR repos. TWO SLICE CHANGES CONFIRMED LIVE: the backups buckets report 'current-expire 30d' while the recordings buckets do not (P23), and the app/instance policies carry s3:AbortMultipartUpload (P22). WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN, and it is the important part: 00-account.sh FAILED at budget creation — 'Unable to load paramfile file:///tmp/tmp.VpLH5zPaEV', because mktemp returns a POSIX path a native Windows aws.exe cannot open. Under set -e that aborted the script, so the monthly budget, the budget-action execution role AND the deny-new-spend policy were all skipped, while 01..05 continued and provisioned everything else. The account therefore currently holds real resources with NO spend guardrail — precisely the RISK-022 failure. Fixed in 824f225 by passing all four JSON documents inline instead of through temp files (no platform seam left); the operator must RE-RUN 00-account.sh, which is idempotent and will leave the existing user and topic alone. STILL OUTSTANDING: the two budget ACTIONS are console-only and unset (AC-085 stays Pending and is nowhere near Met); the SNS subscription is unconfirmed so no alert can fire yet; the operator is STILL RUNNING AS ROOT — acmp-admin exists but MFA is not attached and the root access keys are not removed; 05-route53.sh was correctly not run, as it needs a public IP that will not exist until P25.

P20 account hygiene + spend controls COMPLETED live on 2026-08-03, and the guardrail is now armed rather than merely documented. Verified by query, not assertion: root MFA enabled (AccountMFAEnabled=1); root has NO access keys (AccountAccessKeysPresent=0 — the 'delete root keys' step was a no-op, because `aws login` issues a session rather than long-lived keys); acmp-admin carries a U2F device and a working key; SNS subscription CONFIRMED (a real ARN, no longer PendingConfirmation). The three keys emitted by the first P20 run were lost when the temp log was deleted before they were copied — all three were Active with unrecoverable secrets, so they were deleted and re-minted (acmp-admin by hand; the two app users by re-running 03-iam.sh, which mints only when a user has none), with the new secrets written to git-ignored deploy/secrets/ instead of a session temp file. Re-running the FIXED 00-account.sh then created what the first run could not: budget acmp-monthly (USD 60/mo MONTHLY COST) with 50/80/100% ACTUAL notifications, the acmp-budget-action execution role, and the acmp-budget-deny-new-spend policy. FINDING 1 — the script was wrong about its own limits: it claimed the CLI could not create the budget actions because that 'needs the role ARN', which is precisely the ARN it had just created, so the human console step was never necessary. The 100%-ACTUAL APPLY_IAM_POLICY action is now created BY the script, idempotently, and is live in STANDBY (action 1ed50a50-7de3-4c49-bd1b-233b77376b80); a guardrail that depends on someone remembering to click is one you find missing during the incident it existed for. Re-running 00 was verified a clean no-op with the action count still 1. FINDING 2 → OQ-064: the EC2 half of the brake cannot be built as specified. `aws budgets create-budget-action --generate-cli-skeleton` shows SsmActionDefinition as {ActionSubType, Region, InstanceIds} — explicit instance IDs, no tag filter anywhere in the API — so 'STOP_EC2_INSTANCES filtered by tag Project=ACMP' was never possible, cannot exist before P25 launches instances, and once created must be re-pointed whenever an instance is replaced. AC-085 is therefore unsatisfiable as written (it also says 120% where the script targets 100% FORECAST) and needs amending once OQ-064 is decided; the misleading line in the script is replaced with the API fact. STILL OPEN: CLI work is still done as root (acmp-admin now has MFA and a key, but the default profile remains the root session); AWS Cost Anomaly Detection is not enabled; AC-085 stays Pending.

P24 part 1 (image publish) landed on feat/p24-cd-pipeline. Two pieces: deploy/aws/06-github-oidc.sh registers GitHub's OIDC provider and a push-only ECR role, and ci.yml gains a `publish` job. The identity choice is the substance — the obvious route is an IAM user with an access key in GitHub secrets, and that is deliberately refused: such a key never expires, every workflow in the repo can read it, and it outlives the machine it was pasted from; this project lost three keys to a temp file earlier the same day. The trust policy is scoped to one repository and to refs/heads/main, refs/tags/* and environment:*, so a fork pull request mints a token whose `sub` matches nothing and cannot push to the registry the servers pull from. Permissions are push+read on acmp/* only — no DeleteRepository, no BatchDeleteImage, no lifecycle writes, because CI publishes images but must not be able to remove the one production is running. The publish job sits INSIDE ci.yml rather than in its own workflow because `needs` is the only gate that makes publishing an untested commit structurally impossible; a separate workflow would trigger on workflow_run and re-derive the head SHA, which is more machinery for a weaker guarantee. id-token: write is per-job so the test jobs cannot mint an AWS token. api/worker/sqlserver-fts build once (environment-agnostic, promoted by digest); web builds twice as <sha>-uat and <sha>-prod because ADR-0037 bakes VITE_OIDC_AUTHORITY in, and the two are never interchangeable. Both authorities are REQUIRED repository variables rather than defaulted — a wrong or empty authority ships a bundle that cannot log in and fails in the browser with nothing in the API logs, the same silent-failure shape as the P22 CSP media-src bug. Digests are recorded to a 90-day artifact because promotion deploys by digest, so what UAT tested and what production runs are the same bytes rather than the same label. The job is guarded by vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != '' so that merging it before the role exists leaves main green instead of red, and setting the variable switches it on with no follow-up commit. NOT DONE, NOT CLAIMED: 06-github-oidc.sh has NEVER BEEN RUN — the AWS session expired mid-slice, so the provider, role and policy do not exist and the publish job has never executed; nothing here is verified beyond YAML/shell parse. DRIFT RECORDED: SL-024 says the digest artefact is 'consumed by promote.sh', but promote.sh is the P18b on-prem warm-standby VM failover script (restore a backup, bring the stack up, stop before DNS cutover) whose premise — a standby VM — does not exist in the cloud topology. Image promotion needs its own script; this is the same class of stale assumption as P23's restore.sh pointing at a container ADR-0036 deleted.

P24 part 1 VERIFIED LIVE. PR #166 squash-merged as 9739632; the publish job ran for the first time and succeeded, and the five images exist in ECR (api 104 MB, worker 100 MB, sqlserver-fts 1.41 GB, web -uat and -prod 22.9 MB each). The digest artifact matches `aws ecr describe-images` on all five, so promotion-by-digest has real bytes to point at. The substantive check was NOT the green tick. The claim that mattered is ADR-0037's premise that the two web images are not interchangeable, and the tempting proof — the two digests differ — is unsound: Docker builds are not reproducible by default, so differing digests are equally consistent with the build-arg being silently ignored. ECR's compressed sizes actively misled in the other direction, reporting the PROD image 5 bytes LARGER although its authority URL is 4 characters SHORTER. The sound test was to open the bundle: the top layer of each web image was pulled via get-download-url-for-layer and grepped. The UAT image contains only https://uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev/kc/realms/acmp, the PROD image only https://acmp.anas7ammo.dev/kc/realms/acmp, neither contains the other's, and the UNCOMPRESSED dist differs by exactly 4 bytes — precisely len('uat.'). Per-environment baking is therefore evidenced, not inferred. Two pre-merge suspicions were checked rather than assumed and both were already correct: ecr:DescribeImages IS in the role policy, so the Record-digests step did not 403 after five successful pushes; and the LIVE trust policy really is narrowed to the single subject repo:A-H-911/acmp:ref:refs/heads/main, because 06-github-oidc.sh is written idempotently (it branches on get-role and calls update-assume-role-policy when the role exists) and was re-run after db7f47c — a create-only script would have left that narrowing on paper. Coupling to protect: the trust matches :ref:refs/heads/main, so if anyone ever adds an `environment:` key to the publish job, GitHub mints sub=repo:...:environment:NAME, which matches nothing and fails at assume-role rather than anywhere that reads like the cause. NOT DONE, NOT CLAIMED: no image has been RUN anywhere. Pull-and-boot on a real instance is entirely unproven and belongs to P25; publishing bytes is not the same as those bytes starting. NEW FINDING (cost): there is no ECR lifecycle policy, and the CI role deliberately cannot create one (ecr:PutLifecyclePolicy is excluded on purpose, correctly). Every push to main therefore adds an immutable SHA tag that nothing ever reaps. Shared layers keep the marginal cost per merge small, but the growth is unbounded against a $60/mo budget and needs an operator-run lifecycle policy. NEW FINDING (governance): SL-024 has NO acceptance criterion. AC-075..AC-085 bind to SL-020/021/022/023/025/026/027; the CD slice alone has none, so its exit is unmeasurable and this verification had no criterion to be recorded against. Surfaced to the operator rather than self-issued, because adding an AC moves the acceptance denominator. TOOLING: GNU tar treats a C:/ path as a remote host spec (host:path, rmt) and tried to network-connect to a host named 'C'; --force-local or a POSIX path is required. That failure was masked by a 2>/dev/null on the verification step and produced an EMPTY grep result, which was one careless sentence away from being reported as 'the authority is not baked in' — a fabricated defect. Suppressing stderr on a check converts a broken check into data-shaped output.

PR #166 squash-merged. P24 part 1: GitHub OIDC role + gated ECR publish. First publish run green; 5 images live in ECR with digests recorded; per-env web baking verified by bundle extraction (uat/prod authorities correct, 4-byte uncompressed delta). Part 2 (promotion + getting compose/scripts/.env onto the box) still outstanding, needs P25's instance.

CORRECTION to PE-142, plus two fixes. (1) PE-142's cost finding — 'there is no ECR lifecycle policy' — was WRONG, and was asserted without reading 04-ecr.sh. The script has applied one since P20 (`put-lifecycle-policy`, keep last 10, re-applied idempotently on every run) and `aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy` confirms it live on all four repositories. Retracted. Checking it did surface the REAL defect underneath, which is sharper than the false one: the rule counts IMAGES (`imageCountMoreThan`), and `web` is the only repository receiving TWO images per merge (<sha>-uat and <sha>-prod, because ADR-0037 bakes the authority in). A flat keep-10 therefore gave web FIVE commits of rollback depth against ten for api/worker/sqlserver-fts. That asymmetry fails precisely where it matters, because promotion deploys BY DIGEST: rolling back roughly six merges would find api and worker present and the matching web images already expired — a partial rollback missing the one image that carries the environment identity. 04-ecr.sh now expresses retention in COMMITS (KEEP_COMMITS=10) and scales the image count per repository, and the corrected 20-image policy was applied live to acmp/web. (2) U3's Arabic CONTAINS() gate, which failed all four runs on 2026-08-03 and was recorded as undiagnosed, is DIAGNOSED and FIXED — and it was never flaky. The populate-crawl poll called FULLTEXTCATALOGPROPERTY('ftc','PopulateStatus') WITHOUT a `USE ftsspike` prefix, and sq() connects with no -d, so it executed in master. Full-text catalogs are scoped to the current database (CREATE FULLTEXT CATALOG: 'unique among all catalog names in the current database'; both Microsoft examples for the function prefix USE <database>), so in master the catalog does not exist, the function returned NULL, and `${pst:-1}` masked NULL as 'still populating'. The loop therefore never broke: the 'wait for the crawl' was a blind 45-second sleep that observed nothing, after which CONTAINS simply RACED the populate. That is exactly why it passed on an idle machine and failed on a loaded one — the gate never had a readiness signal at all. Every OTHER statement in the block carries an explicit USE; this one line was the sole omission. Secondary defect found in the same place: PopulateStatus is deprecated, and Microsoft warns that looping on the CATALOG-level property 'takes CPU cycles away from the database and full-text search processes, and causes timeouts', directing callers to the table-level property. The poll now asks OBJECTPROPERTYEX(OBJECT_ID('dbo.t'),'TableFulltextPopulateStatus') in the right database, treats a NULL/non-numeric read as LOUD ('!') rather than indistinguishable from 'busy', and reports a crawl that never reaches idle instead of silently handing CONTAINS a race. NOT CLAIMED: the fix is reasoned + syntax-checked (bash -n) but has NOT been re-run — Docker Desktop is not running in this session, and re-running the spike is the operator's call. The diagnosis stands on the code and the vendor documentation; the green re-run does not yet exist. (3) AC-086 created to close the governance gap PE-142 raised: SL-024 was the only PH-5 slice with no acceptance criterion, so its exit was unmeasurable. Recorded Met on the live evidence as AV-087.

U3 poll hardened again after review caught a REGRESSION in the first fix — recorded because the near-miss is the useful part. PE-144's replacement gated on OBJECTPROPERTYEX(...,'TableFulltextPopulateStatus') = 0. That is wrong in a way that reads correct: status 0 means 'no population in progress', which is ALSO true BEFORE the crawl has started, and CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... WITH CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO queues the crawl asynchronously — the DDL returns before the FTS host picks up the work. The loop could therefore read 0 on its FIRST iteration, break in under a second, and hand CONTAINS the identical race it was written to remove. On a fast or idle machine that is strictly WORSE than the 45-second blind sleep it replaced, because the old code at least burned real time the crawl could use. Same defect class as the original bug: a readiness signal that is not evidence of readiness. The gate now reads BOTH properties as 'status:itemcount' and breaks only on idle AND at least one row indexed — TableFulltextItemCount is documented as 'the number of rows that were successfully full-text indexed', so it asserts the row is actually searchable rather than that the server is merely quiet. '0:0' is now explicitly the not-started state and is NOT success; a NULL/empty read (wrong database or missing object) stays LOUD. Verified by exercising the state machine over 0:0, 0:1, 1:0, empty, NULL and 9:3 — only 0:<non-zero> breaks. STILL NOT RE-RUN: Docker Desktop is not running in this session, so U3 remains DIAGNOSED and HARDENED, not proven. The single assertion the whole gate now rests on — that TableFulltextItemCount reaches >=1 on this box once the crawl lands — is exactly the one that cannot be obtained from the code, and it needs a live run in the isolated `acmpspike` project. Do not let 'diagnosed' become 'fixed' in a later summary without a green run.

U3 CLOSED — root-caused, fixed, and re-run GREEN (17 passed / 0 failed). The Arabic CONTAINS() gate was never flaky; it was three stacked defects, and finding each one required fixing the instrumentation that was hiding the next. (1) The populate poll queried FULLTEXTCATALOGPROPERTY without `USE ftsspike`, and sq() connects with no -d, so it ran in master where the catalog does not exist; NULL came back, `${pst:-1}` masked it as 'still populating', and the wait degenerated into a blind 45-second sleep that observed nothing before CONTAINS raced the crawl. (2) The first replacement gated on TableFulltextPopulateStatus = 0 — wrong in a way that reads correct, because 0 also means 'the crawl has not started', and CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO queues it asynchronously, so the loop could break on iteration one and reproduce the race FASTER than the original bug. Caught in review before it shipped. (3) The second replacement used CONCAT over OBJECTPROPERTYEX, which returns sql_variant, raising 'Msg 257: implicit conversion from sql_variant to varchar'. sqlcmd prints errors on STDOUT, so sq()'s 2>/dev/null never filtered it and the error string arrived as the value, falling through the catch-all case to print '.' — the poll reported healthy progress for 80 seconds while executing nothing. Same family three times over: an error wearing the costume of data. The catch-all now treats ONLY a literal <digits>:<digits> as populating and everything else as LOUD. With the instrumentation finally honest, the REAL defect became visible and is recorded as DEF-018: SQL Server EXPRESS forces AUTO_CLOSE ON for user databases (not inherited from model — verified live, model=0 while Acmp, keycloak and the scratch db were all 1), and an auto-closing database tears down the asynchronous full-text population. Every poll was connecting, restarting the database, and killing the crawl it was polling for. AUTO_CLOSE OFF took the same row through 1:0 → 1:1 → 4:1 → 0:1 with CONTAINS = 1 in about 15 seconds. This is an EDITION-CHANGE defect that arrives with PH-5 — the on-prem Developer edition never did it — and it would have shipped: global search (AC-060/AC-061) would have returned nothing in the cloud with no error anywhere, since the index exists, IsFullTextInstalled reports 1 and the word-breaker is present. Fixed in deploy/scripts/sqlserver-init.sh for BOTH the app and Keycloak databases behind an is_auto_close_on guard (no exclusive access needed, so no ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE), and the spike sets it on its scratch database so U3 exercises the shipped configuration. Also re-confirmed live in the same run: AC-077 (Keycloak 26 production mode on mssql, 87 tables, realm survived restart) and the U4 backup/restore drill 3→0→3 on Express with Keycloak healthy afterwards.

OQ-064 resolved: the EC2 budget brake keeps the native SSM action, and P25's launch script owns the InstanceIds. Re-verified from the LIVE API rather than from notes — `aws budgets create-budget-action --generate-cli-skeleton` confirms SsmActionDefinition is {ActionSubType, Region, InstanceIds}, with no tag filter anywhere, so the premise stands and 'STOP_EC2_INSTANCES filtered by tag Project=ACMP' was never expressible. Chosen: option (a) plus automation. Rejected (b), an EventBridge/Lambda that really can act on tags, as disproportionate — a function, an execution role, an SNS subscription and code to maintain, for a fleet of exactly two instances only ever created by a sanctioned script; it stays the answer if instances ever start being created outside that path, which is the single case (a) does not cover. Rejected (c), dropping it, because the IAM deny action does not reduce EXISTING spend: attaching a deny policy blocks new API calls but a running t3.medium keeps billing, so (c) would leave the brake with no lever that actually lowers the bill. The reason for automating the re-point rather than documenting it is the failure mode — a stale InstanceId does not error, it silently protects nothing, the same shape as DEF-017's unwritable backup mount and DEF-018's AUTO_CLOSE. The launch script already knows the ID it just created, so ownership costs one create-or-update call and deletes a manual step nobody would remember. TWO FINDINGS surfaced while resolving this, recorded rather than folded in. (i) The IAM deny action attaches to the IAM USER acmp-admin, and the account ROOT user cannot be restricted by IAM policies at all — only an Organizations SCP could, and this is a standalone account. The operator is still doing CLI work as root, so while that remains true the brake reads armed and constrains nobody. That is a live gap, not a theoretical one, and it raises the priority of the P20 'switch off root' item from hygiene to guardrail-critical. (ii) The account carries a second, pre-existing budget 'My Monthly Cost Budget' at $10 which is not ours and will alert well before acmp-monthly's $60 — expect the noise and do not read its alerts as the ACMP brake firing. AC-085 is amended in the same pass: it named 120% while the script targets 100%, and 'dry-run verified' is not achievable as written because budget actions have NO dry run — `execute-budget-action` genuinely fires. The verifiable substitutes are describe-budget-actions-for-budget for definition/threshold/status and `aws iam simulate-principal-policy`, which is a real dry run, for proving the deny policy actually denies.

AC-083 / AC-080 / AC-085 advanced from Pending to Partial WITHOUT provisioning anything, correcting an earlier framing of mine that was too coarse. I had said all four remaining PH-5 ACs 'need a live environment'; on inspection only AC-085's leg 4 genuinely requires an EC2 instance. The S3-facing halves of AC-078 and AC-083 need a bucket and an IAM identity, both of which have existed since P20, not a server. AC-083's S3 isolation was settled with `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` rather than by handling the app access keys and writing probe objects into a production bucket: the simulator runs the same evaluation engine IAM uses at request time, so it is authoritative, and it touches no credential and creates no object. Both directions were checked, not just the one the AC names — acmp-uat-app is allowed Put/Get/Delete on acmp-uat-recordings and implicitDeny on acmp-prod-recordings, and acmp-prod-app is symmetric, which covers the more damaging prod-writes-to-UAT direction the AC omits. The result is conclusive for same-account access because get-bucket-policy returns NoSuchBucketPolicy on both buckets, so the identity policy is the only grant path and no resource-based policy can widen it. Recorded as a hardening note rather than a failure: the denial is IMPLICIT, i.e. it rests on least privilege continuing to hold, and any future broad s3:* grant on either app user would flip it to allowed silently; an explicit Deny on the opposite environment's bucket ARNs would make the isolation self-defending instead of merely unpermitted. The Webex leg is satisfied only at template level (WEBEX_ENABLED=false in .env.cloud.example with every space/token variable commented, plus AC-071 already Met so a disabled adapter is unregistered entirely and enqueues nothing); a template is not a deployed configuration, so confirming the UAT box's real .env remains outstanding. AC-085 moved to Partial on three of its five amended legs, including the only genuine dry run available anywhere in this area — simulate-principal-policy showing the deny policy flipping RunInstances, AllocateAddress and CreateDBInstance to explicitDeny while leaving StopInstances ALLOWED, which matters because a brake that blocked its own remedy could not reduce spend. AC-080 moved to Partial on the keycloak restore leg proven live in the same session's spike run. Remaining and honestly scoped: AC-078 needs the application's file-store path exercised against a real bucket (no instance required, only credentials and a bucket that exist); AC-080 needs the same drill against the Acmp database plus the S3 copy leg (no instance required); AC-083 needs the deployed UAT .env; AC-085 leg 4 needs P25's instances and leg 1 needs an observed alert.

AC-078 harness built and AC-078 moved to Partial; the live execution is handed to the operator rather than faked. tests/Acmp.Integration.Tests/MinioFileStoreLiveS3Tests.cs drives the whole AC in one test — upload, StatObject, presign, a REAL HTTP GET of the presigned URL compared byte-for-byte against the payload, delete, and a confirmation that the object is gone — with a finally-block cleanup so a mid-way assertion failure cannot litter a real bucket. The playback leg is an actual HTTP fetch on purpose: a presigned URL that merely parses proves nothing, and only a 200 carrying the bytes demonstrates that a browser <video> element would play it. It also asserts against the live service that the presigned origin is https://s3.amazonaws.com — the P22 CSP finding, which MinioFileStoreCloudTests could only pin offline. The Minio client is constructed exactly as SharedKernelExtensions constructs it in production so the test exercises shipped wiring rather than a bespoke arrangement built to go green. Opt-in by design: a ten-line LiveS3FactAttribute sets Skip when the credentials are absent, chosen over an early-return guard because a guard reports a PASS for a test that never ran — the precise failure shape this session has now hit four times. Verified 2 skipped / 0 passed with no environment set, and rejected taking a dependency on Xunit.SkippableFact for one file. DELIBERATELY NOT RUN AS ROOT. A root-credentialed pass would be worthless and actively misleading: AC-078's substance is that the app's LEAST-PRIVILEGE IAM policy grants exactly what the adapter calls at runtime, and root can do anything, so a green run would prove nothing while looking like evidence — the same class of unearned green as 'differing digests prove per-environment baking'. Reading the app key from deploy/secrets/ was refused by the sandbox classifier, which is the correct outcome for a credentials file; the run is the operator's, as acmp-uat-app. Second clause of AC-078 is Met outright: docker-compose.cloud.yml contains no minio service, only S3 client configuration keys and comments recording the deletion. SIDE FIX: the secrets gate failed on this file because gitleaks' generic-api-key rule matched `const string SecretVar = "..."` — the value being an environment variable NAME, not a credential. Allowlisted narrowly to the ACMP_LIVE_S3_ prefix family, which cannot conceal a real key (an AWS secret is 40 characters of base64 and would never match that shape), and verified by running gitleaks v8.21.2 locally with the exact CI config and flags: 221 commits scanned, no leaks found.

C3 pre-flight found DEF-019 before a single cent was spent — the option was chosen precisely because unrun code in this repo keeps hiding silent defects, and it paid off on inspection rather than needing the boot. Preparing the first-ever local run of the cloud stack meant deciding which images to run, and the strongest choice was the ACTUAL artefacts P24 published rather than locally built ones. That immediately exposed the mismatch: deploy/docker-compose.cloud.yml drives all four ACMP images from one ${ACMP_IMAGE_TAG}, but only api, worker and sqlserver-fts are environment-agnostic and published as a plain <sha>. `web` is published as <sha>-uat and <sha>-prod because ADR-0037 bakes the OIDC authority into the bundle, so there is no plain web:<sha> to pull. Proven against the live registry rather than argued: list-images on acmp/web returns exactly the two suffixed tags, describe-images for the plain <sha> answers ImageNotFoundException, and docker manifest inspect resolves api/worker/sqlserver-fts plus web:<sha>-uat while failing on web:<sha> — the pre-fix deploy failure reproduced exactly. A commit-pinned deploy would have pulled three images and died on the fourth, on the instance, mid-deploy, which is the worst place to learn it. The defect is structural, not a typo: one shared tag variable cannot express a topology where one image is per-environment BY DESIGN, so this could never have worked. It is a seam failure between slices written correctly in isolation — P21 wrote the line before P24 chose per-environment web images — exactly like SL-024's 'consumed by promote.sh' and P23's restore.sh targeting a container ADR-0036 had deleted. The file even contradicted itself: the comment directly beneath the offending line already described the -uat/-prod scheme. ROOT CAUSE of why it survived: the cloud topology had NO CI validation whatsoever. The compose job validates docker-compose.yml — the ON-PREM file — and never mentioned docker-compose.cloud.yml, so the entire PH-5 topology was unchecked, not even for syntax. Fixed and guarded: web reads ${ACMP_WEB_TAG:-${ACMP_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}} so the local build path still works while cloud requires an explicit per-environment tag; .env.cloud.example documents it with the reason and the warning never to point production at a -uat image; ci.yml now config-validates the cloud compose and runs scripts/check-cloud-images.mjs, which pins BOTH halves of the P24-publishes/P21-consumes contract so they cannot drift apart silently again. The guard was itself tested by re-introducing the bug (exit 1, message names the required variable and why) and restoring it (exit 0) — a check nobody has watched fail is not a check. Post-fix, all four tags resolve in the registry and the cloud compose validates.

C3 COMPLETE — the cloud stack has now been booted end to end for the first time, from the ACTUAL images P24 published, and it works. Every service reached its target state: sqlserver healthy, sqlserver-init exited 0, db-migrate exited 0 (the EF migrations ran against a fresh cloud database), keycloak healthy, keycloak-config exited 0 (the acmp realm imported), api healthy, worker up, web healthy, seq healthy after the fix below. Crucially the checks were FUNCTIONAL, not self-reported: web served HTTP 200 with a real bundle over the published port, api answered /healthz 200, and Keycloak's in-network discovery document resolved and reported issuer http://localhost:18080/kc/realms/acmp — the EXTERNAL path, confirming the ADR-0037 same-origin /kc arrangement is wired correctly, which was the single most likely thing to be subtly wrong. Running the real ECR artefacts rather than local builds also re-proved the DEF-019 fix in situ: all four images pulled by their published tags, web by <sha>-uat. FOUND AND FIXED DEF-020. Seq crash-looped on the SEQ_FIRSTRUN_ADMINPASSWORDHASH placeholder that .env.cloud.example ships — Seq needs a Base-64 salted hash and aborts with FormatException on CHANGE_ME. The crash is not the severity; the invisibility is. api declares depends_on seq with condition service_started, and service_started is satisfied by a container that started and then died, so a restart-looping Seq blocks nothing: api, web and keycloak all reported HEALTHY while observability was completely dead. A deployment that looks green with no log aggregation is the state you cannot diagnose your way out of, and it is the same silent-degradation family as DEF-018 and DEF-017. It exists only in the cloud path because on-prem leaves the variable commented out and runs Seq unauthenticated. Fixed in gen-secrets.sh, which already runs before every compose up, so it fails loudly at secret-generation time instead of after deploy; tested for all three cases (CHANGE_ME fails with the remediation command, a real hash passes, unset passes for on-prem) and then proven by generating a real hash and recreating the container, which came up healthy. TWO HARNESS ARTEFACTS, correctly NOT recorded as product defects after checking rather than assuming: my boot env file left the cron value unquoted so sourcing it executed the crontab fields — the shipped template quotes it correctly, verified; and sqlserver flipped to unhealthy late in the run with 'Login failed for user sa' because I restored deploy/secrets under a still-running stack, so the healthcheck read the dev password while the server held the boot password. Both were diagnosed from evidence, not guessed. Safety held throughout: isolated acmpboot project with its own volumes, only free high ports, deploy/secrets backed up and restored by an EXIT trap — which fired correctly on the first failed attempt — and the operator's running dev stack was untouched.

C4 memory check run against the booted cloud stack, and the DEF-020 guard hardened after it failed its own purpose. Two results. FIRST, the instance-size question that option C existed to answer: t3.medium looks viable. Compose v2 really does enforce deploy.resources.limits outside swarm — verified from HostConfig.Memory rather than assumed, because a silently-ignored limit would make the entire 3584 MiB budget fictional. At idle sqlserver sits at 68% of its 2 GiB, api 15%, worker 22%, web 31%; all comfortable. Keycloak is the outlier and the one to watch: 442.6 MiB of a 448 MiB cap, 98.8%, at idle, stable across a 60-second settle so not a startup transient. A burst of 150 concurrent token requests pushed it DOWN to 93% rather than over — the JVM collected under pressure — and nothing recorded OOMKilled. Recorded as AC-084 Partial, explicitly NOT Met: the AC demands an e2e run on t3.medium and this was neither, since the web image has the UAT authority baked in (ADR-0037) so Playwright's login flows cannot complete locally, and a workstation is not a 4 GiB box with swap. The actionable output is narrow and useful: if AC-084 fails on the real instance, Keycloak's 448 MiB is the first allocation to raise and the 512 MiB of host headroom is where it comes from. SECOND, and more instructive: the DEF-020 guard I wrote this session FAILED TO CATCH THE EXACT FAILURE IT WAS WRITTEN FOR. This boot used the placeholder 'unused', gen-secrets accepted it, and Seq crash-looped again — 11 restarts — which only came to light because RestartCount was visible in an unrelated OOM check. The regex validated the base64 ALPHABET but not the LENGTH, and 'unused' is six characters that all happen to be legal base64. Base-64 is always a multiple of four characters, so length is the half that actually discriminates a real hash from a word spelled in the base64 alphabet. Hardened and re-tested across five cases including the one that slipped: CHANGE_ME fails, 'unused' fails, 'abc' fails, a real 108-character hash passes, unset passes for the on-prem path. The lesson is worth more than the fix: a guard tested only against the inputs its author imagined is not yet a guard, and this one was caught by accident rather than by design — the same way DEF-018 surfaced.

P24 part 2 scripting + the boot gate landed, and one scope correction that matters. THREE SCRIPTS. (1) deploy/scripts/promote-image.sh finally closes the SL-024 drift: the slice said the CI digest artefact was 'consumed by promote.sh', which it cannot be, because promote.sh is the P18b on-prem warm-standby VM failover script that restores a backup, runs up.sh --prod and stops before DNS cutover — confirmed by reading it — and its premise, a standby VM, does not exist in the cloud topology. The new script verifies every image for a commit EXISTS in ECR before touching anything, then pins ACMP_IMAGE_TAG and ACMP_WEB_TAG in the target env file. It encodes the subtlety that makes promotion non-obvious here: api, worker and sqlserver-fts are environment-agnostic so the same bytes UAT tested are what production runs, and their digests are printed for audit, but `web` CANNOT be promoted that way and it is not a defect that it cannot — ADR-0037 bakes the authority in, so UAT and prod web are different artefacts from the same commit by design, and promotion means selecting the <sha>-prod build, never re-pointing the -uat one. Getting that wrong ships a production bundle authenticating against UAT, which fails in the browser with nothing in the API logs. Tested: refuses an unpublished commit AND leaves the env file untouched (verified), and the happy path pins both variables with the correct -prod suffix. (2) deploy/aws/07-launch.sh implements the OQ-064 resolution literally — it launches the instance and arms the EC2 spend brake IN THE SAME RUN, collecting instance ids across BOTH environments so launching prod cannot silently drop uat from the action, and creating-or-updating so a replacement re-points automatically. That automation is the whole point: a stale InstanceId does not error, it silently protects nothing, the same failure shape as DEF-017 and DEF-018. It resolves the AMI through the SSM public parameter rather than pinning an id that would rot, requires IMDSv2, encrypts the root volume, and is idempotent on the Name tag so it can never launch a second instance for an environment. Its header records what it does NOT protect against: the IAM deny binds the acmp-admin user and root cannot be constrained by IAM policy at all. (3) deploy/scripts/cloud-stack-boot.sh promotes this session's throwaway harness into the repo — the argument being empirical rather than tidy-minded: DEF-018 was found by re-running a spike that EXISTED, while DEF-019 and DEF-020 were found by a script living in a temp folder that would have evaporated. It boots the full cloud topology from the published images and asserts functionally rather than by self-reported health: five services healthy, migrations/db-init/realm-import all exit 0, web serves HTTP 200 on the published port, api /healthz 200, the Keycloak issuer is the EXTERNAL url (an in-container issuer would break SPA token validation), and nothing was OOM-killed inside the 3584 MiB budget. It generates a REAL Seq hash rather than a placeholder so it exercises the configuration we ship. Run green: 16 passed, 0 failed. SCOPE CORRECTION, recorded rather than quietly worked around: AC-079 cannot be advanced because deploy/scripts/seed-users.sh DOES NOT EXIST. AC-079 is not a test awaiting execution, it is unbuilt SL-026 slice work — writing the seeding script, its idempotency and the UPDATE_PASSWORD requirement. I had listed it as a free win reachable without an instance; that was wrong and is withdrawn.

SL-026 built and AC-079 advanced to Partial without an instance, plus two harness corrections. deploy/scripts/seed-users.sh now exists — it did not before, which was the scope correction recorded in PE-153: AC-079 was never a test awaiting execution, it was unbuilt slice work. The script creates the committee accounts and assigns realm roles, and it was designed around three properties that each earn their place. Idempotent, because a fresh box gets rebuilt several times before it settles and a run that aborts half-seeded is worse than one that never ran, since a partially seeded realm LOOKS done. Temporary-password-only, because without requiredActions=UPDATE_PASSWORD the operator's chosen string silently becomes a permanent shared credential — intolerable in a system where every vote is attributed by identity (ADR-0010), since attribution means nothing if several people can hold one login. Role-correct and VERIFIED rather than assumed from a 2xx, because a user seeded without a role logs in fine and then sees an empty application, which reads as a broken app rather than a seeding bug. It deliberately does not touch the application database: the app JIT-provisions its CommitteeMember row from the token's sub, and duplicating membership here would create two records that can disagree. Proven against the real Keycloak from cloud-stack-boot.sh, so no AWS spend was involved: two consecutive runs gave 4-created/0-present then 0-created/4-present with roles re-asserted on the second pass, and all four accounts read back with UPDATE_PASSWORD pending and enabled=true. Running it immediately found a defect that review had not: Keycloak's person-name validator rejects lastName '(seeded)' with error-person-name-invalid-character, so the script would have failed on its very first use on a real box. AC-078 MET live, and the run that proved it exposed DEF-021 — a silent-data-loss defect in the running product, not in deployment. F was completed first and made the rest possible: the acmp-admin access key turned out NOT to be on disk at all (both 00-account.sh logs record 'IAM user acmp-admin already exists', so the script never emitted one — it only prints a key when it CREATES the user, and aws-app-keys.log holds only the uat/prod S3 app keys), so a second key was minted straight into the git-ignored deploy/secrets/ and the profile configured by command substitution, with the secret never entering the transcript. A named profile plus AWS_PROFILE was used deliberately instead of `default`, because `aws login` OVERWRITES the default profile with root credentials and would have silently un-done the switch with no signal. Identity is now user/acmp-admin, and simulate-principal-policy confirms the budget deny now returns explicitDeny for RunInstances against the identity actually in use while leaving StopInstances allowed and all P25 actions permitted — for the first time the brake binds the operator rather than binding nobody. AC-078 then ran with the acmp-uat-app key and PASSED: upload, StatObject, presigned URL, a real HTTP GET returning the payload byte-for-byte, delete, gone. The critical legs were confirmed OUTSIDE the SDK — the playback bytes over raw HTTP, the deletion by an admin list-objects-v2 — which matters because of what the same run found. DEF-021: the belt-and-braces cross-environment isolation check failed, and the failure was not isolation. S3 enforces it correctly (the AWS CLI answers AccessDenied for the identical identity, bucket and action, and an admin listing shows nothing stored, so AC-083 stands), but MinioFileStore.UploadAsync returned NORMALLY for the refused write and ExistsAsync then reported TRUE for an object that does not exist. Instrumenting rather than theorising gave the exact shape: 'upload threw NOTHING, ExistsAsync returned True, Exists threw NOTHING'. The Minio client as configured swallows permission errors on both PutObject and StatObject, so a refused upload reaches the caller as stored — 201 to the API, success in the UI, no file. It also falsifies, in writing, the comment inside EnsureBucketAsync claiming 'PutObject immediately after is the real authority and its own failure surfaces to the caller'. A post-write existence guard was written, tested, and REVERTED because it inherits the same blindness — the second guard-that-does-not-guard this session, but caught before shipping this time, and a guard that cannot fail is worse than none because it manufactures confidence. DEF-021 is recorded OPEN, not fixed: the remedy is the AWSSDK.S3 fallback that P22 deferred as 'nothing observed requires it', it touches every file operation in the product, and it should not be rushed at the tail of a long session. A deliberately RED regression test is committed, opt-in so CI is unaffected, and it goes green only when the defect genuinely is.

DEF-021 FIXED by a one-line SDK bump, after two wrong turns worth recording. The defect was real and severe — on Minio 6.0.3 the file store reported success for uploads S3 refused, which in production means 201 from the API, success in the UI and no file. The first attempted fix, a post-write ExistsAsync guard, was written, tested and reverted because it inherits the same blindness: StatObject swallows the denial too, so the guard could never fail, and a guard that cannot fail is worse than none because it manufactures confidence. That was the second guard-that-does-not-guard this session, caught before shipping. The second wrong turn was the one recorded as the remedy: 'the AWSSDK.S3 fallback P22 deferred', a client rewrite touching every file operation in the product. Before starting it the cheapest rung was tried — the SDK was pinned at 6.0.3 and 6.0.5 existed — and the bump fixes the defect outright. The isolation regression test, red by design on 6.0.3, is green on 6.0.5 because UploadAsync now throws on the refused write, and the FULL integration suite passes 43 of 43, including the Testcontainers-MinIO on-prem path whose container start was confirmed in the Testcontainers log rather than inferred, after a suspicious sub-millisecond duration turned out to be a reporting artefact. Trying the upgrade first saved a rewrite of the entire storage layer at the tail of a long session. A CONSEQUENTIAL CHANGE came with it, and it is not optional. 6.0.5 also fixed the AWSS3Endpoints rewriting that P22 had documented as a permanent quirk: presigned URLs now use the CONFIGURED endpoint, https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, rather than the legacy global https://s3.amazonaws.com. Two tests failed on exactly that assertion, and the correct response was NOT to relax them — it was to update ACMP_MEDIA_ORIGIN, the compose default and the nginx CSP media-src commentary to match what the SDK now signs for. Leaving the old value would have blocked <video> playback in the browser with nothing in the API logs, which is precisely the silent shape the original P22 finding existed to warn about. AC-083 never moved: S3 enforced isolation correctly throughout, and the CLI's AccessDenied plus an admin list-objects-v2 showing nothing stored were the proof that the fault lay in our adapter rather than in the permissions.

AC-080 MET and the orphaned admin key removed. HOUSEKEEPING first: acmp-admin held two access keys, and the 2026-08-03 one was the credential nobody could use — its secret was never on disk (the 00-account.sh logs record 'IAM user acmp-admin already exists', so the script never emitted one). The two stated limits of the 2026-08-05 integrity audit are now CLOSED, and closing the second one changed what the finding was. LIMIT 1 — the trace check had been a 6-of-218 sample, which could not rule out a requirement reaching only one bucket. Rather than issue 218 trace_query calls, the complete edge export was swept directly: trace_edges.csv holds 1042 edges (379 derives_from, 336 tests, 232 implements, 85 verifies, 8 relates_to, 2 supersedes), and the requirement population was enumerated from the ID SPACE (FR-001..155, NFR-001..063) rather than from the edges themselves — deliberately, because deriving the population from the edge list would make an unreferenced requirement invisible and the check vacuous in exactly the way the audit was asked to guard against. Result: 218 of 218 requirements reach a decision-layer row AND a work item AND a test. Zero missing any bucket, zero isolated. The sample generalised; the gate was sound. LIMIT 2 was phrased as 'requirements reach ADRs, never the 30 DEC- rows', implying requirements were mis-wired. They are not, and the real finding is one layer higher: ALL THIRTY DEC- rows have ZERO trace edges in either direction — not one of the 1042 edges touches a DEC- id. The decision layer sits entirely outside the trace graph. The relationships those rows assert exist only as prose; DEC-030 states in its text that it 'Authorizes scope change SC-002 and ADRs 0034-0037', but nothing encodes that as an edge, so trace_query('DEC-030') returns nothing and neither 'what did this decision authorize?' nor 'which decision authorized this ADR?' can be answered mechanically. G-TRACE does not catch this because it evidently walks requirements only, which means thirty governance decisions pass every gate while being unreachable — structurally the same vacuity risk the audit was commissioned to look for, one level up. Recorded as OQ-065 with two options (type the roughly forty DEC->ADR / DEC->scope-change edges, which are recoverable from the existing prose since each decision already names its authorizations; or accept the decision layer as narrative-only and say so, so no future reader mistakes silence for absent authorization). Deliberately NOT actioned: adding forty edges is a substantive change to the record, and the audit that surfaced it was commissioned read-only.

Attempted to wire the decision-layer trace edges as OQ-065 option (a) requested; the attempt DISPROVED my own finding and the work was not done, deliberately. Two discoveries, in order. FIRST, there is no sanctioned write path to trace_edges in tamheed 2.6.0: the table is not exposed to entity_query, and entity_upsert rejects both 'trace-edge' and 'trace_edge' as unknown entity types. The 1042 existing edges must therefore have been produced by the original migration parser rather than by MCP writes, and AGENTS.md forbids hand-editing tamheed-package/ files, so option (a) is simply not executable through any legitimate route. SECOND, and more importantly, it should not be executed even if it were. Checking how the DEC->ADR relationship might be expressed revealed that 18 of the 30 decisions ALREADY carry it, as a typed promoted_to field naming the ADR each was promoted into. My audit finding — that the relationships 'exist only in prose' — was therefore WRONG for the large majority of them, and I have corrected OQ-065 rather than leaving the overstatement standing. The decision->architecture link is captured as structured data, in the right place; what is missing is only that promoted_to is never materialised into trace_edges, the table trace_query reads. That is a derivation gap in the tooling, not absent knowledge in the package, and it means the authorization chain IS queryable today via entity_query on the decision rows — just not via trace_query. Duplicating promoted_to into edge rows would have created two records of one fact that can drift apart, which is the same two-sources-of-truth anti-pattern seed-users.sh deliberately avoids by refusing to mirror Keycloak identity into the application database. The lesson is the one this session keeps re-teaching: the audit reported trace silence and inferred absence, when the data was simply held somewhere the query did not look. A gap in a VIEW is not a gap in the RECORD, and the two demand opposite responses — fix the view, or you corrupt the record by writing a second copy of what it already knows. Revised options recorded on OQ-065: derive trace_edges from promoted_to at export time, which is an upstream tamheed change rather than a package change; or record that promoted_to is authoritative and trace_query is not expected to reach it. A genuinely open third item remains: 12 decisions have promoted_to null, and DEC-030 authorizes SC-002 plus ADRs 0034-0037 by its own text — four targets a single-valued field structurally cannot hold.

OQ-065 RESOLVED, and the resolution is that there was no data gap at all — only a view limitation plus one honest modelling edge. Reading all 31 decision titles against their promoted_to values makes the convention self-evident: promoted_to is populated exactly when a decision was PROMOTED INTO an ADR, which happened 18 times, and is null when the decision landed as a different KIND of artifact. The nulls are not omissions, they are correct: DEC-009 'Single committee — exactly one committee, no multi-committee' and DEC-017 'Scale ceiling — <=20 total users' are hard CONSTRAINTS, DEC-014 'Availability target 99.9%' is an NFR, DEC-029 'Model the cross-cutting slices P16-P19 as their own phase PH-4' is a planning decision that produced phases and slices, and DEC-031 is a reading rule that produces no artifact at all. A decision that never became an ADR should have a null promoted_to; filling it in would be fabrication. So my earlier concern that 12 decisions were 'missing' their link was wrong for essentially all of them, and the audit's original claim that the relationships 'exist only in prose' was wrong for the 18 that were promoted. What remains true is narrow and worth stating plainly: trace_query cannot reach the decision layer because promoted_to is never materialised into trace_edges, the table trace_query reads. That is a DERIVATION gap in the tamheed export, not absent knowledge — the chain is fully queryable today via entity_query on the decision rows. Recorded as an upstream note rather than a blocker, since fixing it means changing the plugin, not this package, and no write path to trace_edges exists in 2.6.0 anyway. ONE GENUINE MODELLING EDGE, accepted rather than deferred: promoted_to models a 1:1 PROMOTION, and DEC-030 did not get promoted — it AUTHORIZED four separate artifacts (SC-002 plus ADRs 0034-0037). 'Authorizes' is a different relation from 'promoted into', the schema has neither a typed edge nor a multi-valued field for it, and the decision's own text names all four targets explicitly. Inventing a representation would require hand-editing tamheed-package/, which AGENTS.md forbids. The population is essentially one decision, the prose is explicit and searchable, and conflating authorization with promotion — by picking one of the four ADRs to stuff into promoted_to — would lose information while looking tidier. Left as prose, deliberately. Corroborating evidence found while generating the review surface: the execution view renders 'Acceptance criteria x audit verdicts (86 rows)' against 95 verdict rows, so the renderer already dedupes to latest-per-criterion, which independently confirms the rule DEC-031 documents. gate_run counts ROWS and the review surface counts CRITERIA; both are correct and they will always differ by the number of supersessions.

SL-025 Stage 0 built and Stage 1 written but NOT RUN. The slice was planned as a linear build and is not one: reading the provisioning path found three blockers that fail before anything reaches a browser, plus a fourth nobody had. THE ONE NOBODY HAD: the delivery mechanism for the entire cloud deployment has never worked. 08-bootstrap-box.sh reads the environment from an SSM SecureString at /acmp/<env>/env; describe-parameters shows /acmp/* is EMPTY, nothing in the repo created it, and the obvious `put-parameter --value "$(cat .env.cloud)"` cannot work either — the file is 5,483 bytes against a 4 KB Standard-tier limit, and with the account default tier at Intelligent-Tiering an oversized value is silently promoted to a BILLED Advanced parameter rather than erroring. Found by running wc -c on a config template, after two exhaustive sub-agent sweeps read the script line by line and missed it: the defect exists in neither artifact alone, only in the interaction between the script and a service limit neither one mentions. Fixed by new deploy/aws/09-put-env.sh, which strips full-line comments and blank lines only (5,483 -> 1,119 B, 27% of the free tier) and passes --tier Standard explicitly so an oversized payload fails loudly instead of quietly billing. Inline '#' is never stripped because a generated password can contain one; verified Str#ong#Pass1 survives. THE OTHER THREE, each evidenced against the live account rather than reasoned: (1) 07-launch.sh could never find its security group — 01-network.sh creates acmp-<env>-web, 07 looked up acmp-<env> and died blaming a script that HAD run; proven live, the old name resolves to None and the new one to sg-0b6d2e67df7af657b. (2) certbot could not renew on the box — 03-iam.sh scoped the Route 53 write to <host>/A while DNS-01 writes TXT at _acme-challenge.<host>, failing both condition clauses; simulate-principal-policy returned implicitDeny, and SL-025 requires an unattended renewal timer, i.e. exactly the denied path. The widened policy was validated with simulate-custom-policy WITHOUT applying it (these scripts are operator-run): TXT at _acme-challenge allowed, A at <host> still allowed, TXT at another host implicitDeny, A at the apex implicitDeny — wider where certbot needs it and nowhere else. (3) There was no 443 listener anywhere in the repo, while the cloud compose has been publishing 443:8443 with nothing behind it and .env.cloud.example has described https endpoints that could not answer. A REJECTED ASSUMPTION worth recording: I reasoned that AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore excludes ssm:GetParameter and was about to add a grant on that premise. Simulation said ALLOWED. The grant added instead scopes it to /acmp/<env>/* so uat cannot read prod's config. kms:Decrypt remains UNRESOLVED and is labelled so: simulation reports implicitDeny but evaluates identity policies only, and the AWS-managed alias/aws/ssm key policy grants Decrypt via kms:ViaService, which simulation cannot see — the first real --with-decryption read on the box is the discriminating test. SIX DEFECTS IN THE NEVER-RUN BOOTSTRAP, whose own header says to treat its first run as a test of itself. It REPRODUCED DEF-017 VERBATIM: it created /opt/acmp-backups while the compose mount is /opt/acmp/backups, so Docker would have auto-created the real path root-owned and every BACKUP DATABASE would have failed at 02:00 in a cron log while the deployment looked backed up — in the very lines whose comment explains why DEF-017 must not recur. It could also report success on a dead stack (it ran `compose ps` and let SSM's exit status decide, so a stack where every container was unhealthy still printed 'bootstrap Success'); replaced with real assertions whose state machine was driven through all eight cases with a docker test double — healthy and running pass, unhealthy, still-starting, absent, exited:1 and still-running all fail, the last being the PE-154 bug of reading an exit code mid-run. Also: the ECR token was a 12-hour docker login against restart:unless-stopped services (now the credential helper), no swapfile existed though the compose file already asserts the P25 bootstrap adds one, the compose plugin came from releases/latest (pinned), and `python` does not exist on AL2023 (python3). TLS: a cloud-only 443 template is MOUNTED rather than baked, because one web image serves on-prem/dev/e2e/cloud and a 443 block with a missing ssl_certificate stops nginx starting at all. All six security headers are repeated in it — nginx's add_header does not merge across server blocks — and /kc/admin plus the master realm are denied 404, since everything under /kc/ becomes public the moment 443 exists. First boot used to deadlock (no cert -> no nginx -> no stack -> nobody to run certbot), so the bootstrap now writes a self-signed placeholder with CN=ACMP-PLACEHOLDER-DO-NOT-TRUST: a neutral-looking placeholder could sit for months while nginx serves it, the healthcheck passes, the stack reports healthy and every browser refuses the connection. certbot-deploy-hook.sh handles what would otherwise break a REAL certificate — privkey.pem is 0600 root:root behind symlinks into ../../archive/ and the container runs as UID 101 — copying with --dereference, installing 0640 root:101, running nginx -t before reload (reloading a bad config leaves the old one running and returns success). Testing the hook found a bug IN the hook: when chown failed part-way, set -e aborted between copy and move and left .privkey.new, a private-key fragment, in the certs directory; the failure was loud, the residue silent. Now trapped and verified 0 fragments. Cost was promoted from a gate to a design constraint: two always-on t3.medium instances are ~$76/mo against a $60 budget, so prod does not launch until UAT is proven (~$38/mo saved across P25+P27), the Elastic IP is allocated at launch per environment rather than up front (an unassociated EIP bills for nothing), CpuCredits=standard is reclassified as the only uncapped line item rather than an ADR compliance item, and no NAT gateway ever (~$32/mo). Verified from AWS docs that associating an EIP RELEASES the auto-assigned address, so it costs nothing extra while running. Projection ~$47/mo. NOT DONE AND NOT CLAIMED: Docker Desktop is not running in this session, so Stage 1 — the local boot gate that proves the 443 listener before any spend — is WRITTEN (12 new assertions: handshake, HSTS, all six headers individually, /kc/admin and master-realm denied, acmp realm still reachable, /api/ proxying) but has NEVER EXECUTED. Nothing in this slice has been booted. The gate's stated limit is recorded in the script itself: a self-signed fixture proves the listener, headers and routing but NOT cert readability, because Docker Desktop bind mounts do not preserve Unix ownership — that is certbot-deploy-hook.sh's problem and Stage 2's test. DEF-022 raised (not SL-025 scope): crontab.example runs backup.sh with no ACMP_ENV_FILE, so it defaults to deploy/.env which the cloud bootstrap never writes, the miss is swallowed by `|| true`, ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET is unset and the off-instance S3 copy is silently skipped — NFR-058 unmet, backups sharing fate with the box they back up. Documented as a required workaround in the new runbook until fixed. Also new: deploy/runbooks/cloud-provisioning.md, because AC-075 says 'bootstrapped from the runbook' and no such document existed — aws/README.md covers 00-05 and stops, and docker-compose.prod.yml points at deploy/runbooks/install.md, which does not exist.

CORRECTION to PE-170, and Stage 1 is now GREEN. PE-170 recorded the pre-spend boot gate as 'WRITTEN but NEVER EXECUTED' because Docker Desktop was not running. It has since been run twice, and the first run FAILED for a real reason — which is the whole argument for having the gate at all. FIRST RUN: 14 passed, 3 failed. web unhealthy, web returned 000, no TLS listener on 18443. Both templates rendered correctly (the log shows envsubst processing default.conf.template AND cloud-443.conf.template), nginx loaded the config, and then died with `cannot load certificate key "/etc/nginx/certs/privkey.pem": BIO_new_file() failed (... Permission denied ...)`. THAT IS THE EXACT FAILURE I HAD DECLARED UNTESTABLE HERE. Both the script comment and PE-170 stated that the self-signed fixture could not cover cert READABILITY, on the reasoning that Docker Desktop does not preserve Unix modes across a bind mount. It does. openssl writes privkey.pem 0600, nginx runs as UID 101, and the mount carried the mode straight through — the same failure shape a real Let's Encrypt key produces (0600 root:root vs a container on 101). The stated limitation was FALSE, and a false limitation is worse than no statement because it tells a future reader not to trust evidence that is actually there. Corrected in the script rather than left standing; the gate is stronger than it was claimed to be. The bug was in the FIXTURE, not the product: `chmod 0644` ran on the host through Git Bash, where it is a no-op on an NTFS file under a Docker-shared mount, so it silently did nothing. It now runs INSIDE the container in the same docker run, where the mode actually applies. The production path was never affected — certbot-deploy-hook.sh installs 0640 root:101 precisely because of this class of problem, which is why the hook exists rather than pointing nginx at /etc/letsencrypt directly. A second fixture problem was fixed on the way: the cert is now generated in a container rather than with the host's openssl, which on this workstation resolves to a PostgreSQL-bundled build whose OPENSSL_CONF names a file that does not exist and which cannot generate anything at all. The gate already requires Docker, so this adds no dependency, and a gate that only runs where the host toolchain happens to be healthy is not a gate. SECOND RUN: 27 passed, 0 failed, against the REAL ECR images for 7ec172a (not local builds). TLS handshake succeeds and the 443 listener serves the SPA; HSTS present on the HTTPS response, which is the block where it actually applies rather than the 8080 one browsers ignore; all six security headers present and checked INDIVIDUALLY, because nginx's add_header does not merge across server blocks so the presence of some is no evidence of the rest; /kc/admin/ and /kc/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration both 404 over TLS; the acmp realm still reachable at 200, proving the deny did not take too much with it; and /api/ proxying to the api over TLS with HTTP 401 — an API-originated status is proof of life, whereas 502/504 would mean nginx never reached the backend. SIX DEFECTS FOUND BY RUNNING WHAT HAD ONLY BEEN READ, and the split matters. TWO ARE PLATFORM-INDEPENDENT and would have failed identically for any operator on any OS. (1) 08-bootstrap-box.sh passed its remote script through `--parameters "commands=[...]"`, the AWS CLI's SHORTHAND syntax, whose parser splits on commas and newlines — the box received a fragment and died with 'line 2: syntax error: unexpected end of file', an error that indicts the script's content rather than its transport. Fixed by passing real JSON via a file. (2) `aws ssm wait command-executed` gives up after roughly 100 seconds (20 polls x 5s) and the script swallowed that timeout with `|| true`, then read a status that was not final — so a cold-box bootstrap, which installs Docker, clones, pulls four images, migrates a schema and imports a realm, ALWAYS reported 'finished with status InProgress' for a run proceeding perfectly well. That is PE-154's defect one layer up: reporting a non-terminal state as a result. Now polls to Success|Failed|Cancelled|TimedOut with a 25-minute deadline. THREE ARE WINDOWS/MSYS PATH BUGS, all invisible on Linux and all surfacing as errors that name the wrong cause: MSYS rewrites a leading-slash argument into a Windows path before the native aws.exe sees it, so PutParameter answered 'Parameter name must be a fully qualified name' for a perfectly qualified name and the bootstrap preflight reported /acmp/uat/env MISSING when it demonstrably existed. The two fixes are OPPOSITE in direction: 09-put-env.sh and 08-bootstrap-box.sh need conversion OFF, while 05-route53.sh needs it ON, because MSYS rewrites bare arguments but NOT paths inside a file:// URL — setting the variable shell-wide to fix the first broke the third, which I did, turning one failure into two. cygpath -m handles the file:// case and is a no-op on Linux. (6) Docker's per-layer progress bars filled SSM's 24,000-character StandardOutputContent cap on a cold box, so the first real failure ended in '--output truncated--' and could only be diagnosed by going back to the instance; --quiet-pull now keeps the tail meaningful. A SEVENTH DEFECT WAS IN THE ENVIRONMENT, NOT THE CODE, and is the sharpest of the set: certbot printed 'Certbot has set up a scheduled task to automatically renew this certificate in the background' and that was FALSE — systemctl reported certbot-renew.timer as `disabled`. The unit file carries Persistent=true, so it was right in shape and simply never enabled; unattended renewal would never have fired and the certificate would have expired in 90 days in complete silence while the tool's own success message said otherwise. Enabled and verified (enabled, active, next run 2026-08-07 19:58 UTC). Same family as DEF-017 (backups never written, deployment looks backed up), DEF-018 (search returns nothing, logs clean) and DEF-020 (Seq dead, stack healthy) — and caught only because the timer was checked rather than the sentence believed. Structurally it is DEF-019's seam class one layer up: realm-export.json was authored for the dev/ngrok topology BEFORE ADR-0037 chose per-environment subdomains, and nothing reconciled them — a single shared realm file cannot express a hostname that is per-environment by design. Recommended remedy is to have the keycloak-config one-shot, which already uses kcadm to reconcile the realm, update redirectUris/webOrigins/post.logout.redirect.uris from ACMP_HOST when set; that leaves dev untouched and reuses machinery already in the stack. DEF-023 FIXED AND PROVEN BY THE CHECK IT WAS DEFINED BY — four real browser logins on a from-scratch box — and the verification run then found two more defects of the same silent-success family. THE FIX went where the defect said it should: reconcile.sh, the keycloak-config one-shot that already reconciles the realm over kcadm, now REPLACES acmp-web's redirectUris and webOrigins from ACMP_WEB_ORIGIN, which only docker-compose.cloud.yml sets. The handoff proposed deriving it from ACMP_HOST; that is WRONG and the reason is worth keeping — cloud-stack-boot.sh sets ACMP_HOST=localhost while the app is on port 18080, so https://${ACMP_HOST} would register a URI matching nothing. KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN is the browser-facing origin and is correct in both cloud and the boot gate, but NOT in the dev compose, where it is keycloak.localhost:8085 while the SPA is on localhost:8088 — which is exactly why the variable is passed from the cloud file only and the block no-ops when unset. post.logout.redirect.uris became the literal '+' in the export instead of a third patched field: environment-independent, and it sidesteps kcadm's dotted-key path splitting entirely. THE ORDER OF VERIFICATION WAS THE POINT. The Keycloak half was proven FREE on the local boot gate before any AWS spend, and negatively: with the fix the configured origin gets a login form (200) while http://localhost:8088 — a URI the committed realm-export DOES register — is refused (400). That single line proves the reconcile genuinely replaced rather than appended, that the new gate assertion greps the real Keycloak error text, and that the check can fail. A check that has never been seen to fail is what this entire slice is about. The SPA half could NOT be rehearsed locally, and that is a real limit of the boot gate now recorded in it: the published web image bakes VITE_OIDC_AUTHORITY per environment (ADR-0037), so the <sha>-uat bundle points at the UAT hostname wherever it runs — a browser there drives the deployed box, not the local stack. DEF-025, raised from DEF-023's previously unassessed second observation: Keycloak's pages were inheriting the SPA's server-level headers under /kc/. Our script-src 'self' blocked the login theme's inline scripts (7 console violations on every login), and our X-Frame-Options deny landed on top of Keycloak's SAMEORIGIN — conflicting values resolve to deny, which blocks the hidden same-origin iframe automaticSilentRenew uses. FINAL STATE: all four accounts log in and JIT-provision with the correct role in a single run, the renew iframe loads, zero CSP violations, a real Let's Encrypt certificate verifying 0 from off the box, and the SPA's own / still carrying all six headers so AC-081's posture is intact. CORRECTION, AND IT RETRACTS A CLAIM I MADE AGAINST A TOOL. PE-179 closes with a 'PACKAGE-WRITE WARNING' stating that two Tamheed package sessions silently lost their writes, that ids were reused, and that package writes cannot be trusted without reading the CSVs. THAT DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, and the real cause was mine. tamheed-package/data/*.jsonl is GIT-TRACKED -- 29 files -- and canonical state is written there, not to a private store. During that run I ran `git reset --hard origin/main` repeatedly while merging PRs. Any package write that had not yet been git-committed was therefore discarded by my own reset, not by Tamheed. The evidence is unambiguous and was checked before this correction was written: only two commits in the entire run ever contained package data (9d27528 and the later restore), `git reflog` shows the resets sitting between the writes and any commit, and `git show <sha>:tamheed-package/data/audit_verdicts.jsonl` finds AV-103 in none of the intermediate commits. Tamheed then behaved CORRECTLY on each re-open: it loaded the canonical state as it actually stood on disk and allocated the next free id from it. What looked like id reuse was the allocator doing exactly the right thing against state my reset had rewound. The 'silent overwrite' of an earlier narrative was the same thing -- the earlier row no longer existed to be overwritten. THE REAL LESSON IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE ONE I RECORDED: a Tamheed package is a git working tree, so `git reset --hard`, `git checkout` and `git stash` are destructive to uncommitted package writes exactly as they are to uncommitted source. Package writes must be git-committed before any branch operation, in the same way code is. The verification habit I recommended -- read tamheed-package/csv/ rather than trusting a tool's return value -- remains sound advice, but for this reason rather than the one I gave. ONE GENUINE TAMHEED DEFECT WAS FOUND while investigating, and it is unrelated to the above: _next_id orders candidate ids with `ORDER BY id DESC`, which is a TEXT sort. Inside the zero-padded width that agrees with numeric order, so it is correct for the first 999 rows of a table and wrong permanently after -- 'PE-999' sorts above 'PE-1000', so every later call returns PE-1000 again, and since id is the primary key the insert raises and the batch rolls back. progress_update and audit_record would fail forever on any package that stays busy long enough; this package is at PE-181 and climbing. Reproduced in isolation rather than argued. NOT fixed here by operator instruction -- the tool is not this project's to change -- and reported upstream instead, with the reproduction and two further hazards, in findings_10.md at the repo root.
