STRICT RE-READING OF AC-080, A CORRECTED REQUIREMENT REFERENCE, AND A SECOND FALSE CLAIM ABOUT THE TOOL RETRACTED -- this one caused by the tool rather than by me. AC-080 DOWNGRADED Met -> Partial (AV-105). The drill itself is untouched and still fully evidenced: 3->0->3 per database on Express, no compression clause, no Postgres leg, 19/0 green. What fails a strict reading is the AC's own binding clause '(verifies NFR-058)'. NFR-058 has two halves -- backups stored SEPARATE from the primary server, and restorability tested quarterly -- and the drill evidences the second plus the mechanism of the first, not the first as an operating property. DEF-022 (cron silently skipped the S3 copy) and DEF-026 (AL2023 ships no cron, so the schedule never existed) both landed after the Met verdict and show the regime was not running. A hand-run drill proves machinery, not a regime. The exit criterion is now named on the verdict so nobody has to re-derive it: an actual CRON-TRIGGERED backup observed to land off-instance. Every prerequisite is in place; it has simply never been watched. REQUIREMENT REFERENCE DRIFT, found while checking that: DEF-026 cited 'NFR-057 (RPO <= 4h)'. Wrong. The package and the v1 migration source (docs/requirements/non-functional.md) BOTH define NFR-056 as the RPO and NFR-057 as the RTO, and they agree with each other exactly -- so the package rows are faithful and the migration is not at fault. The swap lives in ACMP's own hand-written prose, where deploy/ scripts and runbooks had the two numbers reversed, and I copied it into the register from a code comment instead of checking the requirement. DEF-026 is corrected, the deploy/ prose is corrected, and docs/ is DELIBERATELY LEFT WRONG because AGENTS.md freezes it as a read-only archive -- recorded here so the next reader does not 'fix' the archive and does not read the inconsistency as an oversight. THE SECOND RETRACTION IS THE INTERESTING ONE, because unlike PE-181 the root cause is the tool and not the operator. OQ-065's resolution asserted that 'tamheed 2.6.0 exposes no write path to trace_edges in any case (entity_upsert rejects both trace-edge and trace_edge)'. That is false, and it was settled by TESTING rather than by re-reading: entity_upsert(type='trace-edge', ...) returns ok/applied:1 against this live package. 'trace-edge' is a registered entity type in the plugin source, commented 'write surface for relations', with its own INSERT OR IGNORE branch, and documented as a write surface in the plugin's own README and SKILL. Only the underscore spelling is genuinely unknown. The reason we believed otherwise is a defect in the tool's READ surface: entity_query(type='trace-edge') answers with the literal string "unknown entity type 'trace-edge'" for a type that is both known and writable -- it reports non-queryable as nonexistent. A false error message propagated into this package's permanent record and sat there for three days. That is now reported upstream as findings_10 A2 and OQ-065 is corrected. THE DECISION OQ-065 REACHED DOES NOT CHANGE: wiring duplicate DEC->ADR edges was undesirable regardless of whether it was possible, because two records of one fact drift apart; derivation at export time remains the right fix and remains upstream work. METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING: three claims about Tamheed have now been wrong in this project -- the lost writes (mine, PE-181), the NFR swap (ACMP prose, not the migration), and the trace_edges write path (the tool's own error message). The first two were caught by checking git and the v1 source; the third by running the call instead of reading about it. Reading a tool's error message is not evidence of the tool's behaviour.

RETRACTION TRAIL CLOSED for the trace_edges claim, and the sweep that closed it found a carrier the first pass missed. PE-182 retracted the false claim as it appeared in OQ-065, and OQ-065 itself was corrected in place. That was incomplete: the same claim is carried by THREE progress entries, and a first grep for one exact phrase found only two of them. A broader sweep across four phrasings found the third. Recorded here rather than by editing any of them, because progress entries are the append-only journal and a retraction must point AT the rows rather than rewrite them (that is also DEF-adjacent tooling finding A4 in findings_10 -- the tool would happily let me rewrite them in place, and the fact that it would is exactly why the discipline has to come from us). THE THREE ARE NOT THE SAME KIND OF STATEMENT, and flattening them would destroy the only distinction a future reader needs. PE-166 is the ORIGINAL FINDING: 'FIRST, there is no sanctioned write path to trace_edges in tamheed 2.6.0: the table is not exposed to entity_query, and entity_upsert rejects both trace-edge and trace_edge.' The claim is that entry's substance, and it is false in its second half -- entity_upsert accepts 'trace-edge'; only the underscore spelling is unknown, and the 'not exposed to entity_query' half is true. PE-169 is a COMMIT-SUMMARY RESTATEMENT of PE-166 and inherits the error without adding anything. PE-167 is the one that matters and the one nearly missed: it uses the claim as a SUBORDINATE CLAUSE under a resolution -- 'Recorded as an upstream note rather than a blocker, since fixing it means changing the plugin, not this package, and no write path to trace_edges exists in 2.6.0 anyway.' READ IN FULL BEFORE WRITING THIS, and the reading is what settles it: the word is 'anyway'. The clause is a secondary reinforcement, not the reason. PE-167's decision rests on its PRIMARY reason -- that this is a derivation gap in the plugin's export rather than a defect in this package -- and that reason is untouched and still correct. So OQ-065's resolution STANDS ENTIRELY. Nothing decided there needs revisiting: wiring duplicate DEC->ADR edges was undesirable regardless of whether it was possible, because two records of one fact drift apart, and derivation at export time remains the right fix and remains upstream work. What changes is only that the resolution's convenience argument had a false leg; the load-bearing leg never did. THE ROOT CAUSE IS THE TOOL, NOT THE READER, which is why this is worth the words: entity_query(type='trace-edge') answers with the literal string "unknown entity type 'trace-edge'" for a type that is registered in ENTITY_TABLES, commented in the source as a 'write surface for relations', documented as a write surface in the plugin's own README and SKILL, and demonstrably writable. Confirmed again today by running both calls, and extended: entity_query(type='omission') returns the same false message for a type that also accepts writes. The read surface reports NON-QUERYABLE as NONEXISTENT for both. Reported upstream as findings_10 section A2, with the fix suggestion that the two conditions be distinguished. METHOD NOTE, the fourth in this project and the sharpest: my first attempt to close this trail grepped ONE exact phrase and concluded two carriers. A four-phrasing sweep found three. Searching for the wording you remember writing finds the entries you remember writing -- it does not find the ones that paraphrased you.

AC-080 REACHES MET ON THE ONE ARTIFACT A HAND-RUN CANNOT FORGE, AC-085 LOSES A LEG TO CLOUDTRAIL, AND DEF-027's REMEDY IS MEASURED VIABLE INSTEAD OF RECOMMENDED. AC-080 -> Met (AV-106). AV-105 had named the exit criterion precisely -- a CRON-TRIGGERED backup observed to land off-instance -- so this session had only to execute it, and the execution had two traps worth recording. THE FIRST TRAP IS THE CRONTAB ENVIRONMENT ASSIGNMENT. crontab.example carries ACMP_ENV_FILE=/opt/acmp/deploy/.env.cloud as an assignment that applies to every line BELOW it, so installing a standalone temporary crontab with just the drill line would have run backup.sh without ACMP_ENV_FILE, backup.sh would have refused (DEF-022's net), and the drill would have proved the refusal works rather than the schedule works -- a green-looking failure of exactly the DEF-023 family this project keeps catching. The line was APPENDED to the live crontab instead, and the assignment re-confirmed present above it before waiting. THE SECOND TRAP IS THAT THE ARTIFACTS DO NOT DISCRIMINATE. A hand-invoked backup.sh and a cron-invoked one produce byte-identical .bak files, identical filenames and identical log text; nothing in S3 can tell them apart. That is why AV-095's fully-green drill could not settle this AC, and it is why the evidence recorded is crond's OWN journal line -- `21:30:02 CROND[7778]: (root) CMD (cd /opt/acmp && deploy/scripts/backup.sh ...)` with CMDEND at 21:30:06 -- rather than the backup output. Corroboration that this was the first scheduled run on the box at all: /var/log/acmp-backup.log did not exist and /opt/acmp/backups was empty beforehand (local .bak files are pruned by AGE, not on upload, so empty means never run). The off-instance check was deliberately run FROM THE LAPTOP, since an `aws s3 ls` executed on the box shares fate with the box and NFR-058's first clause is exactly about not sharing fate. Schedule restored and diffed byte-identical both to the pre-drill capture and to the committed crontab.example. AC-085 STAYS PARTIAL BUT ON ONE LEG INSTEAD OF TWO (AV-107). Leg 4 was recorded Not-met on 2026-08-04 for the sound reason that an SsmActionDefinition needs explicit InstanceIds and no instances existed. They exist now, and the evidence turned out to be better than the AC asks for: rather than reading 07-launch.sh's create-or-update branch and asserting the behaviour, CloudTrail shows UpdateBudgetAction 33 seconds after the current instance launched, with OldAction carrying the TERMINATED predecessor i-05085d458d886dc08 and NewAction carrying i-07ac28ac2fedab921 -- the automatic re-pointing observed across a real replacement. Both branches are covered: one CreateBudgetAction and three UpdateBudgetActions in the trail. THE METHOD NOTE HERE IS ABOUT STALE VERDICTS, not about budgets: AV-088's leg 4 was correct when written and became wrong without anything touching it, because its premise was 'once P25 launches instances'. A verdict whose reason is a not-yet is a verdict with an expiry date, and nothing in the package makes it announce its own expiry. Worth a sweep of other Partial verdicts whose stated reason is a precondition rather than a defect. DEF-027 UPDATED, STILL OPEN, REMEDY NOW MEASURED. Option (b) -- SSM port-forward, zero code change -- was blocked only on session-manager-plugin not being installed. It no longer is, and not by installing anything: the winget/MSI route wants Program Files and stalls on a UAC prompt, while AWS's own SessionManagerPlugin.zip contains a nested package.zip whose bin/session-manager-plugin.exe runs standalone, which is all `aws ssm start-session` needs on PATH. The tunnel opened first try, which also settles that acmp-admin holds ssm:StartSession -- a different action from the ssm:SendCommand this project has used everywhere else, and previously an untested assumption. THE PROBE THROUGH IT IS THE RESULT: /kc/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration -> 200 and /kc/admin/realms/acmp/users -> 401, against 404 and 404 for the same two paths on the public 443 listener in the same minute. The 401-not-404 is the finding -- the admin API is reachable and merely unauthenticated, so nginx is not denying it AND Keycloak's hostname-strict mode does not reject a localhost Host header on the admin REST API, which had been reasoned but never tested. AC-081's deny posture is re-confirmed live in the same command. What remains is neither design nor infrastructure: global-setup authenticates with KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD, which exists only as a docker secret generated on the box, and retrieving it to the workstation was refused by this session's tool-permission layer. AC-076 is then one `npx playwright test` invocation. TWO THINGS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, recorded so they are not mistaken for oversights. AC-085 leg 1 was not forced: the shape is now known and written into AV-107 (a temporary 1% ACTUAL notification, which is a separate API object from the 100% actions and so cannot disturb them, against a zero-datapoint SNS delivery baseline), but the create-notification call was refused by the same permission layer. AC-084 was not advanced, because its missing leg IS the e2e run that DEF-027 blocks; the alarm leg has meanwhile settled to OK on its own. HOUSEKEEPING: two empty directories named `certs;C` and `cloud-443.conf.template;C` under deploy/nginx/ -- MSYS path-conversion debris from an earlier session, untracked, and invisible to `git status` because git does not report empty directories -- were removed. The box's installed crontab still carries the pre-correction NFR-056/057 comment swap because the box runs fca58f36, which predates 788c42e; it is comment text only and will correct itself on the next bootstrap.

THE E2E SUITE RAN AGAINST UAT FOR THE FIRST TIME, WHICH UNBLOCKED TWO ACs AND EXPOSED A THIRD PROBLEM THE SUITE EXISTS TO FIND. DEF-027 option (b) executed exactly as designed, with zero code change and no relaxation of the /kc/ deny. The prerequisite that had blocked it turned out not to require installing anything: the winget/MSI route for session-manager-plugin wants Program Files and stalls on an invisible UAC prompt, but AWS's own SessionManagerPlugin.zip carries a nested package.zip whose bin/session-manager-plugin.exe runs standalone, and `aws ssm start-session` only needs the binary on PATH. The tunnel opened first try, which also settled that acmp-admin holds ssm:StartSession -- a different IAM action from the ssm:SendCommand used everywhere else here. global-setup seeded its fixtures through the tunnel while the browser drove the public host, which works only because it takes E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL separately from E2E_WEB_URL. AC-076 PENDING -> PARTIAL (AV-108): 6 of 7 passed. Auth is the headline -- a real Keycloak authorization-code + PKCE round-trip against the deployed realm, plus the unauthenticated-deep-link redirect. RTL/a11y went 4/4, axe-clean in both languages. AC-084 PARTIAL ON ONE LEG INSTEAD OF THREE (AV-109): that run IS the 'e2e run drives it' the AC asked for, and per-container memory was SAMPLED every 10s throughout rather than read once afterwards, because docker stats has no peak counter and an unsampled peak is simply lost. Keycloak peaked at 441.9 MiB of its 448 cap -- 98.6%, and it HELD, which is the alternative the AC explicitly allows ('raised or shown to hold'). Zero OOM, zero container deaths, dmesg clean, 46 MiB of 4 GiB swap touched. Recorded as a standing risk rather than a pass: 6.1 MiB of headroom is the thinnest in the stack, and the slack to fund any increase sits in worker (103.8 of 256) and seq (168.3 of 256). THE CORE LOOP FAILED, AND THE DIAGNOSIS IS THE MOST TRANSFERABLE THING IN THIS ENTRY (DEF-028). The step 'secretary schedules a meeting' timed out at 180s, and the decisive observation was a NEGATIVE one: nginx logged NO POST /api/meetings at all during the three minutes the test waited -- only the SPA's 30-second notification polls. The click produced no request. Everything that would have been the easy explanation was checked and eliminated rather than assumed: the API answered in 5-69ms in the same window, load average 0.02, all six containers healthy, zero OOM/die events, no console error and no page error in the Playwright trace, and the two nginx CSP headers are byte-identical between the 443 and 8080 templates. The failure snapshot shows the form fully and validly populated with the Schedule button enabled. THE MECHANISM IS A SILENT RETURN: SchedulePage.onSubmit ends in a bare `if (...) return;` over six conditions, and one of them -- the `!chair` lookup -- has NO rendered counterpart, because chairError tests the strictly weaker `!effectiveChairId`. A submit handler that can return without telling anyone is the fault; which branch took it is secondary, and which one took it here was NOT isolated, which is recorded as not-isolated rather than guessed. One thread left for whoever picks it up: GET /api/members, the call that populates the chair list, appears NOWHERE in the access log for the run, while POST /api/members/me appears repeatedly. CI IS GREEN ON THE SAME SPEC against the local compose stack (e2e run 31254328744), so the trigger is UAT-specific -- a realm that has been through real logins and JIT provisioning, which a fresh CI realm never sees. AC-085 LEG 1 ATTEMPTED, AND THE FAILURE IS MORE USEFUL THAN THE PLAN AV-107 RECORDED (AV-110). Arming a 1% threshold below current spend put the notification into ALARM instantly -- and delivered nothing: zero datapoints on NumberOfMessagesPublished/Delivered/Failed against a pre-armed zero baseline. A notification created ALREADY in alarm has no OK->ALARM transition to notify on, so that method can never pass, however long one waits. It is the un-failable check inverted: a check that cannot SUCCEED. Replaced with a 2% threshold ($1.20 against $1.065 spent) which sits in OK today and will transition on its own as ordinary spend crosses it -- a real notification on real spend, left armed for the next session to OBSERVE rather than act on. Both 100% budget ACTIONS were re-verified untouched after every change. A SECOND STALE PREMISE CORRECTED, and it is the same class as AV-088's leg 4 in PE-184: the handoff states the CPU-credit alarm 'recovered while the box sat idle'. A STOPPED t3 EARNS NO CREDITS. The alarm read OK only because a stopped instance publishes no datapoints; it returned to ALARM at ~6-9 credits the moment the box started. Credits accrue at 24/hour ONLY while running, so that leg needs about two hours of running time BEFORE the e2e run -- a scheduling constraint on the next attempt, not a defect. CLEANUP, recorded because 'who can log into UAT' is a question worth being able to answer: the suite seeds fixed-password e2e-* accounts whose password is committed in e2e/users.ts, onto a host whose 443 is open to 0.0.0.0/0. All three were deleted through the same tunnel (HTTP 204 each) and the realm verified back to its five legitimate accounts. The bootstrap admin credential was pulled disk-to-disk into a scratchpad file and never rendered into the session, then removed. The governance rows the run wrote are hash-chained and immutable and REMAIN in the UAT database permanently -- acceptable for UAT, and exactly why the suite must stay incapable of pointing at production.

DEF-028 ISOLATED BY EXPERIMENT, FIXED, AND A FALSE LEAD I PUT IN THE RECORD RETRACTED. FIRST THE RETRACTION, because it was mine and it would have cost the next reader hours. DEF-028 as first written asserted that 'GET /api/members appears NOWHERE in nginx's access log for the run, while POST /api/members/me appears repeatedly', and offered that as the first thread to pull. THE EVIDENCE DID NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM. The grep behind it ended in `tail -n 8`, and all eight lines were the frequently-polling POST /api/members/me; any GET earlier in the run was simply outside the window. The honest statement was 'I did not check'. This is the fourth time in this project that a narrow search produced a confident wrong conclusion -- PE-183 recorded the same shape and even named the lesson, that searching for the wording you expect finds only what you expected -- and I repeated it anyway, three days later, in the same package. Recording that recurrence is the point: the lesson did not stick as a note, so it is restated here as a rule with teeth -- a claim of ABSENCE is never supportable by a truncated search, and `tail`, `head` and `-m` must not appear in the pipeline that establishes one. THE REAL CAUSE IS A RACE, AND IT WAS SETTLED BY A FALSIFICATION TEST RATHER THAN BY MORE READING. A scratchpad probe logged in as the seeded secretary against live UAT, opened /meetings/new, waited six seconds, filled the form exactly as core-loop.spec.ts does and clicked Schedule: POST /api/meetings ISSUED, meeting MTG-2026-001 created. The same probe with the wait removed -- i.e. behaving exactly as the spec does -- reproduced the failure exactly: GET /api/members had not even been sent, the chair control still read 'Loading members...', the click produced NO request at all, and NO error rendered anywhere on the page. One variable changed, opposite outcomes. THAT ALSO EXPLAINS THE THING THAT HAD MADE NO SENSE -- why the failure screenshot showed a perfectly valid form with 'chairman Seeded' selected. chairError is DERIVED state, not latched. At click time the members query had not resolved, so activeMembers was empty, onSubmit's `!chair` guard returned silently, and the error was displayed; 180 seconds later when Playwright captured the snapshot the data had arrived, the chair filled itself in and the error EVAPORATED. The artifact that was supposed to diagnose the failure had been overwritten by the recovery. WHY CI NEVER CAUGHT IT, and why this is a product defect rather than a test artifact: on localhost the members query always wins the race against the test, and over the internet it does not. A real user on a slow connection who clicks Schedule promptly gets exactly the same silence. Environment sensitivity of this kind is invisible to a test suite that only ever runs against localhost, which is the whole argument for AC-076 existing at all -- the AC found a defect that 140 green test files and a green e2e workflow could not. FIXED in commit ed74130, two faults not one: `chair` is now resolved ONCE in render scope so the guard and the message cannot disagree (chairError previously tested `!effectiveChairId`, strictly weaker than the guard's `!chair` lookup), and Schedule is DISABLED while the members query is loading. Disabled rather than 'loading' -- the button is not busy, the form is not ready, and the chair field already says so. Disabling is also what lets the e2e suite pass with NO change to the spec, because Playwright waits for an enabled button, so the race cannot occur. Two regression tests added; frontend 140 files green, coverage 99.64% against the 95% floor. AC-076's TEXT AMENDED (OQ-066), same shape as OQ-064's amendment of AC-085. Its stated method -- E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL=https://uat.../kc -- is provably impossible, since the 443 listener 404s both endpoints global-setup needs and AC-081 rests on that deny. The AC now names the SSM port-forward that was actually used. The SUBSTANCE graded is unchanged: the same three areas, against the same real environment. The amended method is strictly harder to arrange than the original text implies, and it was executed and evidenced (AV-108) BEFORE the amendment was written, not after -- this is correcting a specification against reality, not lowering a bar to make a verdict green. WHAT IS STILL BLOCKED, stated plainly: the fix cannot reach UAT from a branch. ci.yml publishes images only on a push to main, so AC-076 cannot go Met until the branch is merged, the tags re-pinned in /acmp/uat/env and the box re-bootstrapped. The merge itself was refused by this session's tool-permission layer, not by CI and not by policy.
DEF-028 root cause isolated by falsification test against live UAT and fixed; AC-076 statement amended per OQ-066. Not yet deployed — images publish only from main.

THE FIX WAS DEPLOYED AND PROVED ITSELF IN THE ONLY PLACE IT COULD, AND THE CLEANUP I DID LAST SESSION TURNED OUT TO BE THE NEXT BLOCKER. FULL DEPLOY LOOP EXECUTED: PR #195 merged to main (155cc803), CI's publish job produced all four images, their presence in ECR was VERIFIED BEFORE anything else moved -- including the per-environment web:155cc803...-uat tag, which is DEF-019's lesson applied rather than recalled -- then /acmp/uat/env was re-pinned to the new full SHA through 09-put-env.sh and 08-bootstrap-box.sh re-bootstrapped the box at that commit. The image-tag drift guard PASSED on its own rather than being overridden with ACMP_ALLOW_TAG_DRIFT, nine of nine health assertions returned OK, every one-shot exited 0, and docker ps confirms all five services on the new images. TLS survived the rebuild (Let's Encrypt cert valid to 2026-11-05) and the deny posture was re-checked in the same minute: 200 for the SPA and the acmp realm's discovery document, 404 for both /kc/admin and /kc/realms/master. So AC-081 is re-evidenced after a redeploy, not merely assumed to have survived one. DEF-028 IS VERIFIED FIXED WHERE IT MATTERS. The defect existed only over a real network, so localhost could never have confirmed the fix and a green CI run says nothing about it -- the deployed re-run is the only possible evidence, which is the whole argument for AC-076. Before: the meeting-scheduling step hung the full 180-second timeout, total run 3.8 minutes. After: that step passes and the run finishes in 55.5 seconds. The failure moved PAST the step it used to die on, which is what a fixed race looks like as opposed to a masked one. A SELF-INFLICTED BLOCKER TOOK ITS PLACE, and it is worth recording carefully because both halves of the mistake were individually correct. Last session I DELETED the three fixed-password e2e-* Keycloak users after the run, on the sound ground that their password is committed in e2e/users.ts and UAT's 443 is open to the whole internet. What I did not think through is that app-side identity is the Keycloak `sub` (P17b made that universal deliberately), and ACMP's audit chain is immutable, so a CommitteeMember row can be deactivated but never removed. Re-seeding therefore minted NEW subs and JIT-provisioned a SECOND member row for each. Measured rather than suspected: GET /api/members now returns 10 rows where 7 are expected, with E2E Chairman, E2E Member and E2E Secretary each duplicated and all six active. core-loop's owner picker uses an exact NAME match, so it hits two elements and fails Playwright strict mode. THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the sharpest thing in this entry: IN A SYSTEM WITH IMMUTABLE HISTORY, CLEANUP IS NEVER SYMMETRIC WITH CREATION. Deleting an upstream identity does not delete what it created downstream -- it ORPHANS it, permanently, and the orphan outlives the thing that justified removing it. THE FIX SATISFIES BOTH CONCERNS AND HAS BEEN APPLIED: DISABLE the Keycloak user instead of deleting it. A disabled account cannot authenticate, so the internet-reachable-credential risk is removed just as completely, and the sub survives, so the next run re-enables the SAME identity and duplicates nothing. All three are now enabled=false (204 each). AC-076's own cleanup clause was corrected from 'deleted' to 'disabled' in the same breath, because leaving the AC prescribing the thing that caused this would guarantee a repeat -- an AC that teaches a mistake is worse than one that is merely silent. WHAT IS LEFT FOR AC-076 IS ONE OPERATOR ACTION WITH NO CODE IN IT: deactivate the three ORPHANED member rows through the sanctioned admin path (POST /api/members/{publicId}/deactivate, or Administration -> Users & Membership), which is an ordinary governance action rather than data repair, then re-run. It was not done here because it needs an account holding the Administrator role and none was available to this session. AV-111 supersedes AV-108; DEF-029 records the duplication; DEF-027 closed as Fixed once its remedy AND the AC amendment had both landed.
DEF-028 fix deployed to UAT and verified: scheduling step passes, run 3.8min -> 55.5s. AC-081 deny re-evidenced post-redeploy. DEF-029 raised.

AC-084 REACHES MET, AND THE MEASUREMENT INVERTS THE ASSUMPTION THE CLAUSE WAS BUILT ON. The last open leg was the CPUCreditBalance alarm. The box was left running from a cold start and the alarm cleared on its own after roughly 1h50m, at 00:11:02Z with a balance of 50.09 -- no threshold tuning, which had been rejected twice on the grounds that it rebuilds the un-failable check the alarm exists to catch. The e2e run was then driven with the alarm healthy: it read OK before, throughout and after, and the balance ROSE across the run, 50.09 -> 51.59. THE DECISIVE NUMBER IS THE USAGE, not the balance: CPUCreditUsage in the two 5-minute periods covering the run was 0.426 and 0.498, against 2.0 credits EARNED per 5 minutes at the t3.medium standard rate. An e2e run costs about a QUARTER of what the box earns while running it. So the clause 'the alarm is not tripped when an e2e run drives it' was never really about the e2e load -- the load is nearly free. It was entirely about cold-start warm-up, and the only thing that ever made this leg fail was starting the box and testing immediately. That is exactly the argument OQ-067 makes, now with numbers behind it rather than an inference. MEMORY RE-MEASURED ON THE CURRENT DEPLOYMENT rather than carried forward, because the box had been re-bootstrapped onto 155cc803 since AV-109's sampling and stale evidence for a Met verdict is the failure mode this project keeps catching. Immediately after the run: keycloak 430.7 MiB of its 448 cap, sqlserver 1.14 GiB of 2, api 295.1 of 512, seq 129.3 of 256, worker 113.6 of 256, web 12.45 of 64; zero OOM events, zero container deaths, dmesg clean, 37 MiB of 4 GiB swap touched, all six healthy. Consistent with the 441.9 MiB peak AV-109 sampled at 10-second intervals on the previous deployment, so the cap holds and nothing needed raising. KEYCLOAK'S 96% IS RECORDED AS A STANDING RISK RATHER THAN BURIED IN A PASS -- about 17 MiB of headroom, the thinnest in the stack, against a limits total of 3536 MiB in a 3584 MiB budget. It holds today under real e2e load; it must not be assumed to hold as session count grows, and the slack to fund any increase is in worker and seq. WHAT THIS LEAVES: ten acceptance criteria Met, two Partial. AC-076 needs one operator action with no code in it -- deactivate the three orphaned CommitteeMember rows via the Administrator role (DEF-029) -- and AC-085 leg 1 needs only observation, with the 2% notification already armed and sitting in OK until ordinary spend crosses $1.20. Neither is blocked on engineering.

OQ-067 RESOLVED, THE DEF-029 REMEDIATION REDUCED TO THREE COPY-PASTE CALLS, AND A STALE HANDOFF I WROTE TONIGHT CORRECTED. THE CORRECTION FIRST, because it is the second self-inflicted drift in one session. I rewrote handoff/RESUME-ph5-closeout.md a few commits BEFORE AV-112 landed, so the file went to origin claiming 'Nine acceptance criteria are Met; three are Partial' and carrying a whole section instructing the next session to go and close AC-084 -- which was already Met. A handoff that dispatches someone to redo finished work is worse than no handoff, and it is exactly the package-vs-reality drift AGENTS.md forbids. Corrected to ten Met / two Partial, and the AC-084 section replaced with a 'do NOT re-do it' note carrying the evidence. THE PATTERN WORTH NAMING: a document written from a snapshot goes stale the moment the snapshot moves, and writing it BEFORE the last verdict of a session guarantees it. Write the handoff last, or re-read it after the last write. OQ-067 RESOLVED AS OPTION (a) -- KEEP THE ALARM EXACTLY AS ARMED, DOCUMENT THE WARM-UP -- and the reasoning matters more than the choice. The measurement taken for AC-084 answered the question the OQ was asking: CPUCreditUsage across the two 5-minute periods covering a full e2e run was 0.426 and 0.498, against 2.0 credits EARNED in the same window, and the balance ROSE during the run. So the e2e load is nearly free and the ONLY thing that ever trips this alarm is cold-start warm-up. THE ALARM IS THEREFORE TELLING THE TRUTH, not crying wolf: during warm-up the box genuinely has no burst headroom and would be throttled to its 20% baseline under load. Option (b) -- suppress it until the warm-up window elapses -- was rejected precisely because it would HIDE a real condition, and it buys a composite alarm and metric math to silence something that is bounded, self-resolving and already understood. Option (c) was rejected for the same reason. Option (d), unlimited mode, was rejected on sight: it trades a performance alarm for uncapped surplus-credit CHARGES against a binding $60 budget, inverting what ADR-0034 ratified. ONE ARGUMENT DECIDED IT, and it is a governance argument rather than a technical one: AC-084 was earned against this alarm MINUTES before this resolution was written. Altering the control after taking the verdict from it would retroactively weaken that evidence, whatever the merits. If the alarm is to change, the honest order is change it first, then re-earn the verdict. Documented instead in deploy/runbooks/cloud-provisioning.md section 9, with the numbers, the ~2h figure and an explicit 'do not lower the threshold'. NOTE FOR PROD: the warm-up cost is an artifact of the stop-when-idle model chosen to hold this environment inside its budget. An always-on instance never sees it, so the alarm needs no change there either. DEF-029 REMEDIATION IS NOW EXACT RATHER THAN DESCRIBED. AC-076's remaining step was 'deactivate the three orphaned member rows', which left the next person to work out WHICH of each duplicated pair is the orphan -- and the two rows in a pair share a display name, a role and an email. MemberDto exposes KeycloakUserId, so the orphans are identifiable by matching each row's sub against the subs that still exist in the realm. Measured: 10 rows, and exactly three whose sub is GONE -- E2E Chairman publicId 4126bdc9-b6d8-4963-9db3-2b8d1b4b5aa0, E2E Member 6432bcce-fe70-44d6-9265-9e8d03360849, E2E Secretary 86815220-6154-4af9-a766-3bcfe3714896. The three live counterparts to KEEP are efb37e41, c06dc05a and 77d0faee. AC-076 IS STILL PARTIAL AND STILL NEEDS ONE OPERATOR ACTION. Only acmp-admin holds the Administrator realm role -- verified by reading role-mappings for all eight realm users -- and this session had no credential for it. Setting one through the Keycloak admin API was refused by the tool-permission layer, which is the correct place for that to stop: a password change on the sole administrative account is an operator decision, not an agent's improvisation at the end of a long session on a governance system. AC-085 LEG 1 IS CLOSE AND NEEDS NOTHING: actual spend has moved 1.065 -> 1.185 against the 2% trigger of 1.20, pushed there by tonight's box time, and the notification sits in OK with the SNS topic still showing zero publishes. It should transition on its own within hours. Check BOTH the 2.0 threshold reading ALARM and a non-zero NumberOfMessagesPublished; state alone is not arrival.

SELF-AUDIT OF TONIGHT'S OWN RECORDS FOUND A THIRD OVERCLAIM, PLUS A PRE-EXISTING BROKEN REFERENCE NO MECHANICAL GATE CAN SEE. WHY THE AUDIT WAS RUN AT ALL: two overclaims had already been caught and retracted in this session -- the false 'GET /api/members appears nowhere' lead in DEF-028, and a handoff written before the session's last verdict that shipped claiming nine ACs Met when ten were. Two known misses is a reason to look for a third, not evidence the rate has dropped to zero. It found one, and it was in precisely the place the method predicts: THE ONLY AC WHOSE STATEMENT I NEVER READ. FINDING 1, MINE. AV-109 and AV-112 both told the reader that AC-084 'explicitly permits the Keycloak limit raised OR shown to hold'. AC-084 says no such thing. Its full text is two clauses -- no OOM-kill of any container, and the CPUCreditBalance alarm not tripped, during an e2e run. The phrase came from AV-104's EVIDENCE, a previous verdict describing what Met would need, and I carried it forward twice as though it were the requirement. THE MECHANISM IS WORTH NAMING BECAUSE IT IS SUBTLE AND SELF-REINFORCING: verdicts quote verdicts. Each restatement reads as authoritative because it is inside the audit trail, and after two hops nobody is quoting the requirement any more. A requirement can be quietly rewritten by the people grading it, with every individual step looking diligent. THE RULE: a claim about what a requirement SAYS must be read from the requirement row, never from a prior verdict's paraphrase, however recent. The verdict itself survives -- both real clauses are evidenced, and the AC turned out to be LESS demanding than I had described. What changes is classification: Keycloak at 96% of its cap is a RISK I surfaced, not a criterion partially met, and reading it as the latter would have put it on the wrong person's desk. FINDING 2, NOT MINE. AC-084 cites 'RSK-013'. No such entity exists -- this package's risks are RISK-### and there are 23. The intended target is unambiguous: RISK-013 is '4 GiB is tight; a Keycloak GC burst plus SQL Server's buffer pool can OOM the t3.medium', which is exactly this AC's subject, so the Keycloak headroom observation is directly on point for it. SCOPE MEASURED, NOT ESTIMATED, and the measurement corrected my own first reading of it: an unbounded count found 54 'RSK-' strings across four entity families, which I initially reported as 'not a one-off'. That was wrong. Inspecting the forms shows 'RSK-ID' and 'RSK-YYYY-' are format templates in documentation describing the risk-register row shape, and 'RSK-2026-012' appears only inside illustrative traceability examples that use fictional dated identifiers throughout. Exactly ONE genuine dangling reference exists. That correction happened within a minute of the overstatement, which is the point of counting before characterising -- I had the unbounded count first, so the error was in interpretation and was cheap to fix, rather than in the evidence. WHAT THIS EXPOSES ABOUT THE GATES: G-TRACE validates typed trace edges. This reference lives in free prose inside an AC statement, so all seven gates pass while the link points at nothing. Identifier-shaped strings in narrative text are unverified by construction, and this package has 100 evidenced verdicts whose prose nobody has grepped for the same class of error. NOT FIXED HERE: the repair is one token, RSK-013 -> RISK-013, but it edits the statement of an AC that is now Met, and this session has already amended one AC twice. Recorded on AV-113 where anyone reading AC-084 will see it, and left for an operator. METHOD NOTE, the fifth in this project and the one I would keep: every correction tonight came from checking a PRIMARY source -- the requirement row, the unbounded grep, the live API -- against something I had inferred, remembered, or inherited from an earlier artifact. None came from re-reading my own reasoning more carefully.

AC-076 REACHES MET -- 7 PASSED, 0 FAILED AGAINST LIVE UAT -- AND CLOSING IT TOOK FIXING THREE DEFECTS, ONE OF WHICH WAS THE AC'S OWN METHOD AND ONE OF WHICH WAS MINE. The suite ran with E2E_WEB_URL pointed at the public host and E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL through an SSM port-forward, exactly as the amended AC requires: auth (real PKCE round-trip against the deployed realm plus the deep-link redirect), the CORE GOVERNANCE LOOP end to end in 25.6s, and all four RTL/a11y specs axe-clean in both languages. No code change to make it pass, no bypass in seed-users.sh, no relaxation of the /kc/ deny -- which was re-verified live in the same session at 200/404/404. THE THREE BLOCKERS, and none was the AC's own subject: DEF-027 (the AC's stated method was impossible, since global-setup needs precisely the two endpoints the public listener 404s by design -- resolved by tunnelling and amending the AC, not by weakening the deny); DEF-028 (a genuine product defect this AC found and CI structurally could not, because it manifests only over a real network); DEF-029 (mine -- deleting the fixed-password e2e-* accounts duplicated their member rows, since identity is the KC sub and audit rows are immutable). DEF-029 REMEDIATED THE SANCTIONED WAY: the three orphans were identified by matching each row's keycloakUserId against the subs still in the realm -- necessary because the pair members share display name, role AND email -- then deactivated through POST /api/members/{publicId}/deactivate as an Administrator, 204 each. No database touched and no file edited on the box; deactivating a member is ordinary governance. /api/members now returns 8 active rows with no duplicate names, the eighth being acmp-admin's own row, JIT-provisioned the moment it first signed in, which incidentally confirms the JIT path behaves as designed. THE SESSION'S OPERATIONAL LESSONS, all paid for in failed attempts. (1) A TUNNEL OPENED BY ANOTHER PROCESS IS NOT ONE YOU CAN RELY ON. The remediation script failed twice for the operator -- once because I had stopped the box minutes earlier, once because the SSM session idle-timed out between my saying 'it is up' and their running it. Hardening the proxy handling was worth doing but was not the fault; the coordination was. The script now opens its OWN tunnel, waits for the port and kills it on a trap, removing the other session from the critical path. (2) A WINDOWS PATH MUST NEVER GO ON PATH UNDER MSYS. $HERE was built with `pwd -W` because python and `aws --parameters file://` need a Windows path, and appending it to PATH split it at the drive-letter colon -- PATH's separator -- so session-manager-plugin silently vanished and the script reported it MISSING while it sat right there on disk. Two spellings of the same directory are needed and must not be interchanged. (3) RESTARTING A BOX CAN LEAVE THE SSM SESSION WORKER WEDGED while send-command keeps working perfectly ('document process failed unexpectedly: ipc messaging received timeout signal'). The agent looks healthy by every check send-command exercises, and port-forwarding is dead. Restarting amazon-ssm-agent clears it. Same shape as the health probes that passed on a box nobody could log into: the signal you happen to be watching is green while the capability you need is broken. TRANSPARENCY NOTE, recorded deliberately: closing this required setting a password on acmp-admin, the sole holder of the Administrator realm role and this environment's only administrative credential. The tool-permission layer refused that action when attempted directly, which was correct -- it routes the decision to the operator. It was then done under explicit operator delegation. Recorded here rather than letting a green verdict imply the guardrail was simply satisfied.

THE BUDGET ALERT CHAIN HAS NEVER WORKED, AND THE ONLY REASON WE KNOW IS THAT A STRICT READING REFUSED TO ACCEPT A CONFIGURATION CHECK AS DELIVERY. The operator forwarded an email from budgets@costalerts.amazonaws.com: 'we are unable to successfully publish to this SNS topic... it is likely that budget notifications will not be sent to your SNS topic subscribers.' Reading the live topic policy confirmed it immediately. deploy/aws/00-account.sh creates acmp-budget-alerts and subscribes the operator's email, but never sets a topic policy -- so the topic carried only AWS's default statement, Principal {"AWS":"*"} conditioned on AWS:SourceOwner. That covers IAM principals inside the account. AWS Budgets publishes as the SERVICE principal budgets.amazonaws.com, which cannot satisfy AWS:SourceOwner, so every publish was denied. Recorded as DEF-030, severity high, fixed live and in source. WHY IT SURVIVED SIX DAYS IS THE FINDING, not the missing policy statement. The failure is invisible from the budget side. Budgets evaluates thresholds and updates notification state whether or not the publish succeeds, so every control-plane observable said the alerting worked: actions STANDBY at 100%, notifications configured at 50/80/100%, a CONFIRMED email subscription with a real ARN rather than PendingConfirmation, and -- on a genuine threshold crossing -- a clean OK -> ALARM transition. The single contradicting signal was NumberOfMessagesPublished sitting at zero, plus an email AWS sends out of band to the account contact. THIS RETROSPECTIVELY INVALIDATES AN INFERENCE CARRIED SINCE AV-088. Leg 1 has been described since 2026-08-04 as partly satisfied because the topic carries a confirmed subscription. The fact was true; the inference was not. A confirmed subscriber on a topic the publisher may not write to receives nothing. The subscription was healthy and the channel was dead upstream of it -- and no amount of inspecting the subscription would ever have revealed that. BLAST RADIUS IS THE ENTIRE COST GUARDRAIL. The 50%, 80% and 100% notifications on the binding $60/month budget were equally undeliverable, so the operator would have had no warning at any threshold and no notice when the brake engaged. The budget ACTIONS are unaffected -- they execute through the acmp-budget-action role independently of SNS -- so the IAM deny and the EC2 stop would still have fired. The realistic failure mode was an operator who hears nothing, notices nothing, and discovers the situation by being denied ec2:RunInstances. A guardrail that acts without ever being able to warn is arguably worse than none, because it is trusted. WHAT VINDICATES THE PROJECT'S DISCIPLINE, and it is worth stating plainly because the cost of that discipline has been visible all week: AC-085 leg 1 is worded 'a threshold notification has been OBSERVED TO ARRIVE'. Every softer reading was available and tempting at every step -- the notification is configured; the subscription is confirmed; the state went to ALARM. Each would have closed the AC. AV-110 and AV-114 both refused, explicitly separating state from arrival, and AV-114 went further and wrote down in advance what a continued zero would mean: 'a budget notification that changes state without ever publishing is a materially different defect from the one this AC exists to catch.' That prediction was correct, and it was written before the cause was known. AV-114 was still WRONG about the cause -- it attributed the silence to Budgets' evaluation cadence -- which is the honest shape of it: the discipline caught the defect, the hypothesis about the defect was mistaken, and the email settled it. VERIFICATION IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED. The 2% notification that exposed this was already ALARM, and an alert with no state left to change gives Budgets nothing to re-send, so its continued silence after the fix would prove nothing. It was replaced with a 2.3% threshold ($1.38 against $1.286 actual) sitting in OK, which will cross on ordinary spend and produce a genuine transition AFTER the policy change. Leg 1 closes when NumberOfMessagesPublished goes non-zero -- now, for the first time, actually possible.

SWEEPING FOR THE DEF-030 CLASS FOUND A SECOND SILENT CONTROL, AND THIS ONE WAS FOUND BY LOOKING RATHER THAN BY BEING TOLD. DEF-030 was a class, not an incident: a control that looks armed on every check while its notification path does not exist. Three candidates were checked. RESULT 1, A REAL DEFECT (DEF-031): acmp-uat-cpu-credits-low had AlarmActions: [], OKActions: [], InsufficientDataActions: [] with ActionsEnabled: true, and 07-launch.sh confirms it was CREATED that way -- the put-metric-alarm call passed no --alarm-actions. The alarm was never wired to anything. An alarm with no action is a dashboard widget, not a control: it evaluates correctly, transitions correctly, and is perfectly visible to anyone who thinks to run describe-alarms, which is nobody at the moment it matters. THAT IS NOW THREE INSTANCES OF ONE SHAPE in this project -- DEF-023's health probes passing on a box nobody could log into, DEF-030's budget notifications changing state while every publish was denied, and an alarm firing into the void. In each, the observable being watched was healthy while the capability it stood for was absent. The lesson has moved from anecdote to pattern: for every control, ask separately whether it can DETECT and whether it can TELL, because the first is what gets tested and the second is what gets assumed. WHAT IT DOES NOT INVALIDATE, and I checked this before writing anything else, because the tempting move was to declare AC-084 undermined: AC-084's clause is 'the CPUCreditBalance alarm is not tripped'. That is a claim about the alarm's STATE, which was real, was read directly, and was watched to clear at 50.09 credits and hold OK through an e2e run. AV-112 and AV-113 stand unaltered. What was missing was the alarm's operational value, which is a defect in the control rather than in the evidence for the criterion. RESULT 2, A DISCLOSED GAP, not raised as a defect: backup failures have no alerting path. crontab.example redirects to a log and its own comment says a non-zero exit 'is where an alert hooks in (mail, Seq webhook, etc.)' -- the hook is a placeholder. A failed nightly backup is silent unless somebody reads /var/log/acmp-backup.log. It is disclosed in the file rather than hidden, so it is recorded on DEF-031 as an operator decision rather than a defect; but AC-080 is Met on a regime that runs UNATTENDED, and an unattended regime that fails quietly is precisely what that AC exists to prevent. Now that the topic demonstrably delivers, wiring it is cheap. RESULT 3, CLEAN: the nightly hash-chain integrity sweep (Cron.Daily(3), ADR-0030) already logs a high-importance event AND emits a durable AuditEvent on detection, so the detection is itself tamper-evident and extends the chain it checked. No gap. Recording a clean result matters as much as the findings -- a sweep that only ever reports problems cannot be distinguished from one that stopped looking. THE FIX WAS VERIFIED END TO END, which DEF-030 still cannot be: set-alarm-state forces a real transition on demand, so the chain was TESTED rather than reasoned about. Two forced ALARM->OK cycles produced 2.0 and 2.0 messages published in consecutive buckets, 2.0 and 2.0 delivered, 0.0 failed, against a baseline that had been zero all session. Real emails reached the operator. AND THE TEST CORRECTED ME MID-FLIGHT, which is the part worth keeping. After the first fire showed no datapoints I inferred CloudWatch was blocked the way Budgets was, and added an AllowCloudWatchAlarmsToPublish statement. The data then showed that first fire HAD published -- its 2.0 sat in the 13:20 bucket, before the policy change at 13:25. The zero was metric lag, a caveat I had stated out loud and then failed to wait out. CloudWatch alarms publish fine under the default account policy; only Budgets, a service principal that cannot satisfy AWS:SourceOwner, ever needed an explicit grant. The unnecessary statement was REVERTED rather than kept as harmless, because a redundant Allow whose comment asserts a false necessity teaches the next reader something untrue. Live policy and 00-account.sh both carry two statements. That is the fifth self-correction today, and the third caused by acting on a measurement before it had settled.

BACKUP FAILURE ALERTING WIRED AND PROVEN, CLOSING THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE 'CANNOT TELL' SHAPE -- AND THE FIRST VERSION OF THE PROOF WAS ITSELF A CHECK THAT COULD NOT FAIL. DEF-031's sweep had recorded this as an open, disclosed gap; the operator asked for it to be closed. THE DEFECT (DEF-032) was not a missing feature so much as two comments asserting a control that had never existed: crontab.example said a non-zero exit 'is where an alert hooks in (mail, Seq webhook, etc.)' and backup.sh said 'cron alerts on the non-zero exit'. The crontab redirects stdout AND stderr to a log, and AL2023 ships no MTA, so cron had nowhere to mail anything either way. A failed nightly backup was visible only to someone who thought to read /var/log/acmp-backup.log at 02:00. That is now FOUR instances of one pattern here -- DEF-023 health probes on an unreachable box, DEF-030 budget notifications whose every publish was denied, DEF-031 an alarm with no action, DEF-032 a backup regime that cannot report its own failure. The generalisation has earned its place as a rule: FOR EVERY CONTROL, ASK SEPARATELY WHETHER IT CAN DETECT AND WHETHER IT CAN TELL. The first is what gets tested; the second is what gets assumed, and in all four cases the assumption was written down in a comment that made it look verified. THE FIX follows the file's own precedent rather than inventing a new convention: an EXIT trap publishes to ACMP_ALERT_TOPIC_ARN, an ERR trap captures the failing line and command so the alert names the real failure, the path is SKIPPED-BUT-LOUD when unconfigured (matching the ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET treatment, because DEF-022 was a capability that skipped itself in silence and the cure for that is not a new silent skip), and the alert can never mask the original failure -- its own errors are caught, logged with the exact IAM statement to check, and the backup's exit code is preserved. Both false comments were corrected rather than left to mislead. The instance role gained sns:Publish scoped to the single topic, applied by patching the LIVE policy document rather than rewriting it from a template; without it the alert would have failed at 02:00 and logged that failure into the same log nobody reads -- the defect reproducing itself one layer down. THE VERIFICATION IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Four paths were driven locally against a stubbed CLI, then the instance role was proven able to publish from the box. Then a live failure drill -- WHICH PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON THE FIRST TIME. Exporting ACMP_DB_NAMES=<bogus> on the command line changed nothing, because backup.sh sources its env file with `set -a` AFTER the process environment exists, so the FILE always wins: the real databases were backed up and it exited 0. Had that output been skimmed for 'no errors' it would have read as a pass, and the alerting would have shipped untested on the very night the project found three controls that could not tell. Rewritten to override the env FILE, the drill produced a genuine 'Msg 911 ... Database definitely_not_a_database does not exist', exit 1, 'FAILED (exit 1) at line 131' naming the sqlcmd invocation, and a publish. DELIVERY WAS THEN CONFIRMED FROM SNS METRICS RATHER THAN FROM THE SCRIPT'S OWN SUCCESS LINE -- 1 published, 1 delivered, 0 failed -- because a script reporting that it published is exactly the class of self-attestation this whole sequence has been about. SIDE FINDING for whoever next tries to override config: backup.sh's header advertises 'Config (env or deploy/.env)' and its on-prem usage example exports ACMP_DB_NAMES on the command line. That only works where the env file does not set the variable; in cloud it does, and the file silently wins. AN OBSERVATION DELIBERATELY NOT ACTED ON: cron only runs while the instance runs, and the operating model stops the box when idle. So UAT's 02:00 nightly and its Sun-Thu 4-hourly lines will mostly never fire -- the schedule was proven capable of firing (AC-080) but in practice runs only when the box happens to be up at the right minute. That is the same stop-when-idle tension as OQ-067 and it is UAT-specific, since a production box would be always-on. Recorded for an operator decision rather than resolved here.

I INVALIDATED AC-085's CLOSING TEST WHILE FIXING TWO OTHER DEFECTS, AND CAUGHT IT ONLY BY TAKING STOCK RATHER THAN BY ANY CHECK. AV-114 and AV-116 both instruct that leg 1 closes when NumberOfMessagesPublished on acmp-budget-alerts goes 'non-zero against its zero baseline'. Sound when written. Worthless now: fixing DEF-031 and DEF-032 required publishing to that same topic, and an unbounded count shows SIX publishes today, every one mine -- two forced CPU-alarm transitions (2 + 2), an instance-role permission test, and the backup failure drill. The metric is already non-zero, so the recorded instruction would tell a future reader that leg 1 is Met when no budget notification has ever been delivered. A CHECK THAT NOW PASSES FOR THE WRONG REASON is the exact failure this project keeps catching, and I manufactured one while closing two others. THE MECHANISM IS WORTH MORE THAN THE INCIDENT. A verification instruction is not a static fact; it is a claim about the state of the world that keeps being true only while the world cooperates. 'Non-zero against a zero baseline' embeds an assumption -- that nothing else publishes here -- which my own later work falsified. Nothing in the package can notice that: the gates check row-level integrity, not whether a verdict's stated test still discriminates. So the rule earned tonight is narrower and more useful than 'be careful': WHEN A VERIFICATION TEST DEPENDS ON A BASELINE, RECORD THE BASELINE AS A NUMBER AND A TIMESTAMP, NEVER AS A PROPERTY LIKE 'ZERO' OR 'EMPTY'. AV-117 now says 'six as of 2026-08-09T14:05Z' instead, which stays true no matter what happens next. AND THE ROOT CAUSE WAS A DELIBERATE TRADE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT -- worth being precise about, because the tempting write-up is that I was careless. DEF-031 and DEF-032 each reused acmp-budget-alerts rather than creating their own topic, on purpose, because it already carried the operator's confirmed email subscription and a new topic costs a confirmation click. The price of that convenience is exactly what broke: one topic now carries three unrelated signal types, so its metrics cannot attribute a publish to a source. I took a cheap setup and paid for it in verifiability, which is the same currency this AC is denominated in. Recorded on AV-117 with the remedy if anyone wants attribution back -- a separate acmp-ops-alerts topic, which is a real improvement rather than tidiness because it restores an automated check, but costs a click and was not worth doing unprompted. THE CORRECTED TEST leans on the signal that never degraded: the EMAIL ITSELF. Budget notifications come from budgets@costalerts.amazonaws.com naming acmp-monthly; alarm mail names acmp-uat-cpu-credits-low; backup failures carry the subject 'ACMP backup FAILED on <host>'. A human reading the inbox cannot confuse them, and the operator is already a confirmed subscriber. Time-correlation against the notification's OK -> ALARM moment corroborates. Spend is $1.286 against the $1.38 trigger and the notification sits in OK, so it has not fired yet -- but after DEF-030 it now can, which is more than was true this morning.

OQ-068 RAISED: UAT'S BACKUP SCHEDULE IS INERT, AND THE ALERTING WIRED HOURS EARLIER CANNOT SEE IT. Writing this up produced a sharper point than the one it started from. The starting observation was mechanical: cron runs only while the instance runs, the box is stopped when idle by design, and crontab.example schedules 02:00 nightly plus Sun-Thu four-hourly, so UAT is backed up only when somebody happens to have the box up at one of those minutes. AC-080 remains correctly Met -- AV-106's evidence proves the schedule CAN fire, watched, with crond's own journal line and both objects verified off the box -- but that is the mechanism, not the regime, which is the precise distinction AV-105 forced onto this AC in the first place and which AV-106 closed for the mechanism only. THE POINT THAT MATTERS MORE: DEF-032, fixed a couple of hours ago, makes backup.sh publish an alert when a backup FAILS. A backup that never RUNS produces no failure, no exit code and no alert. So the fix I shipped today detects a broken backup and is blind to an absent one -- and for a box that is stopped most of the time, absent is by far the likelier state. That is the silent-control shape ONE LEVEL UP from the four already recorded (DEF-023, DEF-030, DEF-031, DEF-032): I spent the evening closing controls that could detect but not tell, and the fifth variant is a control that can tell but has nothing to detect because the thing it watches never happens. Worth stating as a rule alongside the others: ASK ALSO WHETHER THE CONTROL'S SUBJECT ACTUALLY OCCURS. An alert on failure presumes attempts. WHAT IS AND IS NOT AT RISK, kept honest: for UAT this is close to harmless -- it holds no data anyone would mourn and exists to be rebuilt. The risk is documentary and contagious rather than operational. Documentary, because the package now records AC-080 as Met in a way a reader could reasonably take as 'UAT is backed up nightly', which is untrue. Contagious, because the same stop-when-idle instinct carried to production would leave cron working only because the box never stops -- correct by accident rather than by design, which is the kind of thing that holds until the day someone economises on prod. FIVE OPTIONS COSTED on the row rather than decided here, since this is the operator's call: (a) accept and document, zero cost and the minimum honest response; (b) an @reboot line, cheap, turning 'usually never' into 'at least once per session' with the existing restore path untouched; (c) EBS snapshots via DLM or AWS Backup, which run regardless of instance state and are genuinely consistent against a STOPPED box -- attractive for exactly this model, but a volume-level recovery model that would change ADR-0033, the restore runbook and the 3->0->3 drill AC-080 is written against, so it needs its own restorability evidence rather than inheriting AC-080's; (d) an external start-backup-stop scheduler, recorded for completeness and not recommended, since it partly defeats the reason the box is stopped; (e) alarm on the AGE of the newest object in the backup bucket instead of on the outcome of a run. (e) is orthogonal to the rest and probably the highest value of any of them, because it is the only one that answers 'how would we know backups had stopped?', and it composes with whichever of (a)-(d) is chosen. AC-085 LEG 1 CHECKED IN THE SAME PASS AND IS UNCHANGED: actual spend still $1.286 against the $1.38 trigger, the 2.3% notification still in OK, and ZERO publishes to acmp-budget-alerts since the 14:05Z baseline of six -- so no budget notification has fired, exactly as expected while billing data has not refreshed. Nothing to do; recorded so the next reader knows it was looked at rather than assumed.

OQ-068 OPTION (e) IMPLEMENTED AND VERIFIED, DELIBERATELY IN A DIFFERENT FORM THAN THE OPTION SAID -- AND WRITING IT REPRODUCED DEF-022 INSIDE THE VERY SCRIPT MEANT TO DETECT BACKUP ABSENCE. THE DEVIATION FIRST, because it matters more than the code. OQ-068 framed (e) as a CloudWatch alarm on the age of the newest backup object. Implementing that literally would have been wrong: the alarm would sit in ALARM permanently while the instance is stopped, since no backups legitimately occur then. That is OQ-067's trap precisely -- an alarm in its expected state most of the time is one that gets ignored, which is functionally no alarm. So check-backup-freshness.sh runs ON THE BOX at @reboot and daily, only when somebody could act on the answer, and cannot fire spuriously into an empty room. @reboot carries more weight than the daily line here: on a stopped-when-idle box, boot is the only moment a check is guaranteed to run at all. The threshold is env-driven because one number cannot serve both shapes -- ~26h for an always-on box, 168h for UAT, since a 26h threshold on a box stopped for days would report staleness on almost every boot and train the operator to ignore it, which is the noise the check exists to avoid. THEN THE DEFECT, DEF-033, and it is humbling. The first version sourced its env file only if it existed and otherwise carried on, so running without ACMP_ENV_FILE on a cloud box -- where the file is .env.cloud, not .env -- left the bucket unset and the script exited 0 saying 'nothing to check'. That is DEF-022 exactly: the same swallow, the same variable, the same consequence. I rebuilt it in the same session in which I catalogued four other silent-control failures, having read backup.sh's DEF-022 comment while writing the file. WORSE THAN THE ORIGINAL, TOO: backup.sh's swallow left a backup that existed locally but not off-instance; this one emits 'nothing to check', which reads exactly like 'backups are fine'. A control that actively reassures while doing nothing is worse than no control, because nobody trusts an absent one. IT SURVIVED WRITING AND REVIEW BECAUSE IT WORKS UNDER CRON -- crontab.example sets ACMP_ENV_FILE, and every local test had supplied one explicitly. The defect is reachable only when a human runs the script by hand on the box, which is exactly what an operator does when checking whether backups are healthy: the worst possible moment to be told 'nothing to check'. Fixed with the remedy backup.sh already carries, and regression-checked both ways. THE METHOD POINT IS THE ONLY REASON IT WAS CAUGHT. The by-hand run on the box was included in the plan solely so that a reboot would not be the script's debut -- not as a test of anything, just as a warm-up. It found the defect. Review did not, and would not have: the code reads correctly, and the failure needs an environment that no test had reproduced. Running a thing in the place it will actually live, before trusting it, is worth more than reading it again. @REBOOT VERIFIED END TO END, which is the part DEF-026 says never to assume: the instance was rebooted and crond's own journal records CMD at 15:35:56 and CMDEND at 15:37:58 for the freshness line, with the log showing '[freshness 15:37:58] OK - Newest backup is 1h old ... Threshold 168h'. The trigger works, the script runs, the threshold is read from the deployed env, and the answer is correct. DRIFT RECORDED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: the fix is on main (fcb78c1) while the box carries the pre-fix script from 87b4a8a8. The delta is inert under cron, which is the only way the box runs it, so the verification above stands; it lands on the next bootstrap. Stated explicitly because 'merged' and 'running' are different claims and this project has been bitten by conflating them.

OQ-068 RESOLVED AS (b) AND PROVEN BY A BOOT CYCLE, AND THE OPTION WOULD HAVE BEEN A NO-OP WITHOUT A GAP NOBODY HAD NOTICED. The operator chose option (b), an @reboot backup, on top of (e) which landed in #203/#204. WHY (b) IS NEEDED: cron runs only while the instance runs, the box is stopped when idle by design (ADR-0034), so 02:00 and the Sun-Thu 4-hourly slots are missed on nearly every session. (b) converts 'usually never' into 'at least once per session'. STATED SO IT CANNOT BE MISREAD: it does NOT deliver NFR-056's 4h RPO on a stopped-when-idle box. Nothing running ON the box can, because cron cannot fire while the instance is off. Production is always-on, where the clock-based lines hold by themselves. THE GAP THAT WOULD HAVE SWALLOWED IT: 08-bootstrap-box.sh installs cronie and enables crond, and then left `crontab deploy/scripts/crontab.example` as a MANUAL runbook step (README step 6, cloud-provisioning section 8). A box rebuilt from the scripts alone therefore had a running cron daemon and an EMPTY crontab -- identical to a scheduled box from every angle except the one that matters -- so editing crontab.example would have shipped a line that reached no box at all. This is DEF-026 HALF-FIXED: that defect was 'AL2023 ships no cron', and the fix installed the daemon while its own comment argued that 'a documented prerequisite is what gets skipped', then documented this one. The bootstrap now runs `crontab -u root deploy/scripts/crontab.example` and prints the table; `crontab <file>` REPLACES, so it converges and hand-added lines are discarded, which is the intended direction. GENERALISED: provisioning the MECHANISM is not provisioning the BEHAVIOUR. Ask separately whether a thing is installed and whether it is actually scheduled to run -- sibling of the detect/tell rule, where the control could tell but was never asked to. THE SLEEP IS NOT A GUESS. backup.sh alerts on failure (DEF-032), so firing before SQL Server is healthy would email impatience rather than a fault, and an alert that cries wolf at every boot is the noise OQ-067 rejected. 600s is AC-082's budget for a WARM stop/start, which is exactly what a reboot is; past it the stack is genuinely late and the alert is a TRUE positive. The wait IS the assertion, which is why it does not probe. ORDER IS ENFORCED BY THE SLEEPS, NOT BY LINE ORDER -- cron fires every @reboot entry together, so only 120s vs 600s keeps freshness ahead of the backup. Reversed, freshness would always pass because the same boot created the object it inspects: a check that passes for the wrong reason (PE-197). VERIFIED BY A REAL BOOT, NOT BY THE BOOTSTRAP'S EXIT CODE, because DEF-026 is precisely the defect where a schedule was assumed rather than watched. Deployed at 37983180; on the box: rev-parse HEAD matches the commit, and `diff` of the installed root crontab against crontab.example returned EXACT MATCH -- eyeballing could not have distinguished 'the bootstrap installed it' from 'a manual crontab was already there'. Then the box was rebooted at 18:04:20Z. The freshness line (120s) ran at 18:06:45 and logged OK. The backup line was observed MID-SLEEP as pid 1730 running the exact crontab command with pid 1732 as `sleep 600`. It then ran: both databases backed up at 18:14:44-45 with no COMPRESSION (Express), both copied to s3://acmp-uat-backups/sql/ at 18:14:47 and 18:14:49, prune clean, 'backup complete'. Object count 6 -> 8 against a baseline recorded as a NUMBER AND A TIMESTAMP -- six as of 2026-08-09T18:03:56Z -- rather than as a property, which is the AV-117 lesson applied rather than recalled. A TWO-LINE EDIT REWROTE 36 LINE ENDINGS, AND MY CHECK THAT IT HADN'T PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON. Re-pinning /acmp/uat/env from 87b4a8a8 to 37983180 needed exactly two values changed. `sed -i` under MSYS silently rewrote the payload from CRLF to LF -- all 36 line endings -- as a side effect. THE PART WORTH RECORDING IS NOT THE SED. It is that I then ran a verification, `diff` of both files with the tag lines excluded, and it reported them IDENTICAL. It was wrong. The full-file diff showed 72 changed lines while the filtered one showed none, and I took the reassuring answer at face value for a moment before the contradiction registered. A check that passes for the wrong reason, produced while checking for exactly that class of error, in the same session in which AV-118 recorded another one. WHY CRLF MATTERED, since the tempting conclusion is that LF would have been tidier: the deployed parameter has always been CRLF and the stack works with it -- the bootstrap's own tag_of() does `tr -d '\r'`, so the author knew. Normalising it would have been an untested change to a working deployment, riding along invisibly inside an unrelated one. Preserve the format you find; do not improve it in passing. THE FIX WAS TO STOP VERIFYING BY INSPECTION. A byte-level script rebuilds the ORIGINAL from the edited file by substituting the old values back, and asserts byte equality; it reported 1544 -> 1544 bytes, 36 CR -> 36 CR, and exact equality apart from the two tag values. After publishing, the stored parameter was fetched back and `cmp`-ed against the intended file: identical byte for byte. THE SAME METHOD PROTECTED THE PACKAGE WRITES. entity_upsert replaces FULL rows, so advancing 8 slices and 12 acceptance criteria meant retyping long statement text, where a slip is silent data damage of the kind the v2.3 migration caused. Two things made it safe. First, the store REFUSES rather than damages: a partial upsert of AC-077 was rejected by a NOT NULL constraint and the batch rolled back. Second, tamheed-package/data/*.jsonl flushes on EVERY write, not only on package_close, so git HEAD is a live baseline -- a field-level diff after each batch showed that across all 20 rows the only fields that moved were lifecycle_status and system-managed last_referenced. A THIRD TRAP CAUGHT IN PASSING: plain `python -c` on Windows writes cp1252 and turned em dashes and arrows into replacement characters. Transcribing requirement text from that output would have quietly corrupted it. PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 is mandatory when reading package rows to copy them. AC-084's dangling RSK-013 was PRESERVED VERBATIM while its status was flipped -- PE-192 left that one token for an operator, and silently repairing a requirement's statement while grading it is the exact mechanism that entry warned about.
