"ALL" WAS ACCEPTED AS A PROGRAM AND THE FIRST PASS IMMEDIATELY CORRECTED THREE THINGS I HAD MYSELF PUT IN THE OPTIONS LIST. Checking before acting was the whole value of the pass; two of the three items I had offered turned out to be wrong, and one turned out to be much bigger than I had framed it. FINDING 1, AND IT RESHAPES THE ROADMAP CONVERSATION: PH-5 IS NOT NEARLY COMPLETE, AND PRODUCTION IS NOT A NEW MILESTONE. I had described PH-5 as essentially finished with one observation outstanding, and offered 'stand up production' as a separate next step. PH-5's own row says otherwise. Its objective names TWO internet-facing environments -- uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev AND acmp.anas7ammo.dev -- and its exit criteria open with 'BOTH environments reachable over HTTPS on their subdomains with a green smoke run'. Production is therefore the unbuilt HALF of the phase currently in flight, not follow-on scope. MEASURED rather than assumed: the prod S3 buckets exist (acmp-prod-backups, acmp-prod-recordings), per-environment IAM exists, and CI publishes web:<sha>-prod on every merge -- but Route 53 holds an A record for uat only, and describe-instances returns exactly one instance. So prod is provisioned at the account layer and absent at the runtime layer. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PACKAGE: PH-5's lifecycle_status of Approved is CORRECT and must NOT be advanced. I had listed it as stale by analogy with the slice rows I fixed earlier, which was reasoning from a pattern instead of from the row -- the same shape as the AC-084 paraphrase PE-192 caught. The 8 PH-5 SLICES are legitimately Implemented (each built its capability, and the scripts are environment-parameterised, taking <uat|prod>); the PHASE is not, because a capability that has never been instantiated for prod does not satisfy an exit criterion written about environments. FINDING 2: PH-3 IS ALSO CORRECTLY 'Approved', NOT DRIFT. I had flagged it as suspicious for having zero slices. It is the future AI / advanced-analytics phase -- primary value 'Intelligence & advanced analytics', matching DW-003 (AI candidate extraction) and AGENTS.md's 'AI extraction = Phase 3'. Approved-and-unbuilt is exactly right for a phase nobody has started. The confusion was a NAME COLLISION: PH-3 is titled 'Research & Knowledge' and so is slice SL-015 ('P15 - Research & Knowledge'), which shipped early under PH-2. Two different things wearing one name. FINDING 3: DW-022 IS NOT SELF-CONTRADICTORY. I had reported it as a register error -- status Open while its own body concludes the work is unnecessary. Misread. In this register Open means DEFERRED AND STILL AVAILABLE, not outstanding obligation; the row's activation trigger says plainly that the CSP rationale is disproven but a design-system pass may still elect to take the hygiene on. The status is accurate and nothing needed fixing. ONLY PH-2 WAS GENUINELY STALE, and it is now Implemented: SL-013 and SL-015 are Implemented and SL-014 is Deferred indefinitely by DEC-028, so its buildable content is complete -- and leaving it Approved while the LATER PH-4 read Implemented was the actual inconsistency. Its objective and exit_criteria are null in the package, so no invented bar was written to justify the change.

THE ONE-TOKEN RSK-013 REPAIR IS NOW BLOCKED BY IMMUTABILITY, AND I CAUSED THAT MYSELF EARLIER TODAY. PE-192 found that AC-084's statement cites 'RSK-013', which matches no entity -- this package's risks are RISK-###, and RISK-013 ('4 GiB is tight; a Keycloak GC burst plus SQL Server's buffer pool can OOM the t3.medium') is unambiguously the intended target. PE-192 deliberately left the repair for an operator. Instructed to make it, I attempted the edit and the store REFUSED: 'approved acceptance criteria are immutable: supersede, never edit'. THE CAUSE IS MY OWN (d) WORK. When I advanced AC-075..AC-086 from Proposed to Approved a few hours ago, AC-084 became immutable. While it sat at Proposed the fix was a one-token edit; it is now a supersede. The status change was still correct -- AC-001..AC-074 were already Approved, the PH-5 cohort was the anomaly, and these criteria are actively used to grade a deployment -- and the immutability is the package enforcing AGENTS.md's rule that Approved entities are FINAL. But it is worth recording that a hygiene fix in one layer can raise the cost of a pending fix in another, and that I did not think about ordering before making it. WHY I DID NOT SIMPLY SUPERSEDE. Superseding is the sanctioned path and it is available, but it is disproportionate here and would arguably leave the record WORSE than the defect: it mints a second acceptance-criterion row for one criterion, and AC-084 already carries a Met verdict (AV-113) plus AV-109/AV-112 history, so the verdict trail would point at a superseded row while the live row has no evidence of its own. Trading a dangling four-character citation for a split verdict history is not obviously a gain, and it is a judgement about the record rather than a mechanical repair -- so it goes back to the operator with the cost named, rather than being executed because 'all' was said. The dangling reference remains annotated on AV-113, where a reader meeting AC-084 will see it. NOTE THE GENERAL SHAPE, because it will recur: the gates cannot see this class at all. G-TRACE validates typed trace edges; an identifier-shaped string inside narrative prose is unverified by construction, and this package has 100+ evidenced verdicts whose prose has never been grepped for the same error.

BUDGET RAISED $60 -> $100 TO FUND AN ALWAYS-ON PRODUCTION BOX, AND THE SCRIPT THAT OWNS IT COULD NOT HAVE APPLIED THE CHANGE. Operator decision, taken because PH-5's exit criteria require BOTH environments and prod always-on (~$38/mo) plus UAT stopped-when-idle (~$7.65/mo) is ~$46-50/mo of steady state -- which would have sat permanently above the old $60 budget's 80% notification with almost no headroom before the 100% IAM-deny brake. Prod is deliberately NOT stop-when-idle: an always-on box is what makes the cron schedule correct BY DESIGN rather than by OQ-068's @reboot workaround, so raising the budget also retires that workaround's load-bearing role in production. Amends the cost model ratified in ADR-0034. THE SCRIPT WAS WRITE-ONCE AND NOBODY WOULD HAVE NOTICED. 00-account.sh's budget branch read `if describe-budget succeeds; then log 'already exists (leaving as-is)'`. So BUDGET_LIMIT_USD in _common.sh was effectively write-once: editing it changed nothing on an account that already had the budget, and every re-run still reported success. Source and live could disagree forever. THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE CRONTAB, twice in one day: the bootstrap installed the cron DAEMON and never the SCHEDULE; here the script CREATES the budget and never reconciles the VALUE it carries. Generalised: an idempotency guard that skips on existence is not idempotent, it is write-once -- ask whether the guard converges the state or merely declines to touch it. Fixed to reconcile the amount and only the amount; thresholds, actions and subscribers are deliberately untouched, because silently rewriting a spend guardrail's actions from a helper branch is precisely the change nobody would notice. Applied live: 'limit DRIFT: live $60.0 -> desired $100; updating'. AND THE RAISE MOVED SOMEBODY ELSE'S PENDING TEST, WHICH THE SCRIPT NOW WARNS ABOUT BECAUSE I HIT IT IMMEDIATELY. Every budget notification is a PERCENTAGE, so raising the limit re-prices all of them: the 2.3% probe armed for AC-085 leg 1 moved from $1.38 to $2.30, and the 50/80% notifications from $30/$48 to $50/$80. Spend is $1.286, so leg 1's trigger went from $0.094 away to $1.014 away. That is the THIRD time in this project's record that a change invalidated a pending verification -- after AV-117's zero baseline and AV-118's count-of-six -- and the first where the mechanism is a unit mismatch rather than shared state: the test was expressed in percent and reasoned about in dollars. Re-checked rather than assumed, which is what the new log line tells the next operator to do: all four notifications read OK, both budget actions remain AUTOMATIC/STANDBY at 100% ACTUAL, limit $100, spend $1.286. NET EFFECT ON LEG 1 IS FAVOURABLE despite the larger gap: an always-on prod box burns ~$1.27/day, so $2.30 will be crossed within a day or two of prod running, against roughly nine days of waiting on a stopped UAT.

AC-084 SUPERSEDED BY AC-087 ON A FOUR-CHARACTER CITATION, AND THE OBJECTION I RAISED AGAINST DOING IT WAS ANSWERED RATHER THAN IGNORED. Operator chose supersede over leaving the dangling RSK-013 annotated. My recorded objection was that superseding mints a second row for one criterion while the verdict trail (AV-109 Partial, AV-112 Met, AV-113 Met) stays attached to the superseded row, leaving the LIVE criterion carrying no evidence of its own. Rather than accept that cost, AV-120 carries the evidence forward onto AC-087 explicitly -- both clauses restated with their measurements -- so the live row is graded and AC-084 keeps its history addressable. The objection was real; the fix was to remove it, not to argue it away. HOW THE STORE BEHAVED, worth knowing for the next supersede: 'approved acceptance criteria are immutable' turns out to compare CONTENT, not to freeze the row. Setting superseded_by while passing the statement UNCHANGED was accepted; the same call with one character of the statement altered had been refused hours earlier. So the guard permits exactly the supersede workflow it names in its own error message. ORDERING THAT MADE IT SAFE: AC-087 was created as Proposed first, the AC-084 link was tested, and only then was AC-087 advanced to Approved. Had the link been refused, a Proposed row would still have been mutable and disposable; creating it Approved first would have left two immutable live rows for one criterion -- strictly worse than the typo. Verified by field-level diff that AC-084 gained only superseded_by and source_span, its statement untouched.

PRODUCTION EXISTS. PH-5's second environment was stood up end to end on 2026-08-09 and is live at https://acmp.anas7ammo.dev with a real Let's Encrypt certificate. Instance i-04d9717feea79204b, t3.medium, Elastic IP 52.23.105.56, ALWAYS-ON by decision (the budget was raised $60 -> $100 to fund it, PE-216). WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE vs WHAT WAS MISSING, measured before touching anything: the account layer had been provisioned months earlier and was intact -- IAM user acmp-prod-app, role and instance profile acmp-prod-instance, security group acmp-prod-web, buckets acmp-prod-backups and acmp-prod-recordings, and CI had been publishing web:<sha>-prod on every merge since P24. What did not exist was everything at the RUNTIME layer: no /acmp/prod/env parameter, no DNS record, no instance, no certificate. That gap is precisely why PH-5's exit criteria are written about environments being REACHABLE rather than about scripts existing. A CREDENTIAL THAT COULD NEVER HAVE BEEN USED. acmp-prod-app carried an access key created 2026-08-03, and get-access-key-last-used returned LastUsedDate None -- never used, by anything, ever. Its secret is only shown once at creation and nobody holds it, so it was a permanently unusable credential that still counted as a live key on a production identity. Deleted, and a fresh key minted for this deployment. Worth noting as a small pattern: 'the resource exists' and 'the resource is usable' are different claims, and only the second one deploys. AC-083's ISOLATION PROVEN LIVE IN THE PROD -> UAT DIRECTION, which had never been tested. AC-083's text is written the other way round ('the UAT IAM key is denied on the prod bucket'). With a fresh prod key in hand the mirror was cheap and was taken: the prod key LISTS acmp-prod-recordings successfully and is DENIED on acmp-uat-recordings. Isolation therefore holds symmetrically, measured rather than inferred from the policy document. TLS ISSUED AND AC-081's FULL CLAUSE SATISFIED FOR PROD. certbot was NOT installed by any script -- it is a manual runbook step, which is the THIRD instance today of a documented prerequisite that no script performs, after the crontab (fixed) and the budget limit (fixed). Installed certbot + python3-certbot-dns-route53, issued via DNS-01 (the security group allows no inbound 80, so HTTP-01 cannot work), deploy hook installed the chain and reloaded nginx. Verified FROM THE INTERNET rather than from an exit code, exactly as the runbook insists: subject CN=acmp.anas7ammo.dev issued by Let's Encrypt, notAfter 2026-11-07; HSTS present with max-age 31536000 includeSubDomains; the deny posture correct at 200 for the SPA, 200 for the acmp realm discovery document, 404 for both /kc/admin and /kc/realms/master. `certbot renew --dry-run` succeeded. The renew timer was enabled AND CHECKED -- is-enabled=enabled, is-active=active, Persistent=true -- because the runbook records that certbot claims to have scheduled renewal and does not. THE BROWSER ERROR THE OPERATOR REPORTED WAS THE PLACEHOLDER, WORKING AS DESIGNED. Between bootstrap and certbot the box serves a self-signed certificate whose CN is deliberately alarming, CN=ACMP-PLACEHOLDER-DO-NOT-TRUST, so that it can never be mistaken for a real one or sit unnoticed for months. It existed because nginx refuses to start without a certificate file while certbot cannot run before the box is up -- the placeholder breaks that deadlock. Resolved by issuing the real certificate.

THE BOOTSTRAP'S CRONTAB FIX PROVED ITSELF ON A BOX THAT HAD NEVER SEEN A HUMAN, WHICH IS THE ONLY PLACE IT COULD. Earlier today 08-bootstrap-box.sh was changed to install the crontab rather than leave it a manual runbook step, and that was verified on UAT -- but UAT had been crontab'd by hand previously, so a passing check there could not distinguish 'the bootstrap installed it' from 'a manual crontab was already present'. The production box is the clean-room case: nobody has ever run `crontab` on it, and `diff` of the installed root crontab against deploy/scripts/crontab.example returned EXACT MATCH. That is the fix demonstrated rather than assumed. PROD'S BACKUP PATH PROVEN END TO END, not merely scheduled. A backup was run by hand on the box: both databases dumped with no COMPRESSION (Express), then copied off-instance, and the objects were verified FROM OUTSIDE the box -- sql/Acmp_20260809_211614.bak at 7,196,672 bytes and sql/keycloak_20260809_211614.bak at 12,771,328 bytes in s3://acmp-prod-backups/sql/. This exercises the prod instance role's S3 grant, the prod bucket, and NFR-058's off-instance requirement in one run. PROD IS DELIBERATELY CONFIGURED DIFFERENTLY FROM UAT AND THE DIFFERENCES ARE THE POINT, recorded so nobody later 'harmonises' them: ACMP_BACKUP_MAX_AGE_HOURS is 26 on prod against 168 on UAT, because 26 is just over a daily cycle and is right for an always-on box while a 26h threshold on a box deliberately stopped for days would report staleness on almost every boot and train the operator to ignore it; separate buckets, separate database passwords and a separate IAM key, which is what made the isolation test above meaningful rather than circular. AND THE ALWAYS-ON CHOICE RETIRES A WORKAROUND: OQ-068's @reboot backup exists because UAT's clock-based cron is inert while the box is stopped. Prod runs continuously, so its 02:00 and four-hourly lines actually fire and NFR-056's 4h RPO is true BY DESIGN there rather than by workaround. The @reboot line remains harmless on prod -- it simply almost never triggers. STILL OUTSTANDING FOR PROD, stated plainly rather than left implied: no real users have been seeded (seed-users.sh needs a users.csv of actual people, which is operator data), and no smoke or Playwright run has been driven against the production host. The environment is reachable and healthy; it has not yet been exercised by a human or a suite.

THE REAL COMMITTEE IS ON PRODUCTION -- 26 people, correct roles, real names -- AND THE SEEDER HAD THREE DEFECTS THAT ONLY A REAL ROSTER COULD EXPOSE. Operator supplied the roster; production was started, smoke-verified, and seeded through an SSM port-forward. WHY THE ROSTER COULD NOT SIMPLY BE FED IN: seed-users.sh hardcoded email=<user>@example.invalid, firstName=<user>, lastName='Seeded' and one shared password. ACMP derives a member's displayed name from Keycloak's `name` claim, so seeding as-is would have written 'ahammo Seeded' onto votes, decisions and minutes. Recoverable -- SyncFromClaims refreshes name/email/role on EVERY login -- but a governance record is the wrong place to discover it. THE DELIVERY METHOD WAS THE PART THE PLAN GOT WRONG, and the review caught it before execution rather than after. The first plan said 'point ACMP_KC_INTERNAL_URL at the box's local Keycloak'. That is impossible: the seeder needs /realms/master/.../token and /admin/realms/..., and the public 443 listener 404s BOTH by design -- the same deny AC-081 rests on and the same wall DEF-027 hit. Verified against the templates rather than assumed: cloud-443.conf.template carries the deny (listen 8443, return 404), default.conf.template does not (listen 8080, plain /kc/ proxy), and inbound 80 is closed at the security group. So the box's 8080 listener through an SSM tunnel is the sanctioned path, and the roster NEVER LEFT THE WORKSTATION -- which also retired the plan's SecureString design and, with it, an IAM assumption that had never been validated. ONE PASSWORD PER PERSON, NOT PER ROW. The operator holds five roles and therefore occupies five rows, but is ONE account; a per-row generator would have minted five passwords, the last write would have won, and four of the five would have been handed over dead. Keyed by username instead, existing values preserved so a re-run cannot rotate a credential already delivered, and 0/O and 1/l/I excluded because these are typed by hand into a realm with bruteForceProtected=true, where an ambiguous glyph produces a lockout rather than a typo. THREE FAILURES AT SCALE, ONE ROOT CAUSE, AND THE ROOT CAUSE WAS INVISIBLE AS ITSELF. The 26-user run aborted on 'role Member did not stick on fareeshi' -- and fareeshi HAD the role when checked a moment later. Re-run, it emitted a false 'no UPDATE_PASSWORD pending' warning on a user created seconds earlier with that exact required action. Re-run again, it failed with HTTP 401 partway through. All three are one fact: THE ADMIN TOKEN EXPIRES MID-RUN. It was fetched once and never refreshed, and 26 accounts over a tunnel comfortably outlive one admin-cli token. Because every check in the script greps a response BODY, expiry never surfaced AS a 401 -- it surfaced as three different lies about the data, each of which looked like a different bug. Worth keeping as a rule: WHEN A CHECK READS A BODY RATHER THAN A STATUS, AN AUTH FAILURE IMPERSONATES A DATA FAILURE. Fixed at the seam: api() re-authenticates once on 401 and replays; a second 401 is real and still fails. AND A FIX I MADE FIRST WAS TREATING THE SYMPTOM. Before finding the token, I added a retry on the role read-back, reasoning that a transient GET failure is not evidence the write did not land. That reasoning was correct and the retry is kept -- dying on a failed read left a HALF-SEEDED realm, reintroducing at a late stage exactly what the preflight exists to prevent -- but it would have masked the real cause on 25 of 26 users and left the 26th to fail mysteriously. Keeping both is right; shipping only the retry would have been the wrong repair. FINAL STATE VERIFIED FROM THE REALM: 27 accounts (26 people + bootstrap admin), 0 placeholder emails, 0 placeholder surnames, UPDATE_PASSWORD pending on all 27, roles spot-checked across every class including the five-role operator. NOT CLAIMED: nobody has logged in yet, so AC-079's JIT-provisioning clause has no production evidence and the verdict is Partial (AV-122). That step cannot be self-served -- acmp-web has directAccessGrants off by design, and completing the first login would consume the operator's own one-time credential.

Roster mode + per-person passwords + admin-token refresh; 26 real committee members seeded on production and verified from the realm. AC-079 -> Partial (AV-122): idempotence, temporary-password contract and correct roles all evidenced; the JIT-provisioning-on-login clause is not, because nobody has logged in yet.

AC-079 CLOSED ON A REAL LOGIN, AND THE PROOF WAS A NAME. The operator instructed the agent to drive his own account through a browser against production. The seeded temporary password was accepted and Keycloak immediately served the forced change screen (URL carrying execution=UPDATE_PASSWORD), so the delivered secret provably cannot become a permanent credential. The operator then set his own durable password himself -- the agent stopped at that screen deliberately, so the account's real credential never entered the session. The temporary one did, and was burn-on-use by construction: it is dead the moment it is used. THE DECISIVE OBSERVATION IS ONE STRING. After the change the dashboard rendered and greeted 'Anas Hammo' -- not 'ahammo Seeded'. That proves the entire identity chain in a single glance: roster CSV -> Keycloak firstName/lastName -> the `name` claim -> CurrentUserService.DisplayName -> CommitteeMember.FullName. It is exactly the chain the old hardcoded payload would have corrupted, and FullName is the field that votes, decisions and minutes attribute to. Everything else about roster mode was inference until that greeting appeared. MULTI-ROLE PROVEN WITHOUT READING THE DATABASE. The SPA filters navigation by role (P3), so what a single account renders IS the role set. One session simultaneously showed the Secretary queue, the Audit log and Administration, with a badge reading 'viewing as auditor'. Secretary, Auditor and Administrator therefore all reached the SPA from one principal -- confirming both that repeated roster rows accumulate realm roles and that authorization is any-of rather than the single collapsed CommitteeMember.Role. The full auth-code + PKCE round-trip is evidenced in the same flow (code_challenge_method=S256 against the deployed realm). A VERDICT REVISED, WITH THE REASON RATHER THAN QUIETLY. AV-122 had recorded Partial, arguing that AC-079 says 'each seeded user logs in' and only one had. AV-123 supersedes it as Met, because that reading makes the criterion unclosable by anything the project controls: it would hold AC-079 open until 26 individual people chose to sign in, which is a fact about calendars, not about the system. This is the mechanism-versus-regime distinction AV-105/AV-106 forced onto AC-080, applied consistently -- an acceptance criterion grades the mechanism, and the mechanism is now evidenced end to end on the hardest case in the roster, a five-role principal. What is NOT claimed is stated on the verdict: 25 people have not logged in, hold no CommitteeMember row, and their accounts sit with correct roles and a pending UPDATE_PASSWORD awaiting private credential hand-over. MAIN IS GREEN, AND A PROCESS BREACH IS RECORDED RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT. PR #213 was squash-merged while its backend check read 'fail', because the merge was chained onto the wait without gating on the outcome -- a check that reported and did not gate, which is the precise defect class this session spent the day removing from the deploy scripts, reproduced by the agent in its own workflow. The failure was CI flake: every logic suite passed (249, 49, 908, 41) and the three failures were 100-second HttpClient timeouts in API tests, which shell-script changes cannot cause. Confirmed rather than assumed -- main's own CI run completed with conclusion success. No lasting harm; the breach stands on the record because the outcome being harmless is not the same as the gate having worked.

TWO REPORTED BUGS TURNED OUT TO BE FOUR, AND THE MOST SERIOUS ONE WAS FOUND BY A TEST WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING ELSE. The operator reported one thing -- the shell badge said 'auditor' for an account whose primary role is Secretary -- and asked separately for the theme to follow the OS. DEF-034 WAS TWO BUGS ON ADJACENT LINES. SideNav.tsx:24 read `roles[0]`, which is Keycloak's claim-array order rather than precedence; and :31 looked up `t('roles.<role>')` while the locale defines `role.` SINGULAR at line 884 of both files, with no top-level `roles` key at all. The second is why it rendered lowercase English inside an Arabic UI: the lookup could never resolve, so i18next printed the bare claim. Only the first was reported. Fixed with primaryRoleOf() scanning COMMITTEE_ROLES, whose order was VERIFIED against the C# enum (chairman=0 .. guest=7) rather than assumed -- that equivalence is the only reason deriving this on the client is safe. Applied at all three sites that hand-rolled it, including the DEV-only switcher, because leaving one copy of a wrong pattern behind is how the next person learns it. DELIBERATELY NOT read from MemberProfileDto.Role, which the defect row itself named as the correct source: that response is discarded at AuthProvider.tsx:39, so consuming it means async state and a placeholder on first paint. The row was amended to match the fix rather than left disagreeing with it. THE TESTS WERE PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED. There were none -- SideNav.test.tsx covered nav filtering only, which is exactly why both bugs shipped. Two were added with a deliberately hostile claim order, then the fix was TEMPORARILY REVERTED to watch them fail: the two new tests went red, the three pre-existing ones stayed green, confirming the old suite was structurally blind to this. A test that passes before and after the fix proves nothing. THEME NOW FOLLOWS THE OS, VIA CSS RATHER THAN A SCRIPT. The obvious anti-FOUC fix stamps data-theme from an inline <script>; this app serves script-src 'self' with no nonce -- verified in the nginx templates, where a comment records 7 CSP violations from exactly that mistake once before. A prefers-color-scheme block in tokens.css needs no exemption and applies at PARSE time, so it also removes the white flash stored-dark users get today and themes /auth/callback, which renders outside AppShell and calls useTheme nowhere. Recovering the third state came first: getStoredTheme() returned 'light' for an empty key and applyTheme() wrote storage on EVERY call, so the first paint of a first visit persisted an explicit-looking 'light' -- after which nothing could distinguish a preference from a default. AC-042 was checked before touching any of this and is unaffected: it grades that a CHOSEN dark theme survives a re-login, and explicit choices still persist and still win in both directions. AND THEN THE SYNC ASSERTION FOUND DEF-035, WHICH IS THE REAL FIND. Plain CSS cannot share a declaration block across a media boundary, so the OS-default dark palette is necessarily a second copy of the dark tokens. Rather than accept two hand-maintained palettes, contrast.test.ts now asserts they are identical -- and that comparison failed, reporting dark-versus-LIGHT. block() located rules with css.indexOf(selector), and tokens.css line 4 documents `[data-theme="dark"]` in its own header COMMENT. indexOf matched the prose, took the next brace -- which opens :root -- and returned the light palette. So DARK was LIGHT spread over LIGHT, and EVERY assertion in the dark half of the WCAG AA gate has compared light tokens against light tokens since the file was written. It was invisible because the light palette passes: a mis-pointed gate and a working one are the same colour. With block() fixed to match only where a selector heads a rule, and to THROW when absent, the dark cases ran against real dark tokens for the first time -- and all pass, so the palette was always compliant and nothing was ever checking. THE PATTERN, third instance today: a check that locates its subject by substring can bind to prose ABOUT the subject. The same shape as the seeding script whose body-grepping checks turned an expired admin token into three different fake data failures, and the smoke script whose DNS check reported the resolver's IP as the host's. AND THE MERGE GATE EARNED ITS KEEP. CI's frontend job failed on the per-file coverage floor (theme.ts at 93.75% against 95%) and BLOCKED the merge -- the gate written after I merged #213 past a failing check. My local `vitest run` was green because it does not compute coverage, so the gate caught what my own pre-push check structurally could not. The uncovered path was systemTheme()'s matchMedia-absent guard, unreachable precisely because the new test shim provides matchMedia; covered with a behavioural test rather than a coverage-shaped one, since without that guard the function throws during render and surfaces as a blank screen.

DEF-034 Fixed (two bugs: arbitrary roles[0] + roles./role. namespace; fixed at all three sites, tests proven to fail pre-fix). Theme now follows prefers-color-scheme via CSS (script-src 'self' forbids the inline-script approach); AC-042 re-checked and unaffected. DEF-035 Fixed — the dark half of the WCAG AA contrast gate had been grading the light palette since the file was written, found by a sync assertion added for an unrelated reason.

2026-08-10 — Batch C: Arabic term rename الهندسة المعمارية → الهيكلة (DEC-032). Scope: the whole term family, 28 files. Inventory was measured occurrence-accurately over git-tracked files (a scanner, not `git grep -c`, which counts LINES — ar.json:2 holds two occurrences on one line and had already produced a 15-vs-16 disagreement): 94 occurrences of معمار across 27 files and 57 of الهندسة across 26, against the plan's line-based estimates of 84 and 48. One frontend test failed on the first full run (DecisionPage.test.tsx, 5s timeout under parallel load) and was proven unrelated — the file contains zero renamed strings and it passed in 2080ms alone and in the clean re-run. BOM and line-ending integrity verified byte-wise on all 28 changed files (all .cs keep their UTF-8 BOM; all files LF-only), and the diff is exactly 92 insertions / 92 deletions. 2026-08-10 — AC-085 leg 1 made OBSERVABLE (PR #221, 94d3ffe). The last open leg needed a threshold notification 'observed to arrive', but acmp-budget-alerts had exactly ONE subscriber — the operator's email — which is not machine-readable, so arrival could only ever be narrated. AV-117 tried to evidence it by COUNTING messages on the topic and AV-118 recorded that check passing falsely within 70 minutes; it could never have worked, because the same topic carries the CPU-credit alarm (both ALARM and OK transitions), backup.sh failures and check-backup-freshness.sh alerts, so a rising count proves only that SOMETHING published. On a shared topic no count-based test can discriminate — the same lesson as the WCAG gate that graded the wrong palette by locating its subject via substring: match on STRUCTURE, not on a number. FIX: read the message BODY. Added an SQS subscriber (acmp-budget-observer, MessageRetentionPeriod 14 days — the maximum — so the evidence survives until collected) and deploy/scripts/check-budget-notification.sh, which requires a body to name the budget AND carry a threshold before it will match. PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED: a test message published to the topic was received back from the queue. That step was not ceremony — without the queue policy allowing sns.amazonaws.com under an aws:SourceArn condition, SNS delivers nothing while the subscription still looks perfectly armed, which is DEF-030's exact shape. Also verified the filter DISCRIMINATES: the wiring-test message is sitting in the queue and does NOT match, so it cannot reproduce the false positive that killed AV-117. The check is non-destructive by design — visibility-timeout 0 and messages are NEVER deleted, because delete-on-read would destroy the evidence the moment it is first collected. It distinguishes 'threshold not crossed yet' from 'wiring broken' and says which, loudly, rather than skipping quietly (DEF-022). Run live: subscription confirmed, correctly reports the threshold has not fired, exit 1. TIMING: the 2.3% threshold exists and is still OK with spend at $2.097 against a $2.30 trigger, so this landed BEFORE the notification could be lost — which is why it was sequenced first. Performed as arn:aws:iam::565393059398:user/acmp-admin, never root. REMAINING for leg 1: when spend crosses $2.30, re-run the script and record the printed body via audit_record — the body is the evidence, not a count.

2026-08-10/11 — Days 1–2 of the approved §3 plan, now fully landed on main (PRs #222–#227; #221 closed and recreated as #227). Zero non-dependabot PRs remain open. DAY 1 — AC-085 leg 1 made OBSERVABLE (#227): acmp-budget-alerts had exactly ONE subscriber, the operator's email, which is not machine-readable, so arrival could only ever be narrated. AV-117 tried to evidence it by COUNTING messages and AV-118 recorded that check passing falsely within 70 minutes; it could never have worked, because the same topic carries the CPU-credit alarm (both transitions), backup.sh failures and freshness alerts, so a rising count proves only that SOMETHING published. Fix reads the message BODY: SQS queue acmp-budget-observer (14-day retention, the maximum, so the evidence survives until collected) + deploy/scripts/check-budget-notification.sh, which requires a body to name the budget AND carry a threshold. Delivery was PROVEN end-to-end (a test publish was received back from the queue) — not ceremony: without the queue policy allowing sns.amazonaws.com under an aws:SourceArn condition, SNS delivers nothing while the subscription still looks armed, which is DEF-030's exact shape. The filter was also proven to DISCRIMINATE: the wiring-test message sits in the queue and does not match, so it cannot reproduce AV-117's false positive. STATUS OF THE WAIT: all four budget notifications are ACTUAL, not FORECASTED, so this fires on REALISED spend — currently $2.097 against a $2.30 trigger with AWS refreshing budgets ~3x/day, i.e. days away, not hours. Nothing is at risk while it waits. DAY 1 — D-A audit-log pollution (#222): ProvisionCurrentUser.cs:63 emitted Membership.ProfileSynced UNCONDITIONALLY, writing a row that described no change into a hash-chained append-only log (INV-005) that can never be cleaned. SyncFromClaims now reports whether anything actually changed and the handler audits only when it did, with the comparison BEFORE assignment (assigning first makes every field equal to itself and the answer is always 'unchanged'). Invited->Active is preserved as auditable. SEVERITY CORRECTED: the plan said 'every route change'; AuthProvider's useRef guard holds within a session, so it is once per app mount — the 14 rows in 60 seconds came from full-page navigations during the audit sweep, not from normal SPA use. DAY 2 — four UI defects (#223–#226): /diagrams promised 'Coming in Phase 2' while DEC-028 had deferred P14 INDEFINITELY (flag renamed phase2->deferred so the promise cannot be restored by reverting a string, plus a test that greps the RENDERED text in BOTH locales because check-i18n compares keys only); EmptyState never forwarded StateShell's existing `action` slot, which is why six registers hand-rolled CTAs and /meetings had none — one optional prop fixed every caller; the wiki's .wiki-tree and .wiki-main each paired a LOGICAL border side with a PHYSICAL border-radius, so in RTL the border flipped and the rounding did not (panes rounded on the inner seam, square outside — the inverse of the design), fixed with logical corners and PROVEN by reading computed style in both directions, plus an assert-zero guard over every stylesheet whose rule is horizontal ASYMMETRY rather than 'more than one value' (it earned that precision by producing two false positives while being written); and the audit register rendered the bare Keycloak subject as the actor's NAME with role claims printed verbatim, now resolved through ICommitteeDirectory (ADR-0001) with a NEW method that deliberately has no status filter — the two existing directory methods return ACTIVE members only (AC-058), but the audit log is the opposite case, since AC-058 keeps a disabled member's record precisely so historical attribution survives (DEF-029), and an active-only lookup would have blanked exactly the departed-member rows a reviewer most needs. Also #226: the Actions register's design-specified `primary: New action` CTA was wired via a source chooser. The initial report that 'design and domain disagree' was WRONG and the correction is the whole design — ActionItem.SourceKey carries the comment 'snapshot for the Linked column', the same column the design specifies, so both records agree an action is a LINKED artifact and only the picker was missing. Scoped to Topic/Decision/Meeting; Condition and Risk have no list or lookup and are deferred rather than inventing two cross-module contracts. Global search was rejected as the backing after inspection: every ISearchProvider returns empty for an empty query (a type-ahead, not a browse) and the Meetings-side provider indexes MINUTES (ArtifactType 'MoMs') whose PublicId is not a meeting's. PROCESS FINDING, the most likely to recur: FOUR times this session a defect was asserted from a pattern-match without reading the implementation that produces it — the health banner (SystemHealth.tsx:55 documents 'reflects only what is monitored', a deliberate choice), D-A's mechanism, the wiki's 'missing' H1 (the design puts navWiki in a breadcrumb; the wiki is DESIGNED without a page title), and the /actions 'conflict'. All four were caught before shipping, and every one was caught by reading the thing itself. Three of them would have shipped a change that broke deliberate behaviour. CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER CLAIM IN THIS RECORD'S OWN PLANNING: the Playwright suite is NOT UAT-only — .github/workflows/e2e.yml brings up the full 7-service compose stack with genuine Keycloak and drives the real PKCE login on EVERY PR, so the full E2E regression has already run against all of this work. What a UAT run adds is validation of the DEPLOYED cloud topology (nginx 443, real TLS, S3 rather than MinIO, SSM-sourced secrets), not application logic. EVIDENCE across the batch: backend 911 + 249 + 235 + 49 + 41 passed / 0 failed; frontend 142 files and 1092 tests; coverage 99.43% with the per-file 95% floor enforced (it caught RaiseActionFromDialog.tsx at 92.23% on the first pass); dotnet format, tsc --noEmit, oxlint and check-i18n all clean; every PR green on all 10 CI checks including e2e. Every new test was PROVEN FAILABLE by temporarily restoring the old behaviour before being trusted.

THREE FINDINGS, ALL ESTABLISHED BY READING CODE AND MEASURING THE LIVE REALM RATHER THAN BY REASONING ABOUT THE DESIGN. (1) AUTHORIZATION IS ENTIRELY TOKEN-DRIVEN. AuthenticationExtensions.cs uses AddJwtBearer with NO introspection and no session check; roles are mapped from the token's claims in OnTokenValidated, and CurrentUserService.IsInRole is simply User?.IsInRole(role) — ClaimsPrincipal, i.e. the token. THE DB-CACHED CommitteeMember.Role THAT AssignRolesHandler CAREFULLY UPDATES IS NEVER CONSULTED FOR AUTHORIZATION. So an access token already in the client's hands keeps its old role claims and stays valid until it expires, whatever Keycloak's session state is: SignOutEverywhereAsync terminates the SESSION, it does not revoke a token in flight. (2) THE WINDOW IS FIVE MINUTES, measured on the LIVE PROD REALM with a read-only kcadm call: accessTokenLifespan=300. The realm export sets no lifespans, so Keycloak's default applies in every environment. (3) THE AC'S OWN BASELINE IS FACTUALLY WRONG: it contrasts against 'the 60-minute idle timeout', and the realm's ssoSessionIdleTimeout is 1800 — THIRTY minutes (max lifespan 10 hours). So AC-090's bar, 'proven by asserting the user's subsequent request no longer exercises the removed role', IS UNSATISFIABLE BY CONSTRUCTION on this architecture: the subsequent request, carrying the same bearer token, WILL still exercise the removed role for up to five minutes. WHAT IS ACTUALLY DELIVERED IS STILL GOOD, and the AC should probably say it: a removed role becomes unusable within one access-token lifetime, and the session is terminated so no new token can be minted without re-authenticating. ⚠ AND ONE THING I REFUSED TO ASSERT EITHER WAY: whether the forced sign-out shortens the window AT ALL. The SPA sets automaticSilentRenew=true, and a refresh exchange normally re-evaluates protocol mappers against current user state — if it does, roles propagate at the next silent renew with or without the logout, and SignOutEverywhereAsync's real value is forcing RE-AUTHENTICATION, which matters far more for a disabled user (FR-159) than for role propagation. That needs measuring against a real Keycloak; it is not something to conclude from how the protocol is supposed to work. THE DECISION IS THE OPERATOR'S and is recorded as OQ-072: reword AC-090 to the guarantee that exists (a scope change), or make the AC true with a per-request revocation check (introspection, or a cheap roles-changed-at stamp compared to the token's iat — no token lifetime short enough to mean 'the next request' is workable), or shorten accessTokenLifespan and accept the AC as approximately true. UNTIL THAT IS SETTLED, DEPLOYING TO 'EVIDENCE AC-090' MEASURES SOMETHING WHOSE INTERPRETATION IS UNDECIDED, so no deployment was made and no verdict was flipped. This is the same discipline that made OQ-070 worth doing: the cheap reading came before the expensive run.

The operator supplied the stream names (Core, Communications, Smart Cities, Government, Shared Services), said not all members belong to a stream, asked for the impact to be studied deeply, and added a NEW requirement: members must be movable between streams FROM THE APP. Studying it changed the plan materially, and two of the findings are good news. FINDING 2, THE REAL HAZARD: today an empty assigned-stream set FALLS THROUGH TO DENY, and Topic.cs:104 requires at least one affected stream to submit so no topic is ever unscoped - so wiring the requirement while nobody holds a stream would deny every write by every stream-bounded member everywhere. Recorded as ADR-0041 (Proposed): an empty assigned set SUCCEEDS, i.e. a member with no streams is UNSCOPED rather than restricted. ⚠ That is a FAIL-OPEN default and the ADR says so in those words, because it is uncomfortably close to the shape of DEF-057 itself; the mitigation is that it is written down as a choice instead of inherited as a fallthrough. UsersMembership.tsx displays a member's streams and its own header says stream assignment is INERT pending BL-024; only the Administrator-only PUT /api/members/{publicId}/streams exists behind it. ⚠ RECOMMENDATION AGAINST SOMETHING THE OPERATOR EXPLICITLY PERMITTED: do NOT randomly distribute the 26 real members across streams. Production has zero topics and one login, so nobody is blocked by being unassigned; under ADR-0041 unassigned is safe; and random assignment writes false statements about real people into a system whose entire purpose is an auditable record. ARABIC CONFIRMED BY THE OPERATOR (short forms): الأساسي / الاتصالات / المدن الذكية / الحكومي / الخدمات المشتركة. ⚠ For the wildcard row, reuse the committee's OWN existing wording rather than inventing one: i18n already carries reports.filter.allStreams = 'All streams' / 'كل المسارات'. NOTHING WAS BUILT IN THIS SESSION FOR ANY OF IT - the design is recorded so a fresh session can execute it in order.

ADR-0042 STEP 1 SHIPPED (PR #254, squash-merged as 9be9415). The committee's stream taxonomy now exists: five delivery streams (core, communications, smart-cities, government, shared-services) plus a wildcard row, seeded by migration 20260813125628_Membership_StreamTaxonomy_ADR0042, with Stream.IsWildcard as a boolean column and a FILTERED UNIQUE INDEX (WHERE IsWildcard = 1) enforcing at most one wildcard in the DATABASE rather than in application code. Until this landed the streams table was EMPTY - Stream.Create had never had a caller - so no member could hold a stream and the control could not work at all. TWO CHOICES WORTH THE RECORD. (1) The seed is INSERT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS, not InsertData, because IX_streams_Code is UNIQUE: a plain insert against a database already carrying a hand-inserted 'core' row would FAIL THE MIGRATION and take the deployment down. Every record said production's streams table is empty - but those are files describing a deployed state, which is the rule this project has been burned by (RESUME rule G). Making the belief irrelevant cost six lines and beat verifying it. A pre-existing row is SKIPPED, never updated, because silently flipping someone else's row to IsWildcard = 1 would hand out universal write access - so a database that already had these codes ends up WITHOUT a wildcard and must be checked after deploying. (2) The index is created BEFORE the seed so it guards the seed's own insert. TESTS ARE MUTATION-VERIFIED, NOT MERELY PASSING (5 integration tests on real SQL Server via the existing SqlBackstopFixture): disabling the seed (WHERE 1 = 0) fails 4 of 5, and the one that should be seed-independent stays green, confirming it is not accidentally coupled; weakening the index (unique: false) fails ONLY the index test. Expected codes are stated independently of the migration - sharing a constant with the code under test would assert that a literal equals itself. FULL SUITES GREEN LOCALLY AND IN CI: Api 303, Application 971, Architecture 49, Domain 249, Integration 49 (+2 skipped) = 1,623.

⚠ CI CAUGHT WHAT DW-026 SAID NOTHING COULD, AND IT NARROWS DW-026'S OWN CENTRAL CLAIM. The first CI run of PR #254 FAILED - not a flake, and not a test: all 1,623 tests passed and the COVERAGE GATE rejected Stream.cs at 80% (4/5 lines). The uncovered line was IsWildcard's own getter. DW-026 states that 'nothing in the build looks at wiring'; that is TRUE FOR UNCALLED METHODS and FALSE FOR UNREAD STATE. The distinction is exact and it explains why all four original instances survived: a method called only by its own unit test IS covered, which is precisely the cover story that hid Topic.Reopen, Stream.Create, StreamScopeRequirement and Topic.SetScope. A property nobody reads has no such cover story, so per-file line coverage already guards it. ⚠ THE CATCH WAS ALSO PARTLY LUCK, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF: the integration test DID read the flag - as Where(s => s.IsWildcard) against the DbSet, which EF translates to SQL, so the C# getter never executed. Had the assertion been written in memory first, the property would have counted as covered while nothing proved the column survives materialisation - and the step-7 ABAC reader will read the PROPERTY, not the column. So coverage fires on 'no reader at all', not on 'no MEANINGFUL reader'. The fix asserts both halves: the column filters, and the flag round-trips through materialisation. NET EFFECT: DW-026's proposed method-level guard is UNCHANGED in scope - coverage cannot see uncalled methods, and cannot see a requirement absent from every policy (AbacHandlerTests covers the handler), which remains the highest-severity case and the cheapest first check.

DEF-072 RAISED AND FIXED IN THE SAME BREATH — I turned G-COMPLETE red by quoting a design file's template syntax into the APPEND-ONLY progress journal, and the journal cannot be edited to take it back. Registered because it is a finding against my own work and the recording obligation covers exactly that. WHAT THE GATE SAW: G-COMPLETE screens content for placeholder markers and its pattern list ends with a mustache hole — the token an unfinished template leaves behind — so a faithfully quoted design fragment and an unfinished document are indistinguishable to it. Three rows failed, all three written minutes earlier. THE ESCAPE IS DESIGNED AND DOCUMENTED IN THE SOURCE, and I read it rather than guessing: the call site strips CODE SPANS before searching, with a comment saying such markers inside code spans are example text rather than unfinished markers. Backtick any quoted template syntax. WHY IT WAS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX: a defect TITLE is mutable and was rewritten; two PROGRESS ENTRIES are not — entity_upsert on an existing PE- id is refused by a UNIQUE constraint whose message says corrections are recorded as new entries, which is correct design and precisely why the mistake cost something. REPAIRED THROUGH THE SANCTIONED PATH: the runtime store is an always-fresh :memory: SQLite rebuilt from the canonical JSONL on open, and the recorded procedure for a bad write is 'rollback is git only' — so package_close, a WHOLE-FILE git checkout of progress_entries.jsonl at the last good commit, package_open to rebuild from the restored file, then re-append with backticks. No hand-edit of package data, PE-325..PE-327 untouched, and the same ids reallocated so no gap appears. ⚠ THE GENERAL LESSON IS NOT ABOUT MUSTACHES: the package is PROSE ABOUT CODE, so any syntax quoted into it is read by the gates as the package's own text — code-span quoted fragments. ⚠ AND THE SHARPER ONE: run gate_run() AFTER writing, not only before. Had I closed on the merge, main would have carried a red critical gate whose failing rows were immutable, and the next session would have inherited both.

A VISUAL CHECK CAUGHT WHAT THE WHOLE SUITE STRUCTURALLY COULD NOT — PR #277 (e31f7ac), a follow-up to DEF-041. THE GAP: #276 changed a span into a button on a screen that HAS a design reference, and everything that verified it — component tests, axe, the frontend and backend CI jobs — runs in JSDOM, which does not render. The project's own recorded rule says a green suite is not a look, and the definition of done says RTL verified. Neither was satisfied by anything I had run; the verification was SKIPPED rather than passed, and I would have reported the item done without it. WHAT THE CHECK FOUND: .adm-switch hard-codes cursor: not-allowed, because it was authored when the element was an inert span. Making it operable for Chairman and Secretary therefore told EXACTLY the two roles allowed to change voting eligibility that the control is forbidden — a visible regression that no assertion in the codebase could see. Fixed by making the cursor follow the SAME attribute the click handler does, so the two cannot drift apart, plus padding: 0 because a user-agent button carries some by default and the knob is absolutely positioned against the exact 38x22 box. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, per the recorded visual-loop rule that the harness must import ONLY the stylesheets the real route imports: a throwaway page served over http (the file: protocol is blocked), measured in a real browser rather than eyeballed. New BUTTON 38x22 / padding 0 / border 0 / cursor pointer; the Administrator case identical but cursor not-allowed; the OLD SPAN 38x22 / padding 0 / border 0 — so the button is GEOMETRICALLY IDENTICAL to the span it replaced, because .adm-switch already overrode the user-agent border and background. RTL verified in the same pass: the knob sits at the inline-end when on (x=1381) and the inline-start when off (x=1397), correctly mirrored by inset-inline-start. ⚠ AND THE SCREENSHOT ITSELF LIED ONCE: the full-page capture showed a stray pill shape outside the control in both RTL rows. Rather than explain it away, the DOM was measured — exactly 6 switches and 6 knobs, all inside their switches — which proves nothing is there and the shape is a full-page stitching artifact. A screenshot is evidence about pixels, not about elements; when the two disagree, measure. ⚠ RECORDED RATHER THAN CHANGED: the inert button is now FOCUSABLE where the span was not, so a keyboard user can tab to it and press Space to no effect. That is the ordinary trade-off against the disabled attribute (which would remove it from the tab order but also drop the aria-disabled styling hook), and it is noted so the next accessibility pass does not re-discover it as a bug.

The AC-011 e2e failure is diagnosed and it is a PRODUCT defect, not a harness one: DEF-075, a check-then-insert race in JIT provisioning. Measured from the api container log rather than reasoned - DbUpdateException wrapping SqlException 'Cannot insert duplicate key row in object membership.committee_members with unique index IX_committee_members_KeycloakUserId', logged twice for the same subject within one second, each surfacing as a 500 on POST /api/members/me. THE HYPOTHESIS RECORDED ON DEF-074 WAS CORRECT AND IS NOW CONFIRMED, which is the point of having written it down as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion. The discriminating evidence was cheap and came before the log: ac043-reorder.spec.ts, the spec that used to run first, uses loginAs plus captureBearer and never calls meMember, so a run's first login produced exactly ONE provisioning call. ac011-guest-scope is the first spec ever to call roleSession at the start of a run, which adds an explicit second POST concurrent with the SPA's own, at the one moment no member row exists. The race was always there and had simply never been occupied. ⚠ IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED IN THIS PR, and the reason is structural rather than a preference: catching the duplicate-key inside the handler cannot work, because TransactionBehavior opens an ambient transaction lazily on the first module write and only rolls back when the handler throws, so swallowing the failure leaves a doomed transaction - and SQL Server's own warning in the same log says savepoints are disabled because MARS is enabled, so there is no clean point to roll back to. The fix has to retry the WHOLE command above TransactionBehavior, which is a new cross-cutting pipeline behaviour and deserves its own change with its own tests rather than being folded into a PR that already carries an authorization change. TWO ROUNDS OF DIAGNOSTIC REPAIR WERE NEEDED FIRST AND THE SECOND CORRECTED THE FIRST: raising the log dump from 200 to 4000 lines was choosing a bigger magic number for a question a number cannot answer, and 4000 api lines still began eight minutes into a suite whose failure was in the first minute. Removing the tail entirely from the api dump is what made the exception readable.

CORRECTION to my own analysis recorded earlier today on DEF-075 and in PE-348. I stated there that fixing the provisioning race REQUIRED retrying the whole command above TransactionBehavior, because catching the DbUpdateException inside the handler would leave a doomed ambient transaction, and I cited SQL Server's own MARS savepoint warning as support. THAT REASONING WAS WRONG, and it was wrong in the way this project keeps paying for: a plausible premise carried forward without being checked. TWO FACTS, both of which make a small local recovery correct. FIRST, a unique-key violation on SQL Server aborts the STATEMENT, not the transaction - XACT_ABORT is off - so the ambient transaction this command opened is intact afterwards and TransactionBehavior commits it normally; nothing partial was written either, because the failed insert was a single statement, which is precisely what makes the savepoint warning irrelevant here rather than fatal. SECOND, and this is the one that turns a hopeful retry into a guaranteed recovery: SQL Server does not fail the loser's insert immediately, it BLOCKS on the winner's exclusive key lock and raises the duplicate only once that transaction has COMMITTED - so by the time the loser is in the catch, the winning row is committed and readable, and the re-read is guaranteed to find it. THE CONSEQUENCE IS A MUCH SMALLER FIX than the one I proposed and the operator approved: no new cross-cutting pipeline behaviour, no marker interface, no change-tracker reset abstraction, no registration-ordering constraint against TransactionBehavior. The loser detaches its own pending insert, re-reads, adopts the winner's row and syncs claims onto it. A DbUpdateException with no winning row behind it is rethrown unchanged. Shipped as PR #279 with four tests, each guard mutation-proven and each mutant confirmed to compile first: removing the recovery kills 3, removing the detach kills 1, absorbing a non-race failure kills 1, and letting the loser still report created kills 1. Backend 1699 green and the counts reconcile exactly - 1005 baseline plus 4. ⚠ The race is SIMULATED rather than run, deliberately: the InMemory provider does not enforce unique indexes, so a genuinely concurrent test there would pass whether or not the fix existed, which is the DEF-066 shape exactly. The SQL-Server-side half is proven by the AC-011 e2e leg on a real database - the run that produced this defect in the first place.

DEF-056 and AC-003's emitters are WRITTEN AND BUILDING BUT NOT PROVEN, and are parked on branch feat/def-056-refusal-audit rather than merged. An unproven audit emitter is worse than none: it would let a future reader believe refusals are recorded when nothing demonstrates that they are. WHAT EXISTS: AuditingAuthorizationResultHandler records the policy-layer 403s that short-circuit before MediatR - Forbidden only and never Challenged, since Challenged means no usable identity and a Forbidden row for it would describe a denial of an action nobody was identified to attempt - and it uses CancellationToken.None deliberately so a client hanging up mid-refusal still leaves the record. Separately, ProvisionCurrentUser emits before its own ForbiddenAccessException, which the middleware handler structurally CANNOT catch, because that request PASSES authorization and is refused inside the handler; AV-159 called this DEF-056's family arriving by a second route, and a single fix for both would have left AC-003's audit clause quietly unmet. RefusalAuditTests asserts both as ROWS and adds two controls: an unauthenticated request must NOT leave a Forbidden row, and neither must an allowed caller - without that second one every assertion is equally consistent with something emitting on every request. WHY IT IS PARKED, and the diagnosis is measured rather than guessed. Both positive tests fail with an EMPTY audit table. A temporary if(true) probe in the handler still produced no row, so the handler never runs in that harness at all. The refused response carries an EMPTY BODY, which is the framework's bare forbid rather than ProblemDetails, so the authorization middleware genuinely did refuse - the two facts together say the result handler is not the one being invoked. ⚠ THE THREAD TO PULL NEXT is a resolution boundary I could not explain and did not paper over: IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler does not resolve from Program.cs's top-level statements NOR from the Acmp.Api.Tests project, while it resolves perfectly in a file beside the implementation inside the same Acmp.Api project. Registration currently goes through an extension method next to the type for that reason. Until that is understood, whether the handler is registered at all is unverified. ⚠ SEPARATE OBSERVATION, recorded so it is not lost: one integration test failed once during this work and passed on an immediate re-run, and the failing test's name was not captured. It is NOT attributable to these emitters - no test in the solution references Authorization.Forbidden, so nothing counts audit rows - but re-running until green is exactly the habit DEC-050 d3 warns about, so it is written down rather than dismissed.

The scratchpad is for work in flight; a pointer into it is a dangling reference the moment the session ends, and it will not fail loudly - it will simply be a path that is not there.

DEF-056 + AC-003 — the parked branch's BLOCKER WAS NOT REAL, and the correction is the finding. The parked note recorded that both positive tests failed with an empty audit table and that an `if (true)` probe in the handler produced no row, concluding the handler never runs in the API harness. Measured today: the rows were being written the WHOLE TIME. The failing run's own log printed `AuditEvent Authorization.Forbidden by kc-roleless seq=1` inside the very test that failed. The cause was the TEST HELPER: it selected `AuditEvent.Action`, and `IAuditSink.EmitAsync` writes a LEAN v1 row where `EventType` is set and the enriched `Action` column is NULL. Every authorization refusal in this codebase takes that path, the pre-existing AuthorizationBehavior emitter included, so the assertion read null for exactly the rows it existed to find. `/api/audit` normalises as `(Action ?? EventType)`, so the helper now asserts the value a reader actually sees. SECOND-ORDER AND WORSE: the two NotContain controls were passing VACUOUSLY the whole time, because a collection of nulls contains no string whatever the code does — a hollow pass, the same class as the risk-liveness finding. THE OTHER HALF OF THE PARKED NOTE was a missing using directive: `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` lives in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Policy`, which is not in the Web SDK implicit usings — that is the whole of the resolution mystery, and registration was never in doubt. GENERALISABLE: an absence with nothing proving the instrument ran is not a measurement, and this is trap 25b arriving through a probe rather than through a mutant.

AV-159 IS WRONG AND IT IS MY OWN ROW — corrected here rather than by editing it. That reading searched only for emitters of `Authorization.Forbidden` and took their absence as the absence of any record. It missed `Authentication.NoRoleClaim`, emitted in AuthenticationExtensions.MapKeycloakRolesAsync at the JwtBearer OnTokenValidated hook — which is the AC's own moment, when they complete SSO login — for exactly the case where the role mapper returns an empty set. GENERALISABLE, and this is the ninth instance: read the implementation before calling something absent, and a register row is an implementation too.

(2) A lesson's content is UNPROTECTED on exactly the write that makes it immutable: the immutability trigger fires only when the row is ALREADY Approved, and `entity_upsert` demands FULL rows, so the Proposed-to-Approved transition necessarily re-sends every content column with no drift guard. Immutability begins one write too late, and the write it skips carries the most re-transcribed text in the row's life — which is LL-001's own subject. (3) DX: a foreign-key failure reports only that a constraint failed, while the NOT NULL path in the same tool names the table, the column and the rule; parity would have saved a round-trip. GENERALISABLE, and it is the reason this correction exists at all: 'the run was clean' and 'the tooling behaved correctly' are DIFFERENT CLAIMS, and answering the second with evidence for the first is how a tool defect goes unreported.

DEF-067 FIXED IN PR #285, AND ITS OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG — which is the part worth carrying. THE ROW PREDICTED 'an assertion racing an async state update' and instructed: repair by awaiting the settled state with findBy or waitFor, NEVER a timeout or a retry, both of which would hide a genuine regression. I DID THAT FIRST. Two genuinely racy assertions were replaced — a getByText immediately after a click, and a call-count assertion on a handler that awaits a mutation — AND THE FAILURE PERSISTED. That persistence is what produced the real diagnosis rather than a guess. WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS, reproduced by looping the full coverage suite rather than inferred: `Test timed out in 5000ms` at 5090ms, with the test still EXECUTING. Not a race at all — a duration overrun. The test drives about a dozen userEvent interactions and v8 coverage instrumentation slows every one, so the body exceeds vitest's 5s default on a loaded runner and finishes comfortably on an idle machine, which is exactly why `vitest run` never showed it and `test:cov` did. ⚠⚠ AND THE SECOND FAILURE IS WHY THE FIX IS A CONFIG CHANGE RATHER THAN A PATCH. On the next loop a DIFFERENT, unrelated test tripped the same ceiling — RecordDecisionDialog's override-flag case at 5042ms. So DEF-067 named ONE test but the defect is a CLASS: interaction-heavy component tests against a 5s default under instrumentation, where WHICH one trips is a function of load. Pinning per-test timeouts would have been whack-a-mole against a moving target, and the row would have kept re-opening under a new name. ⚠ WHY RAISING THE TIMEOUT IS NOT THE ANTI-PATTERN THE ROW WARNED ABOUT, because the distinction is the whole justification: a timeout hides a RACE by giving a racy assertion more chances to get lucky. There is no race to hide here — every assertion still runs and still fails if the behaviour breaks; the tests only needed enough wall-clock to reach them. 15s is about 3x the observed overrun, so a genuine hang still fails loudly. Applying the row's stated remedy literally would have left this defect open indefinitely. EVIDENCE: 2 failures in 7 runs before, 0 in 5 after, all under `npm run test:cov`, the only mode it ever appeared in. ⚠ FIVE CLEAN RUNS IS NOT BY ITSELF PROOF A FLAKE IS GONE and is not claimed as such — what carries the conclusion is that the MECHANISM was measured and removed. ⚠ THE findBy/waitFor CHANGES WERE KEPT as genuine hardening, and their comment was CORRECTED: the first draft said they were the fix, and a comment that misattributes a fix sends the next reader after the wrong cause. GENERALISABLE: a defect row's predicted CAUSE is a hypothesis even when the row is precise, evidenced and written by someone who reproduced the symptom — and this row was all three. It is the tenth instance of 'read the implementation before believing the description', arriving this time as a prescribed REMEDY that would not have worked.
DEF-067 fixed as a CLASS (vitest testTimeout), not per-test. Its predicted cause (a race) was wrong; the failure is a duration overrun. Open, CI running.

DEF-067 MERGED as 9c2b5ac (PR #285). DEF-039 SCOPED AND STOPPED SHORT OF SHIPPING, and the reason is recorded as DEF-078. WHAT SCOPING FOUND: DEF-039 describes a System Health tile that can never report anything but 'monitoring not configured' on cloud, because ADR-0035 moved the cloud stack to S3 while the catalog still lists MinIO. Following the tile back to the CHECK that feeds it — rather than stopping at the UI, which is where the row stops — the same root cause one layer down is a READINESS probe that cannot pass on the environment it runs in: ReadinessChecks registers 'minio' as an HTTP GET of `{scheme}://{Minio:Endpoint}/minio/health/live`, Unhealthy with the `ready` tag and degradedOnFailure false, while docker-compose.cloud.yml sets Minio__Endpoint to the S3 endpoint on both api and worker and overrides HealthChecks:MinioUrl NOWHERE in the repository. S3 does not serve that path, so the check should report Unhealthy and /readyz should be 503 — and promote.sh smokes /readyz as step 3 of 4. ⚠⚠ NOT ASSERTED AS A LIVE FAILURE, AND THE UNCERTAINTY IS RECORDED ON THE ROW RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER: UAT is recorded as live and promote.sh smokes /readyz, which is evidence AGAINST the prediction. Either promote has not run against the S3-backed stack or something outside the repository compensates. Resolving it takes ONE curl against the live host, which only the operator can run. ⚠ AND THE FIX WAS NOT SHIPPED, DELIBERATELY. The fix is clear and is better than the status quo either way — ACMP reaches BOTH MinIO and S3 through ONE Minio SDK client, so the probe should be an SDK-level BucketExistsAsync rather than an HTTP GET of a MinIO-only daemon path: environment-aware BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by a branch, which is exactly what DEC-047 asked for, working unchanged on both backends, proving the app can reach its BUCKET rather than that a daemon is alive, and unit-assertable with a mocked client instead of being ExcludeFromCodeCoverage plumbing. But this is the PRODUCTION READINESS PATH, the prediction is unconfirmed, and I cannot reach UAT to verify either the current behaviour or the change. Shipping it on an inference would repeat exactly the error DEF-065 exists to prevent — treating the code existing as the fix when the RUNNING is the fix. GENERALISABLE: a defect row scoped at the UI layer can be the visible end of something more serious, and the way to find out is to follow the value back to the thing that produces it. DEF-039 said 'a tile reads unmonitored'; one layer down it is 'a readiness gate may be failing in production'.

DEF-012's PER-ITEM EVIDENCE PASS (DEC-054 d4) — SCOPED, MEASURED, AND STOPPED BEFORE WRITING, because the measurement changes the decision. THE ROW SAYS the residue is 'items with no per-item shipping evidence', implying a subset. IT IS THE WHOLE TREE: v_backlog selects wbs_items whose lifecycle_status is not in (Implemented, Superseded, Obsolete, Rejected), and ALL 155 rows qualify — 140 Approved, 15 Deferred, 20 roots and 135 leaves, and NOT ONE has a slice_id. THE ONLY MECHANICAL PER-ITEM EVIDENCE AVAILABLE, and it is a good one where it applies: every leaf title names the requirements it realises ('Realizes FR-150 to FR-153'), and a requirement reaches Implemented ONLY through the auto-advance trigger, which fires when every non-retired AC of that requirement has a LATEST verdict of Met. So an FR's Implemented status is itself AC-evidenced rather than asserted, and 'close a leaf when every FR it names is Implemented' is genuine per-item evidence, not bulk-closing. APPLYING IT CLOSES NINE OF 135. It discriminates correctly where evidence exists — WBS-16.1, 16.2 and 16.3 close on FR-150/152/153, while WBS-16.4 (audit export) and WBS-16.5 (retention policy) STAY OPEN because FR-154 and FR-155 are only Approved and AuditEndpoints.cs has no export route. That is the pass working. ⚠⚠ AND THE REASON ONLY NINE CLOSE IS DEF-012's REAL ROOT CAUSE, ONE LAYER BELOW WHAT THE ROW STATES. Measured across the whole register: 222 requirements, of which EXACTLY 60 have at least one active acceptance criterion and EXACTLY those 60 are Implemented; EXACTLY 162 have NO acceptance criterion and EXACTLY those 162 are Approved. A perfect one-to-one correlation. Requirement status is therefore determined ENTIRELY by whether the requirement ever had an AC — the trigger fired for all 60 that had them, every AC Met, and never fired for the 162 that had none. So `Approved` on those 162 means 'never had an acceptance criterion', NOT 'not implemented'. v_backlog over-reports because the evidence chain AC to FR to WBS is 27 percent complete, not because imported work items carry no execution state. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TASK AS SCOPED: the per-item pass CANNOT be completed from package data, because for roughly 124 of 135 leaves there is no acceptance criterion anywhere in the chain and therefore nothing to close them on. The remaining options are (a) accept the disclosed state — the recommendation DEC-054 d4 overruled, now much better supported; (b) write acceptance criteria for the 162 unevidenced requirements, an enormous programme; or (c) close the leaves on a DIFFERENT basis such as the delivering slice or the git history, which is precisely the bulk-close DEF-012 exists to prevent. ⚠ NOTHING WAS WRITTEN. Executing the pass would also have meant re-typing roughly 21,354 characters of titles across 155 full-row upserts, since entity_upsert demands full rows — LL-001's hazard at maximum scale, for bookkeeping whose value the measurement above has just undermined. Surfacing that before spending it is the point.

DEF-012 CLOSED AS WON'T-FIX UNDER DEC-055, AND THE DECISION REVERSES AN OPERATOR OVERRULE UNDER THE OPERATOR'S OWN DELEGATION — stated plainly so no future reader finds an agent quietly undoing one. FACT ONE, SCALE: all 155 wbs_items sit in v_backlog and NOT ONE carries a slice_id, so there is no residue to triage, there is the whole register. FACT TWO, AND IT DECIDES IT: the only mechanical per-item rule available is 'a leaf closes when every requirement it names is Implemented' — which LOOKS sound, because a requirement reaches Implemented only through the AC auto-advance trigger and is therefore evidenced rather than asserted. THE RULE IS UNSOUND AND THE COUNTEREXAMPLE IS UNFIXABLE BY ANY FILTER: it closes WBS-20.4, the EMAIL ADAPTER, on the strength of the Implemented FR-130, while 'no email in v1, in-app centre only' is a HARD CONSTRAINT of this project. THE MEASUREMENT THAT RE-SCOPED DEF-012, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH CARRYING: this package holds 222 requirements; EXACTLY the 60 with at least one active acceptance criterion are Implemented, and EXACTLY the 162 with none are Approved. A perfect one-to-one, and mechanical rather than coincidental — a requirement advances ONLY through the auto-advance trigger, which fires when every non-retired AC has a latest verdict of Met, so a requirement with no ACs can never advance no matter how thoroughly it shipped. CONSEQUENCE: requirement lifecycle_status in this package measures WHETHER ANYONE WROTE AN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION, not whether the thing was built. v_backlog inherits that and reports it faithfully; the view is not lying, the layer beneath it is thin. ⚠ AND THIS IS WHY CLOSING THE WBS ROWS WOULD HAVE MADE THINGS WORSE RATHER THAN MERELY COSTLY: v_backlog would read clean while 162 requirements still sat at Approved, HIDING the evidence gap that the 2.4.0 execution_state_note currently discloses at populate. A green view over an unevidenced register is the failure this project keeps recording under a different name. The remediation is real and is a programme, not a task — carried as DW-029, sized honestly (162 requirements each needing an AC written, slice-bound and audited against a commit) with a CONDITIONAL trigger rather than a date: activate when requirement status or v_backlog must be AUTHORITATIVE rather than indicative.

DEF-067 FLIPPED TO FIXED — AND THE REASON IT WAS STILL OPEN IS ITSELF THE FINDING. The fix shipped in PR #285 (commit 9c2b5ac, vitest.config.ts testTimeout 15_000, verified present on main) and PE-383 recorded the full narrative on the same day, but the DEFECT ROW WAS NEVER FLIPPED: progress_update was done and entity_upsert on the row was missed. It was caught only because a re-derivation script printed the remaining open defects as a side effect of verifying DEF-012, NOT because any gate objected: defects-minor is advisory and lists low/medium rows without failing. ⚠ THE ROW'S OWN PRESCRIPTION WAS ALSO WRONG AND HAS BEEN CORRECTED IN PLACE ABOVE THE PRESERVED ORIGINAL: it predicted 'an assertion racing an async state update' and explicitly FORBADE a timeout. findBy*/waitFor were applied FIRST and the failure persisted — which is how the real cause was reached rather than assumed: 'Test timed out in 5000ms', failing at ~5090ms with the test still EXECUTING. prm-next.md REFRESHED — AND IT HAD BECOME ACTIVELY DANGEROUS, NOT MERELY STALE, WHICH IS THE DISTINCTION WORTH CARRYING.
