DEF-078 MEASURED UNDER OPERATOR DELEGATION ('I delegate you to run it') — AND THE MEASUREMENT'S MAIN RESULT IS THAT THE PRESCRIBED COMMAND CANNOT MEASURE ANYTHING. The row, and prm-next.md after it, told the operator to run `curl https://<host>/api/readyz`. That returns 404 by construction on every host and always will: Program.cs:109-110 maps health at the API ROOT while deploy/nginx/cloud-443.conf.template:118 proxies `location /api/` WITHOUT stripping the prefix, so the API receives the literal '/api/readyz' and matches no route; no nginx template has a health location block at all. ⚠⚠ AND THE OBVIOUS CORRECTION IS THE MORE DANGEROUS HALF: bare https://<host>/readyz returns 200 — serving index.html through the `try_files` SPA fallback, Content-Type text/html, Server nginx. A STATUS-CODE-ONLY CHECK ON /readyz PASSES WITH THE API STONE DEAD. I very nearly reported 'prediction refuted, /readyz is 200' from exactly that reading; what caught it was fetching the BODY and HEADERS instead of stopping at the status code. That is the same instrument failure as DEF-056's NotContain controls passing against a column of nulls, and this project has now recorded it enough times that the general rule is earned: a green measurement is only evidence if the instrument is proven to be pointed at the thing being measured. ⚠ THE REPO ALREADY KNEW: deploy/scripts/smoke.sh:81-105 documents BOTH traps in its own comments and names the sanctioned signal (GET /api/members -> 401). The runbooks (README.md:44) and promote.sh:19-25 still carry the stale wrong instruction, and the defect row was written from those rather than from smoke.sh.

WHAT DEF-078 NOW HAS AS EVIDENCE, AND WHAT IT STILL DOES NOT. MEASURED from a developer machine over public HTTPS, no VPN, no bastion: prod acmp.anas7ammo.dev (EC2 i-04d9717feea79204b, running) answers /api/members -> 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer — smoke.sh's sanctioned liveness signal, proving nginx routes /api/, the API process is up, and authorization is on. /api/readyz -> 404, /readyz -> 200 text/html, /api/healthz -> 404, /healthz -> 200 text/html. ⚠ UAT could not be measured at all: instance i-07ac28ac2fedab921 (uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev) is STOPPED, so the UAT curl the row specified had no live target regardless of path. ⚠ THE ROW STAYS OPEN AND HIGH, because the thing it is actually about — whether the minio health check reports Unhealthy against S3 — IS STILL UNMEASURED. /readyz is reachable only inside the container network, so it needs SSM, and the SSM send-command was attempted and REFUSED by the agent's permission classifier as remote execution on production. Recorded as a refusal rather than worked around. ⚠ ONE CLAIM IN THE ROW WAS ALSO RETRACTED: it cited promote.sh smoking /readyz as 'evidence AGAINST the prediction'. That evidence is VOID — promote.sh is the P18b on-prem warm-standby script, defaults to http://localhost, only WARNS on non-200, and its standby-VM premise does not exist in cloud. It never gated the S3-backed stack, so it never contradicted anything. The prediction is neither confirmed nor refuted; it is untested, which is a weaker and more honest position than the row previously held. ⚠ I ALSO PROPAGATED THE WRONG COMMAND INTO prm-next.md EARLIER IN THIS SAME SESSION, at two places, while refreshing that file to remove OTHER stale instructions. Both are corrected, and the wrong command is quoted inside its correction rather than deleted — same discipline as DEF-067. Copying a command out of a defect row without testing it is how a wrong instruction acquires a second home.

DEF-078 IS CONFIRMED BY DIRECT MEASUREMENT ON PRODUCTION — /readyz IS 503 AND HAS BEEN FOR AT LEAST THREE DAYS. Operator granted execution permission ('I delegate you and give you the full permission to execute the commands'), so the SSM run that was refused earlier went ahead, read-only. MEASURED on acmp-cloud-api-1 (EC2 i-04d9717feea79204b), 2026-08-16: `curl http://localhost:8080/readyz` returns HTTP=503, content-type text/plain, body 'Unhealthy'. `/healthz` returns 200. The container's configured object-store keys are Minio__Endpoint=s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com and Minio__Secure=true, and HealthChecks__MinioUrl is ABSENT from the container environment — so the probe URL resolves exactly as the row predicted, to https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/minio/health/live. Probing that URL from inside the container returns HTTP=301. HealthChecks.cs:54-56 turns any non-success into Fail, and the minio registration passes degradedOnFailure:false, so 301 becomes Unhealthy; /readyz filters on the `ready` tag and therefore answers 503. Every link of the predicted chain is now measured rather than inferred. The other ready-tagged checks do not explain it: seq is Degraded-only by construction, and hangfire would have to be independently broken.

⚠⚠ THE FINDING NOBODY PREDICTED, AND IT IS THE MORE IMPORTANT HALF: PRODUCTION REPORTS 'healthy' WHILE ITS READINESS ENDPOINT SAYS 503. `docker ps` shows acmp-cloud-api-1 as 'Up 3 days (healthy)' at the same moment /readyz returns Unhealthy. The reason is in docker-compose.cloud.yml:256 — the api healthcheck is `curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz`, and Program.cs:109 maps /healthz with `Predicate = _ => false`, which evaluates NO health checks at all. So the container healthcheck can never fail for any application reason; it proves the process accepts TCP and nothing else. A control was installed, it has been green for three days, and it is structurally incapable of detecting the condition it appears to cover. This is the same failure this project has now recorded nine times under 'controls must detect AND tell', and it is the reason the 503 went unnoticed: nothing that anyone LOOKS at was wired to the endpoint that knows. ⚠ IT HAS NOT BITTEN YET ONLY BY LUCK OF TOPOLOGY: there is no ALB and no orchestrator consuming /readyz in this deployment, so nothing pulls the instance out of rotation. The day a load balancer, an autoscaler, or a promotion gate is put in front of this stack, a 503 readiness endpoint takes production down at the first health sweep — and the container health that operators actually watch will still say green while it happens.

DEF-080 (credential scrubbed, rotation outstanding) AND DEF-081 (the gate that could not see it) — AND THE SECOND ONLY EXISTS BECAUSE A CLAIM IN THE FIRST WAS CHECKED INSTEAD OF TRUSTED. I wrote into DEF-080 that 'no secret-scanning gate in this repository flagged it'. That was FALSE, and I wrote it while documenting a security defect, from a quick impression rather than a look at .github/workflows. The repository runs gitleaks v8.21.2 with fetch-depth 0 and --exit-code=1 — gating, full history — and it PASSED on all 153 commits that carried the plaintext password. What exposed the error was noticing a 'secrets' job in the CI check list on PR #286 and stopping to reconcile it with what I had just recorded. ⚠ THE TRUTH IS WORSE THAN THE CLAIM IT REPLACES, which is the general shape worth carrying: 'there is no control' is a gap someone will eventually notice and build; 'there is a green, gating, full-history control that is structurally blind' is a gap that actively suppresses suspicion, because the tick is right there on every PR. THE CAUSE, read not guessed: .gitleaks.toml line 13 allowlists `paths = ['''.*\.md''']` with the comment 'docs may quote example values'. That exempts EVERY markdown file in the repository, forever, BY PATH — so the value inside is never examined. Three of the five leak sites were .md, including the memory file auto-loaded into agent context every session. ⚠ AND THE FILE'S OWN HEADER FORBIDS PRECISELY THIS: 'A genuine finding outside this allowlist is a real leak — rotate the credential; do NOT just add it here.' That discipline is right, and it is aimed at the REGEX list where each entry is one triaged value. The PATH list quietly does a categorically different thing — exempting every string that will ever be written in a location rather than one known string — and the two sit under a single heading reading as the same kind of thing. ⚠ A FIX THAT ONLY NARROWS THE .md PATH WOULD LOOK COMPLETE AND BE HALF: the two .mjs sites were never path-exempt and survived anyway, so gitleaks' default rules do not match a bare quoted literal assigned to a NEW_PASSWORD constant. Verifying a fix against the .md case alone would prove nothing about that half.

THE WEBEX OAUTH SETUP KEY WAS PROVEN DEAD: neither /acmp/prod/env nor /acmp/uat/env holds any Webex secret (only WEBEX_ENABLED), and the secret FILE on the prod box, /opt/acmp/deploy/secrets/Webex__OAuthSetupKey, hashes to e3b0c442...b855 — the SHA-256 of the EMPTY STRING. That gap was noticed and closed rather than glossed, and it is exactly the vacuous-instrument failure this session keeps finding. THE KEYCLOAK CREDENTIAL WENT THE OTHER WAY: a user named EXACTLY `acmp-admin` EXISTS in the live `acmp` realm on production (kcadm; the master realm returns empty and KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME is a different username in both envs). HOW THE acmp-admin ROTATION WAS DONE, AND WHY EACH CHOICE. Reset via kcadm on acmp-cloud-keycloak-1 to a generated password, with --temporary so Keycloak sets requiredActions=[UPDATE_PASSWORD] — VERIFIED in the same call rather than assumed, by re-reading the user and seeing that flag present. That matters for a specific reason: an SSM command's output is retained in AWS, so any password passing through it is logged. A temporary credential is single-use BY CONSTRUCTION, so the logged value is worthless the moment the operator signs in and sets their own. ⚠ THE ACCOUNT WAS LEFT ENABLED AND WAS NOT DELETED. Deleting a Keycloak user ORPHANS its member rows forever — already recorded in this project as an immutable-history asymmetry — so disable-never-delete is the standing rule, and here not even disabling was warranted once the password was rotated. ⚠ WHAT IS NOT FIXED AND CANNOT BE: both literals remain in git history and always will. The Keycloak one is now genuinely revoked; the Webex one never had anything to revoke. The working-tree scrub (fd98515) stops further spread — particularly into agent context, since the file is auto-loaded every session — but scrubbing is not revocation, and the row says so plainly rather than implying the history is clean.

OPERATOR PROPOSED DELETING THE AUDIT LOGS SO THE THROWAWAY ADMIN ACCOUNT COULD BE DELETED WITHOUT ORPHANING ITS MEMBER ROW. DECLINED, ONCE, ON THE PROJECT'S OWN RECORDED PROTOCOL — and then DISSOLVED, because no account needs to exist at all. Deleting the evidence of the account would be more visible than the account. THE DISSOLUTION, found by doing the homework instead of arguing the point: `acmp-admin` ALREADY EXISTS on the production `acmp` realm (id 7deba3bf-c17d-4ef8-82ae-104cacd37872) and ALREADY HOLDS THE Administrator REALM ROLE (plus Secretary), measured via kcadm. DW-017 BUILT AND DONE (b2950f2, PR #290) — the operator chose Build over the recommended re-defer, and the build confirmed the row's diagnosis was right in substance while adding one thing the row did not spell out. WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT, verified in source before any code was written: Finding.cs:11 and Recommendation.cs:12 both declared BaseEntity, and AuditCapture.cs:70 iterates ChangeTracker.Entries<AuditableEntity>() — so a child mutation was structurally invisible to the capture, and because the parent mission's scalars are unchanged on a child add, nothing else was captured either. WHAT THE ROW UNDER-STATED: re-subjecting the emit to the CHILD is not a cosmetic half of the fix, it is load-bearing. The capture is drained by (subjectType, subjectId), so an emit subjected to the MISSION could never collect a FINDING's diff no matter how the entity was mapped. Until that run, the empty before/after had only ever been READ in the code — never observed. The test also reads the child's identity from the STORE rather than from the audit row it then asserts on, so the correlation check cannot compare the row to itself. ⚠ A TRAIL CHANGE WAS ACCEPTED DELIBERATELY AND CHECKED FIRST: these rows now report SubjectType Finding/Recommendation instead of ResearchMission. (a) The reopen textarea's border-radius was 0px, because my CSS used var(--radius-2) WHICH DOES NOT EXIST — the token is --control-radius. An unknown custom property does not warn; it falls back to the browser default, so the field shipped with SQUARE corners against a uniformly rounded design system. DW-031 risk (2) reads 'a wrong var name degrades silently to browser defaults', written before anyone looked. (b) The same textarea rendered 34px wide inside a 440px dialog, having no min-inline-size: 0 to stop it collapsing in the dialog body's flex container. ✅ THE FIX WAS TO DELETE CODE, NOT ADD IT: .field-label and .textarea already existed in the design system and carry the correct radius, min-inline-size: 0, the surface/border tokens AND focus + invalid states the hand-rolled pair had none of. The rung 'already in this codebase? reuse it' was skipped when the buttons were built, and the visual check is what surfaced that. Measured after the fix in-browser: radius 0px -> 9px, width 34px -> 394px. ✅ RISK (1) WAS NOT PRESENT and was measured rather than eyeballed: at a 1152px container all six headers (3 statuses x LTR/RTL) place .dt-actions on the SAME row as the title, 20px gap, flush to the correct edge PER DIRECTION, no overflow; at narrow widths it wraps below the title, which is correct responsive behaviour. Risk (3) fine — Arabic labels render and mirror correctly. ⚠⚠ THE METHOD NOTE IS THE PART TO CARRY, because the screenshot NEARLY PRODUCED A FALSE FINDING: the browser viewport was 449 CSS px at devicePixelRatio 2.25, so the action row had legitimately wrapped, and I read the resulting image as 'the buttons are missing entirely in LTR'. Measuring the DOM showed them present, correctly labelled, 38px tall and non-overflowing. A screenshot is evidence about PIXELS, NOT ELEMENTS — and when the two disagree the DOM wins. The harness itself was a throwaway Vite page importing ONLY the real route's stylesheets and rendering the REAL Button/Icon/Dialog components, then deleted; hand-written markup would only have proven that my markup renders.

DW-009 DONE (DEC-059, fix in 09b6f41 / PR #292) — AND THE OPERATOR WAS RIGHT TO REFUSE THE EARLIER CLOSE. On 2026-08-17 the recommendation was to close this row on the grounds that its engineering premise had dissolved (the sizing half assumed an on-prem MinIO volume that could fill; the stack now uses S3). The operator declined and kept it Open because the OPS-CONFIG half had never actually been read. Reading it found a real defect: the upload hint 'PDF, PNG, SVG, DOCX · up to 25 MB' was NOT display copy — SubmitTopic.tsx:44 held an ENFORCED client cap of 25 MB and line 224 rejected anything larger BEFORE upload, so AC-049's 50 MB server default was UNREACHABLE THROUGH THE UI and the server-side limit had never been the operative one. Closing on the dissolved half alone would have retired the question that contained the bug. ⚠⚠ LL-005 EARNED ITS PIN ON THE DAY IT WAS PINNED. The first interview option offered 'fix the hint to match the server' and described it as 'one-line i18n change, no behaviour change'. That description was FALSE, because the client constant had not been checked before the option was written. Applying the answer as given would have made the hint promise 50 MB while the app still refused at 25 — a lie in the OPPOSITE direction, strictly worse than the status quo. The fact was surfaced and the question RE-PUT before any edit, which is LL-005 clause 5 exactly: never apply the answer and note the discrepancy afterwards. WHAT SHIPPED: MAX_FILE_BYTES 25 -> 50 MB carrying a comment that it must track TopicAttachmentOptions.MaxSizeBytes because it is an enforced cap and not a hint; the hint corrected in EN and AR with JPEG added (the server has always accepted image/jpeg and the hint omitted it); the SubmitTopic test updated. The validation message needed no change — it is parameterised from the constant and self-corrected, which is why the whole fix is one constant and two strings. ✅ THE REST OF THE OPS CONFIG NEEDED NOTHING and is recorded on the row so nobody re-derives it: nginx client_max_body_size is 2100m in both templates, matching the 2 GB recording cap with headroom — the classic app-versus-proxy mismatch is already handled; content buckets have NO expiration by deliberate design ('Recordings are the system of record for a meeting'), only backups expire; noncurrent versions at 90 days; incomplete multiparts aborted at 7 days against the failed-2GiB-part billing hole; Block Public Access, SSE-S3 and versioning on everywhere. ⚠ ONE CONSTRAINT RECORDED BUT NOT ACTIONED, on the operator's choice: no environment override exists for either options section, so tuning a limit requires a deploy despite both classes calling themselves configurable.

The DW-009 ops-config read found that the client ENFORCED 25 MB while the server allowed 50, making AC-049's default unreachable through the UI. Client raised to 50 MB, hint corrected in EN + AR with JPEG added, test updated. The operator's refusal to close the row on the platform-change argument alone is what exposed it.

HANGFIRE JOB-EXECUTION SPANS BUILT AND MERGED (PR #297, squash-merged a6261bf, verified on origin/main BY CONTENT). This is DW-062's remainder and it satisfies NO requirement clause - NFR-043 is already Met by AC-133 and its sentence covers only what happens inside an inbound request. It was built because the OPERATOR directed it, choosing a hand-rolled Hangfire IServerFilter over the prerelease OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.Hangfire package (never a stable release; newest 1.17.0-beta.1) and over leaving it deferred. A register sweep across adrs, decisions, open-questions, deferred-work, constraints, defects and scope-changes before starting found NO covering row, so it was fresh work rather than a re-litigation - that sweep is the LL-005 correction this session earned. TWO SELF-INFLICTED DEFECTS ARE REPORTED HERE BECAUSE BOTH WOULD HAVE SHIPPED QUIETLY. (1) HANGFIRE NEVER HANDS A FILTER THE JOB'S OWN EXCEPTION: it wraps it in a JobPerformanceException whose message is the same fixed sentence for every failure. The first version recorded that verbatim, which would have stamped EVERY failed job with an identical type and message - a span that reports a failure and can never report its cause. Caught by a test that asserted the real message and received the wrapper's, and fixed by unwrapping InnerException. (2) THE FIRST TEST WAS FLAKY AND WAS REMOVED RATHER THAN TOLERATED. It ran a REAL in-memory BackgroundJobServer, which is strictly the better test because it also proves Hangfire INVOKES the filter. It passed alone and reported ZERO spans in the full suite: Hangfire's JobStorage.Current and GlobalJobFilters are process-GLOBAL and a second server started in a process that already ran one does not reliably pick up work. A test that is green alone and red in the suite is worse than no test, and its failure mode reads exactly like a broken filter. ⚠ WHAT THAT RETREAT COSTS IS STATED IN THE TEST FILE RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the surviving tests prove the filter's LOGIC, not its REGISTRATION. That Hangfire actually calls it rests on the UseFilter line in AddAcmpHangfireStorage and is verified by inspection only - the same class of gap as the AddSource lines in each host's Program.cs, and named as such in AV-211. DESIGN POINT WORTH KEEPING: the Activity travels through PerformContext.Items and never a field, because Hangfire resolves a filter ONCE and reuses that instance across every worker thread - an instance field would be shared state across concurrent jobs and each would stop whichever activity was stored last. Dispatch and execution spans are deliberately NOT parented: Hangfire serializes a job as type, method and arguments with no header for a W3C traceparent, so linking them would mean changing the serialized job payload. Both mutations killed with the mutant confirmed to COMPILE - removing the unwrapping fails exactly one test, flipping ActivityKind.Consumer to Producer fails exactly one. 1880 tests pass; coverage 99.58% global with both new files at 100%.

BATCH 17, THE STACK BATCH. A STACK WAS STARTED - THE FIRST TIME IN THIS PROGRAMME - AND IT WAS DONE THE SAFE WAY. The operator authorised it and chose the isolated option over reusing the dev stack, which mattered: docker ps showed no ACMP containers but docker volume ls showed FIVE populated volumes including acmp_mssql-data, and containers last exited three weeks ago. That is precisely the dev-stack rebuild pitfall - SQL Server keeps the VOLUME's original SA password and ignores the env value, so a recreate against a populated volume fails its healthcheck and the recorded recovery is down -v, destroying all five volumes. dev-up.sh is up -d --build, the exact operation. Instead: an isolated compose project on FRESH volumes, same compose file and same env file, so the configuration under test was the shipped one while the dev stack's data was structurally unreachable rather than merely avoided. One further care: the sqlserver service builds a 3.62 GB FTS image, so an existing CI-built image was tagged to the name compose expects and the build was skipped. sqlserver and seq were brought up alone and confirmed healthy BEFORE the api was started. Everything came up healthy and /readyz returned 200 on all four checks - sqlserver, objectstore, hangfire and seq.

DEF-099 - OTLP TRACES HAVE NEVER REACHED Seq IN ANY ENVIRONMENT, AND DW-065 HAS BEEN CARRYING THE WRONG EXPLANATION FOR SEVERAL BATCHES. DW-065 says no trace has ever been OBSERVED, and it has been read as nobody having looked. Nobody could have looked. Both compose files set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT to the bare /ingest/otlp and NEITHER sets OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL, which is set nowhere in the repository; the .NET OTLP exporter defaults to grpc and posts to the endpoint verbatim. Probed against the running Seq: POST /ingest/otlp is 404, POST /ingest/otlp/v1/traces is 200. The OpenTelemetry SDK swallows export failures unless its self-diagnostic log is on, which it is not, so this has been silent since the instrumentation shipped. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHAT MAKES IT A FINDING RATHER THAN A SUSPICION: under shipped configuration, eight /readyz calls grew Seq's event count from 679 to 739 while the DB span count stayed at EXACTLY 72 with an unchanged newest-span timestamp. Same host, same port, same container - the log pipeline delivers and the trace pipeline does not. Setting the protocol to http/protobuf and restarting made 51 DB spans appear at once. Severity high and deliberately not softened: nothing malfunctions for a user, but a shipped capability is wholly non-functional in production, AC-133 rests on spans that never arrive, and the next agent told to read a trace could not have told an empty pipeline from a quiet one.

NFR-028'S RESIDUAL IS SETTLED BY OBSERVATION, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT PE-501 SAID WOULD SETTLE IT. The residual was that EF Core can INLINE constants into generated SQL, so a user value could in principle appear inside db.query.text, and that this could not be ruled out from a package README - only by capturing a real trace. Captured. Every literal in every observed statement is rendered as a question mark, and the decisive case is not a parameter at all: the health check issues SELECT 1, a compile-time constant that was never a parameter, and it arrives as SELECT ?. So SqlClient instrumentation sanitizes LITERALS, not merely parameters, which is the stronger property and the one the residual needed. Six distinct statements were captured across 72 DB spans, including an EF Core query rendered as SELECT TOP(?) ... WHERE [o].[Id] = ?. THE SERILOG HALF IS ALSO DONE, and it needed no stack: 24 structured-logging call sites exist in all of src across 680 files - confirmed by two counting methods that differ on receiver breadth - and NOT ONE names a person, an email, a vote or content. The masking enricher is registered in BOTH hosts and has a test, though it matters less than it looks: it matches by property name and its list covers email while containing nothing for full names or vote content, so two of the three things NFR-028 names hold by convention rather than by mechanism. Confirmed live too - the request-log events in Seq carry only Application, ConnectionId, Elapsed, RequestId, RequestMethod, RequestPath, SourceContext and StatusCode. NO VERDICT WAS RECORDED, DELIBERATELY: writing 'no PII reaches the traces' while DEF-099 means no trace reaches anything would be a Met verdict resting on a pipeline that does not deliver. NFR-028 waits for DEF-099.

MY OWN INSTRUMENT WAS WRONG TWICE INSIDE THIS ONE INVESTIGATION, AND THE SECOND FAILURE ALMOST PRODUCED A CONFIDENT WRONG DEFECT. First: I scanned Seq's events for property names beginning with db. and got zero, and concluded no DB spans existed. Seq nests OTLP attributes as STRUCTURED OBJECTS - db, then query, then text - so a flat dotted-name test could not have seen a span if one were there. I formed the protocol hypothesis on the strength of that zero. The hypothesis turned out to be correct, but it was reached from evidence that did not support it, which is the read-before-calling-it-a-defect failure arriving from an unusual direction: not a wrong conclusion, but a right conclusion held for a wrong reason, which is indistinguishable from luck until it is re-derived. Second: a before-and-after comparison built from an inline python -c inside a shell substitution FAILED SILENTLY on this Windows shell - both sides returned empty, compared equal, and printed the verdict 'shipped config does NOT export'. That verdict was an artifact of the broken measurement, produced before any evidence existed for it. Trap 2 exactly: a measurement that indicts is measuring itself. Both were caught by rebuilding the instrument - a reader that understands the nested shape, and a script FILE that prints event count, span count, newest timestamp and the wall clock together so a silent failure cannot masquerade as a result.

BATCH 18 - DEF-099 FIXED AND MERGED (#300 -> 1da0e05, all 10 checks green), AND IT HAD A SECOND HALF NOBODY HAD SEEN. WORKER HALF, which needed a different discriminator because both hosts write to one Seq: with the worker running and ZERO api requests, DB spans still grew 676 to 722 with the newest timestamp advancing - production that cannot come from an api nobody is calling. Both containers were confirmed carrying all three OTEL_ variables. One more check worth naming: docker compose config exits 1 on the cloud file, and I confirmed that is PRE-EXISTING by running the identical check against the unmodified file from HEAD - missing ACMP_S3_* variables, not my change. A measurement that indicts a change is measuring itself until proven otherwise.

NFR-028 CLOSED - AC-138 and AV-216 Met, against 1da0e05. The evidence was complete in batch 17 and the verdict was deliberately NOT written then, because 'no PII reaches the traces' while no trace reached anything would have been a Met verdict resting on a dead pipeline - true for the wrong reason, and indistinguishable from the real thing to every later reader. With DEF-099 merged, traces demonstrably arrive and the same evidence now means what it says. The trace half rests on the SELECT 1 case: the health check issues a compile-time constant that was never a parameter, and it arrives as SELECT ?, so SqlClient sanitizes LITERALS and not merely parameters - the stronger property, and the exact residual PE-501 said only a captured trace could settle. The log half rests on a census, not on the enricher: 24 structured-logging call sites in all 680 C# files, none naming a person, an email, a vote or content, confirmed by two counting methods that differ on receiver breadth and carrying a positive control. THE VERDICT SAYS PLAINLY THAT THE MECHANISM IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS: SensitiveDataMaskingEnricher matches by property NAME, and its list covers email while containing nothing for full names or vote content. Two of the three things the requirement names hold by CONVENTION, which is why the census is load-bearing and the enricher is only defence in depth.

PR #300 squash-merged, all 10 CI checks green. Adds OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL to api and worker and the missing OTEL_ block to the worker, in both the dev and cloud compose files. Config only. Verified by the span-count discriminator on an isolated stack, not by a clean start-up. Unblocks NFR-028 (AC-138 Met) and removes the cause DW-065 was really carrying.

BATCH 19 OPENED WITH AN OPERATOR INTERVIEW, AND THE INTERVIEW EXPOSED A PROCESS FAULT OF MY OWN. Four questions were put and all four answered: the next batch goes to NFR-019 TLS verification; the org security policy DOES specify the 8-hour session ceiling, confirming NFR-023 (DEC-065); the DW-029 programme is DONE when only externally-blocked requirements remain, at which point SL-031 goes to Review; and work continues in this session. THE FAULT: I put the NFR-023 question to the operator BEFORE sweeping the registers for it. LL-005 says sweep before offering the operator an option, and this is the first time I have broken it from the interview side rather than the disposition side. The sweep - run only when I went to execute the answer - found the register already held TWO answers nobody had connected to NFR-023: OQ-003, Deferred, resolving to a 60-minute idle timeout set in ACMP's own realm; and OQ-076, Approved and BUILT on 2026-08-13, which measured the live production realm and records that real app-side inactivity detection was constructed because automaticSilentRenew meant an open tab was never idle. Had I swept first I would have asked a better question. The cost this time was nil, because the three numbers in play turn out not to conflict - but the shape is the expensive one.

NFR-023 CLOSED - AC-139 and AV-217 Met, against fed82f4, with SC-027 first removing the [unverified] marker that had made it look unverifiable for several batches. THE THREE NUMBERS LOOK CONTRADICTORY AND ARE NOT, which is the reading that unlocked this: NFR-023 says 8 hours, OQ-003's resolution says 60 minutes, and both the Keycloak realm and the application say 30. NFR-023's Target states CEILINGS - idle at most 8 hours, absolute at most 24 - so a product sixteen times stricter satisfies it. The idle half is genuinely built rather than inherited: useIdleSignOut.ts sets a 30-minute timeout wired unconditionally in AuthProvider, and its wiring is mutation-tested because the silent-renew suppression must happen BEFORE the redirect or the next renew tick resurrects the session. The absolute half rests on ssoSessionMaxLifespan measured at 36000 seconds on the LIVE production realm - ten hours, inside twenty-four - and that clause has to rest on the lifespan ceiling rather than on refresh-token behaviour, because revokeRefreshToken was measured false and refresh tokens are therefore not rotated at all.

DW-073 - THE HALF OF NFR-023 THAT IS TRUE BUT NOT CHOSEN. Evidencing AC-139, the idle clause was straightforward and the absolute clause looked equally so: a measured number comfortably inside a stated limit. Then the obvious question - where is that number configured - returned nothing. deploy/keycloak/realm-export.json sets NEITHER ssoSessionIdleTimeout NOR ssoSessionMaxLifespan, and a grep for either key across every json and shell file in the repository finds no occurrence at all. So the value satisfying a Must-priority security requirement is not ACMP's decision; it is whatever the Keycloak image defaults to, observed once, eight days earlier. A Keycloak image bump could raise it past twenty-four hours and every test, gate and acceptance criterion would stay green, because nothing reads it. Same shape as NFR-050 - true across everything measured, guarded by nothing - but sharper, because NFR-050's property is a fact about migrations already written while this one is a fact about a third party's default that changes on a version bump. Recorded rather than absorbed into the verdict, and the verdict names it too.

DEF-100 DISPOSITIONED (DEC-066): NFR-019 IS KEPT AS WRITTEN AND THE GAP IS TRACKED AS DW-074. The operator was offered four dispositions and REJECTED the easy one - narrowing NFR-019 to the public endpoint plus the database hop, which would have extended OQ-024's mTLS reasoning to ordinary TLS and closed a Must-priority security requirement immediately with zero work. Their reasoning is worth keeping: ordinary TLS and mTLS are different questions, OQ-024 settled only the second, and an on-prem governance platform should not downgrade a security requirement because the current deployment happens to put everything on one host. CONSEQUENCE, STATED RATHER THAN SOFTENED: NFR-019 stays Approved and UNVERIFIABLE and correctly has no acceptance criterion, exactly where NFR-054 sits behind DW-066. DEF-100 stays OPEN deliberately - the decision reconciles which side is the AUTHORITY, it does not remove the disagreement, and marking it Fixed would be manufactured status. This is the SECOND time this session the operator has declined to relax a requirement to make it closeable; SC-024 was the first. The pattern is worth noticing: the register is being kept as a statement of the target, not of the status quo.

THE PROGRAMME'S OWN DERIVATION RULE IS BROKEN, AND MY OWN PROSE IS WHAT EXPOSED IT. prm-next section 2b states the candidate rule as: Approved Must-priority non-functional ids, MINUS EVERY ID NAMED IN A DEFERRED-WORK ROW, minus the ops group. Running it after writing DW-074 returned a single id, NFR-038 - NFR-018 had vanished. Nothing about NFR-018 changed. DW-074's activation trigger contains the phrase 'if an external security review or the NFR-018 ASVS assessment examines transport security', and that passing CROSS-REFERENCE was enough for the rule to treat NFR-018 as covered. THE RULE CONFLATES A MENTION WITH A COVERAGE - which is the exact sentence prm-next already carries about NFR-027 ('A mention is not a coverage'), arriving from the deferred-work side where nobody had thought to apply it. Re-derived with the strict reading - an id counts as covered only when it appears in the DW row's TITLE, that is when the row is ABOUT it - the answer is TWO: NFR-018 and NFR-038. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ARITHMETIC: the loose rule silently SHRINKS the candidate set every time a row cross-references a requirement, so the better the register's prose gets at linking things, the more requirements quietly disappear from the programme's own worklist. A well-cross-referenced register would eventually report itself finished.

SL-031 IS Review - THE DW-029 PROGRAMME IS DONE-CLAIMED AFTER TWENTY BATCHES, ON THE OPERATOR'S DEFINED END CONDITION. They set that condition in the 2026-08-20 interview: done when only externally-blocked requirements remain. Derived with the strict coverage rule, TWO remain and neither can be closed by any work in this repository - NFR-018 needs an external OWASP ASVS 5.0 Level 2 assessment, and NFR-038 rides Tarseem, whose phase was deferred INDEFINITELY by DEC-028 and which has no endpoint in the product at all. The slice's own objective carried a STATUS NOTE saying it was 'deliberately NOT Review', so flipping the status alone would have left the row asserting something untrue about itself; the note was rewritten in the same write, and the title and every other field round-tripped byte-identical against a generated pre-image. Review means done-CLAIMED and not verified, and readiness_check counts it as open - which is correct and deliberate. THE PROGRAMME'S REAL YIELD WAS NEVER THE VERDICTS. Fourteen requirements were found built on one side only, each invisible precisely BECAUSE it had no acceptance criterion to fail, and the register now carries them as deferred-work rows with activation triggers instead of as silence.

SL-031 IS Implemented AND PH-6 IS CLOSED - EVERY PHASE IS NOW Implemented EXCEPT THE ONE THAT IS FROZEN ON PURPOSE. The operator accepted the DW-029 programme on 2026-08-20, and that acceptance IS the verification Implemented requires: nothing mechanical could supply it, because no gate can judge whether twenty batches of acceptance-criterion work were done well. Phase readiness passed all four blocking rules - acs-met, slices-closed, wbs-done and defects-closed - with one advisory failing, defects-minor naming DEF-100, which DEC-066 carries DELIBERATELY because the operator kept NFR-019 as a target rather than narrowing it to match what shipped. That advisory failure is the intended state of this phase at close and is recorded as such in the phase row itself. TWO ROWS WERE AMENDED RATHER THAN JUST RE-STATUSED, because a status flip alone would have left both asserting something untrue about themselves. SL-031's objective carried a STATUS NOTE reading 'deliberately NOT Review'; it now records the acceptance and what Implemented means here. PH-6's exit_criteria named only SL-029 and SL-030 - they were written before SL-031 joined the phase - and now state that a third slice arrived whose exit is an operator acceptance rather than a shipped feature, because its output is verdicts and register rows, not code. Both edits round-tripped byte-identical against generated pre-images, and every field not being changed was preserved by omission. PH-3 remains Approved and must stay that way: WBS-20.4 is the email adapter against a hard constraint (DEC-055), and repairing it is the manufactured-status move DEF-010 records.

SECOND OPERATOR INTERVIEW OF THE SESSION, FOUR QUESTIONS, ALL ANSWERED - AND THE PREMISES WERE VERIFIED BEFORE ASKING THIS TIME. The first interview taught that lesson the hard way: I put the NFR-023 question to the operator before sweeping the registers for it, and the sweep would have changed the question. So this round began by reading PH-6's slice states, every phase's status and the deferred-work counts, which is what surfaced that SL-031 was the ONLY thing holding PH-6 open - a milestone that would not have been visible from the question alone. THE ANSWERS: accept SL-031 as Implemented and close PH-6, done here; triage the 53-row deferred-work backlog as the project's next milestone; fix BOTH blind controls, assumptions-current and DEF-087, rather than the cheaper one alone; and continue in this session, picking up DW-065's stale title in passing. Three of the four are still ahead.

DW-065'S TITLE CORRECTED - MY OWN DEBT, FLAGGED TWO BATCHES AGO AND NOT DONE UNTIL NOW. The row asserted that NFR-043 'HAS NEVER BEEN OBSERVED AS AN ACTUAL TRACE'. True when written; false since batch 17 captured real traces; and DEF-099 turned out to be the REASON none ever had been - OTLP export was posting to a path Seq answers 404 on, in every environment, silently. Leaving that standing was the register asserting something untrue, which is the exact class this whole programme exists to end, and I had flagged it in prm-next as 'the first item of the next batch' and then run two more batches without doing it. THE STATUS DID NOT CHANGE and should not have: the row's actual ask - trace completeness across ALL MODULE ENDPOINTS - is genuinely undone, because the traffic driven in batch 17 was unauthenticated and exercised almost none of them. Only the title was wrong. WORTH RECORDING: the row's own body had already listed a sub-check nobody had done - 'whether the WORKER's traces reach the same collector. Its OpenTelemetry registration is new and has never run anywhere.' Batch 18 answered exactly that, finding the worker had no OTEL_ variables at all. That sub-answer is now folded in, and what remains is span PARENTING across modules, which code inspection structurally cannot settle: registration proves spans are created, not that they join one trace.

DEFERRED-WORK TRIAGE SLATE BUILT - 53 OPEN ROWS GROUPED BY WHAT ACTUALLY BLOCKS THEM, WHICH IS THE AXIS THE ADVISORY'S QUESTION NEEDS. deferred-work-reviewed asks a human whether each activation trigger FIRED, and severity cannot answer that; what a row is waiting FOR can. Grouped with ordered rules, most specific first: (A) OUT OF SCOPE by hard constraint or an indefinitely deferred phase - Webex, AI extraction, the email channel, Tarseem - 11 rows whose triggers CANNOT have fired; (B) blocked on a running stack or production observation, 17 rows, mostly the P95 performance set; (C) blocked on a browser, 8 rows, the WCAG group and the browser matrix; (D) blocked on the operator or an external party, 4 rows; (E) ACTIONABLE NOW in this repository, 13 rows - the ONLY bucket whose triggers can have fired today. MY FIRST VERSION OF THIS INSTRUMENT WAS TOO LOOSE AND I DID NOT HAND IT OVER: a keyword bucket on 'render|visual' swept the alpine/distroless migration and the P95 page-load rows into 'needs a browser', and the default bucket became a dumping ground holding Webex, AI extraction and the email channel - none of which is self-contained, all three out of scope by hard constraint. The second version uses ordered first-match rules. ONE KNOWN MISFILE REMAINS AND IS STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: DW-066, the alpine/distroless migration, sits in the browser bucket and does not belong there. A triage slate with one acknowledged error is usable; one with an unknown error rate is not.

CORRECTION - I PUT TWO UNMEASURED NUMBERS IN A COMMIT MESSAGE, IN THE SAME BATCH WHOSE OTHER ENTRY PRAISED ME FOR NOT HANDING OVER A LOOSE INSTRUMENT. Commit 46821d6 states the deferred-work triage split as 'A. out of scope 11 / B. blocked on a running stack 17'. The correct split is A=10 and B=18. The script has always said 10 and 18; I never saw those two lines, because the command that ran it piped through tail and the visible output began part-way down bucket B. I then wrote the counts into the commit message from recollection. C, D and E were on screen and are right. HOW IT WAS CAUGHT, and it is the reason the discipline exists: preparing the resume prompt for a fresh session starts by RE-MEASURING every number the prompt will assert, which is prm-next's own standing rule after ten stale tallies. The re-measurement disagreed with what I had written an hour earlier, and re-running the original script settled which was true. WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A CORRECTION RATHER THAN A SHRUG: the numbers are small and nothing downstream depends on them, but a commit message is durable and unamendable, and the failure mode is exactly the one this session has been documenting all day - a count asserted from memory rather than from output, produced immediately after congratulating myself for rigour about a different instrument. The rule that would have prevented it is mechanical: if a number is going into a durable artifact, it must come from output visible in the same breath, not from what I believe the output said.

prm-next.md REWRITTEN END TO END FOR A FRESH SESSION - 783 LINES TO 498, BECAUSE ITS SPINE HAD BECOME FALSE. The file was organised around 'the DW-029 acceptance-criterion programme is the active work', and that programme closed today. Section 2b was titled 'What is NEXT: the DW-029 programme' and section 1 opened by saying it is where you start. A fresh session would have acted on both. WHAT WAS PRESERVED AND HOW: sections 3 and 4 - the two misleading registers, and 175 lines of traps that each cost real time to learn - were carried over BYTE-IDENTICAL by SLICING the original text rather than retyping it, and the slice was hash-checked before and after (sha b41761ef5feb0450). That is LL-001 applied to prose: the hand is the untrusted transport, and retyping 175 lines of hard-won warnings to preserve them would have been the least safe way to keep them. WHAT WAS REWRITTEN: section 1 (state, the corrected candidate rule, the advisories including the two BLIND ones, and a compressed record of batches 14 to 21), section 2 (things already built that get re-proposed), section 5's programme-specific rules - which outlived the programme and now say so - and section 6, the carried list, which now opens with the operator's chosen next work rather than with items they had already dispositioned.

THE HANDOFF VERIFICATION FOUND THREE THINGS THE MECHANICAL CHECK COULD NOT, WHICH IS THE POINT OF DOING BOTH. The id sweep passed cleanly - 99 governance ids in prm-next and 60 in the memory index, zero dangling, and 31 explicitly asserted row states all matching live. Reading the prose then found three real faults. FIRST, A DANGLING SECTION REFERENCE: section 3 said 'measure them (2b says how)' and section 2b no longer exists; repointed at section 1. SECOND, AND THE WORST OF THE THREE: the new measurement block told a fresh session to run entity_query on requirements, and THAT CALL FAILS - 226 rows is about 82 KB and overflows the tool's token limit, which I had hit myself earlier in this very session. The file would have sent a fresh session straight into an error as its first act. It now points at the canonical JSONL, which is what trap 13 already says to do for payloads, and states plainly that the columns argument does not narrow the response. THIRD, a preamble sentence left ungrammatical by my own insertion. NONE of the three is an id or a status, and none would have been caught by any amount of mechanical checking - which is the same lesson the file's own tenth-fix paragraph records, arriving again one batch later.

Deferred-work disposition session, part 1 of the operator's 2026-08-20 choice. Re-derived the grouping over all 53 open DW- rows rather than trusting the batch-21 slate, as prm-next instructs. Partition verified mechanically against the live register: 53/53, zero gaps, zero duplicates, split 19 repo-adjudicated / 12 operator-adjudicated / 22 structurally blocked. My grouping differs from batch 21's bucket E on twelve rows because I split by WHO ADJUDICATES rather than WHERE THE WORK LIVES - the demand-triggered rows (DW-028, DW-033, DW-035, DW-063) moved out of the actionable bucket into the operator tier where they can actually be answered, and DW-001, DW-011, DW-014, DW-029, DW-034, DW-037, DW-047, DW-054, DW-071, DW-072 moved in. Batch 21's one acknowledged misfile (DW-066 in the browser bucket) is placed with the operator-plus-heavy-verification group instead.

FIVE FINDINGS THAT CHANGE THE QUESTIONS, all from sweeping adrs/decisions/scope_changes BEFORE the interview rather than after (LL-005, LL-008, trap 32) and from reading implementations rather than the rows describing them (LL-006).

1. DW-037 IS NOT A PENDING JUDGEMENT - IT IS DRIFT. DEC-064 clause d2, Approved at the operator interview of 2026-08-19, reads 'DW-037 is ACTIVATED... It becomes real work.' The row still reads Open. I swept every Approved decision, ADR and Merged scope-change naming a DW- identifier and cross-checked each named row's live status: of DEC-064's five clauses, d1 (DW-020 and DW-030 to Done) and d4 (which produced DW-038) were applied and d2 alone was not. DW-037 is the only deferred-work row an approved decision explicitly activated that is still Open.

2. AND THE REQUIREMENT BEHIND IT SAYS THE OPPOSITE. SC-020, Merged 2026-08-18, moved FR-035 to Deferred - the label meaning not in v1 - and its own approval note records that FR-035 and FR-036 were added to that set after I disclosed they had been misclassified from file existence. DEC-064 d2 activated the work the next day. Both stand and neither cites the other.

3. NFR-013 MANDATES A TECHNOLOGY A RATIFIED ADR REMOVED. DW-054 carried its own instruction to check whether the columnstore index the requirement assumes was ever actually created, and nobody ran it. It was not: zero columnstore hits across migrations, and dashboardAgg.ts line 4 says 'no columnstore (ADR-0022, right-sized for under 20 users)'. ADR-0022 is Approved and its decision clause 1 reads 'No Reporting read-model tables, no columnstore, no aggregation endpoints in v1'. The keyword sweep also surfaced DEC-020 and ADR-0003, both older and both still naming columnstore reporting as part of why SQL Server was chosen, and OQ-040, which asks which SQL Server edition production runs - relevant because columnstore is not available on every edition. This is the LL-008 shape a fourth time: neither NFR-013 nor ADR-0022 contains the other's identifier.

4. DW-052'S PREMISE IS WRONG, SO ITS 'CLOSEABLE TODAY' HALF IS NOT CLOSEABLE. The row states that MeetingRecordingOptions and the topic attachment options carry NFR-011's per-file ceiling and concludes an acceptance criterion over the upload validators would verify it. They carry a ceiling, not that ceiling: TopicAttachmentOptions.cs line 10 defaults to 50 MB, MeetingRecordingOptions.cs line 10 to 2 GB, and a search for MaxSizeBytes across every json, yml, env and sh file in the repository returns nothing, so neither is overridden anywhere. NFR-011 says 100 MB. Whichever way that text reads - a floor to support or a ceiling not to exceed - one of the two upload paths diverges from it.

5. DW-037'S DATA CLAIM WAS WRONG IN ONE DIRECTION AND RIGHT IN ANOTHER. The row says P6 shipping made the scheduled-meeting date available. On the Topics side it did not: Topic.Schedule(meetingId, ...) at Topic.cs line 185 does not persist the meeting id - it raises TopicScheduledEvent, which has zero consumers anywhere outside Topics.Domain, and Topic has no MeetingId property or column. But the date IS reachable from the Meetings API, where MeetingDetailDto.ScheduledStart pairs with AgendaItemDto.TopicId. So the work is genuinely unblocked and must read from Meetings, never from the Topics API the row names. The same fact partially clears DW-001's stated blocker.

MECHANICAL FACT WORTH CARRYING: the deferred-work-reviewed advisory CANNOT go green from reviewing. I read its predicate rather than assuming it - it selects every row whose lifecycle_status is Open, Activated or Scheduled, with no reviewed field and nothing recording a judgement. Only closing a row removes it. The deliverable of a review is therefore the recorded judgement, not a colour change, and the advisory staying red afterwards is correct rather than a failure.

SMALLER VERIFIED VERDICTS: DW-014 not fired - ICommitteeDirectory projects CommitteeRecipient(UserId, FullName) and CommitteeMemberRef(PublicId, AccessExpiresAt), no email anywhere. DW-048 sub-fact confirmed - NFR-006, FR-032 and FR-153 are all still exactly 200 characters in both title and statement. DW-072 not fired - tokens.css last changed at b66695c on 2026-08-10, before the row was written. DW-071 not fired - routes last changed at ca3bf05 on 2026-08-14. DW-073 not fired, and its stated risk is smaller than the row claims: the Keycloak image is digest-pinned at 26.0 with an explicit sha256 in both compose files, so the unchosen session default cannot drift on a silent pull, only on a deliberate edit. DW-004, DW-006, DW-007, DW-008 and DW-010 not fired - their trigger prose says Phase 2 or Phase 3 meaning the PRODUCT ROADMAP era, not a package phase row, and reading PH-2 or PH-3 statuses for them gives the opposite answer.

NOTHING WRITTEN TO THE REGISTER. No disposition applied, no row status changed. The slate was published as an operator-facing artifact and the interview offered.

OPERATOR CORRECTION, and it is the most durable output of this part of the session. The operator refused the interview and rejected the slate on the ground that it referenced roughly forty package entities by identifier alone - every deferred-work row by number, plus DEC-064, SC-020, ADR-0022, DEC-020, ADR-0003, OQ-040, AC-049, AC-105, NFR-011, NFR-013, FR-035 and others - and then asked them to rule on them. Their words: do not just mention DW-x and expect me to go and check it myself; when referring to a tamheed entity of any type, LL, DW, SC and so on, do not just use its id to reference it, you have to get its details so I can read it fully and make a decision.

The failure is not cosmetic. An identifier is an index into a store the reader may not have open, so citing one transfers the retrieval work to the person the artifact exists to serve, at the exact moment they are being asked to decide. The practical effect is either a decision made on my summary of the row rather than on the row, or no decision at all. Both are worse than a longer document. It is easy to get wrong because identifiers READ as precision - a slate dense with them looks rigorous, and it is genuinely traceable for the agent, which has the store open and can resolve every one in a tool call. The asymmetry is invisible from my side: I had already read all 53 rows, so the identifiers felt like references; to the reader they were homework.

Recorded as LL-011 (Proposed - awaiting the operator's confirmation interview, since an agent never approves its own lesson). Remediation applied in the same breath: the slate is being regenerated with the full canonical text of every entity it cites, quoted verbatim from data/*.jsonl by a generator rather than transcribed by hand, which is LL-001's rule applied in the outbound direction.

entry: Squash-merge of PR #301 - the not-optimized-for-mobile notice. AC-140 Met via AV-218 against this commit. NOTE FOR ANYONE READING THIS COMMIT'S CONTENTS: it is larger than the feature, because local main held ten unpushed package commits that the feature branch carried, so the squash folded them in. No content was lost; the granularity was.

DW-040 / FR-037 BUILT - PR #302 open, awaiting CI. AND THE ROW'S SIZING WAS WRONG IN TWO WAYS, both found by reading the code before writing any, which is the whole return on that habit.

WHAT DW-040 SAID: 'the capability FR-037 exists to guarantee IS delivered; only the input gesture differs... No card-level drop handler exists.' That framed the work as pure frontend wiring. It was not.

FIRST ERROR: THE OPERATION WAS A SWAP AND A DRAG IS A MOVE. MoveTopicPriority swapped the topic with the element at index+delta. For the keyboard's plus-or-minus one that is correct AND INDISTINGUISHABLE from a move, which is exactly why nobody noticed. For a drag from index 4 to index 0 they diverge completely: a move shifts 0..3 down one place, a swap exchanges 4 and 0 and leaves the middle sitting where it was. Shipping the widened delta without replacing the swap would have delivered that surprise silently. The handler now lifts the topic out and re-inserts it at the target index; because the two operations agree at plus-or-minus one, AC-043's keyboard path is untouched BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by hope, and a test asserts precisely that.

SECOND ERROR, AND THE ROW COULD NOT HAVE ANTICIPATED IT: THE CLIENT CANNOT COMPUTE THE POSITION AT ALL. The kanban renders data.items - the FILTERED, SORTED and PAGE-TRUNCATED backlog result. Three independent things break the mapping between the index a user sees and the canonical column the handler orders by (Priority, CreatedAt, Key). The filter bar is rendered in kanban view, so hidden cards sit between visible ones. The kanban hides the pager but still sends pageSize, so it displays a PREFIX of the column and there is no way to reach the rest. And the sort chosen in table view persists into kanban, so the visual order may not be priority order at all. A delta computed in the browser would therefore ask the server to move the topic N places through a DIFFERENT sequence, and would land wrong whenever any of the three applies.

THE FIX IS ADDRESSING BY IDENTITY. The drag path sends the TARGET TOPIC'S ID and the server resolves both endpoints inside the column it already materializes, which makes the client's ordering irrelevant. The command now carries exactly one addressing mode - a non-zero Delta for the keyboard or a TargetTopicId for the drag - enforced by an XOR in the validator, because accepting both would leave the handler picking a winner silently and accepting neither is a request that asks for nothing.

MUTATION-CHECKED AT BOTH LAYERS, and both mutants were reverted and re-verified. Restoring the swap fails Move_by_more_than_one_MOVES_rather_than_swapping and NOTHING ELSE - so the new test discriminates, and the plus-or-minus-one test passing against that same mutant is independent proof that AC-043 is unaffected by the change. Removing the same-bucket guard in Kanban fails exactly the cross-column test - so one gesture cannot silently fire both a reorder and a status transition, which FR-033 owns.

THE e2e EARNS ITS COST BY DRAGGING ACROSS MORE THAN ONE POSITION. A single-position drag would pass against the OLD swap semantics too and therefore could not tell the fix from the bug it replaced. LESSON RECORDED, AND THE CHECKING BEFORE RECORDING IS ITSELF THE POINT. The operator asked whether the repeated false-green pattern was a lesson. Rather than mint one on the strength of the question, I read the existing register first - LL-006, LL-007 and LL-009 all live in this family - and that read changed the answer.

WHAT I EXPECTED TO FIND: that this was LL-007 firing again and the honest move was to record an instance, not a new row. LL-007 says: before trusting a clean scan, prove the scanner looked at something - inject a deliberate fault and watch the count move.

WHAT I ACTUALLY FOUND: I HAD DONE THAT. The mutation IS LL-007's remedy, and it still produced a false green. LL-007 treats the SCANNER as the thing that might have no subject; its cure proves the FAULT was injected and says nothing about whether the DETECTOR exists. A mutation check stacks two instruments and LL-007 only inspects one. So this is not a duplicate - it closes LL-007's own blind spot, one level up. Recorded as LL-012, Proposed, awaiting the operator's confirmation interview.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES IT WORTH A ROW: a mutant that FAILS is self-proving - something ran, saw the fault, objected. A mutant that PASSES proves nothing at all, because a missing test, a mis-targeted file, a filtered-out test, a stale build and a genuinely uncovered branch all produce the identical observation. And it is the direction that FEELS like a completed check, because you did the work of writing the mutant.

THE DISAMBIGUATOR IS THE COUNT, and it is cheap: 13 tests where there were 10, of which 2 fail under the mutant. Two counts, both moving, in both directions. 'The mutant passed' is not a result.

A SECOND MECHANISM WORTH KEEPING, because it is not specific to tests: in a multi-command invocation an early step can fail while a later step still runs and prints a healthy number. Here a `cd` failed, the heredoc that wrote the test file never ran, and the vitest call on the next line executed anyway against the pre-existing suite. When a command chain writes something and then measures it, the measurement is not evidence that the write happened - the same family as reading an exit status after a pipe and getting the pipe's last command rather than your gate's.

HONEST QUALIFICATION, recorded so the row is not read as self-flagellation: the instinct worked. The passing mutant was flagged as suspicious and investigated rather than accepted, which is how the cause was found. The lesson is not that the judgement failed; it is that the judgement should not have to carry it, because the count check is mechanical and costs one command.

WBS-23.3 / DW-038 CSP SPIKE — RUN AND ANSWERED. VERDICT: PNG export of the CSS report cards IS possible under the shipped CSP with NO header change, but NOT with the library that was pre-selected. Nothing was installed; package.json is untouched.

HOW IT WAS RUN (so the result is reproducible, not asserted). The SPA was built with `npm run build` (exit 0). A throwaway harness was placed in the gitignored `dist/`: `spike.html` linking the REAL built stylesheet `assets/index-Ge1n7iiV.css`, `spike/cards.html` carrying one card of each of the five `rpt-*` kinds (bars, columns, stack, stat, matrix) using the real class names, and `spike/run.js` which applies the zone colours the way the app does — through CSSOM writes (`style.setProperty`), which is how react-dom applies the `style` prop, never through a style ATTRIBUTE. `dist/` was served by a small Python static server whose CSP header is EXTRACTED from `deploy/nginx/default.conf.template` and envsubst-ed from `deploy/.env.example`, never re-typed (LL-001). The header the browser actually received is recorded in the run report and is byte-identical to the shipped one for the on-prem topology: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self' data:; media-src 'self' ; connect-src 'self' http://keycloak.localhost:8085; frame-src http://keycloak.localhost:8085; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none'. The DEV topology was chosen deliberately because it is the STRICTER frame-src case: in cloud, KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN equals the site's own origin, so frame-src there effectively contains 'self'; in dev it is a foreign origin, so it does not. Chromium 149.0.7827.55, both locales, en/ltr and ar/rtl with dir+lang on <html> as the app sets them.

THE RUN WAS GATED ON THREE NEGATIVE CONTROLS, and they all fired before any capture was believed. (a) `setAttribute('style', ...)` was BLOCKED — a style-src-attr violation event, and the colour did not apply. (b) An injected `<style>` element was BLOCKED — style-src-elem. (c) A CSSOM `setProperty` DID apply. Without these three a clean capture would only prove the server had forgotten the header — the DEF-078 shape. They also independently re-confirm DW-022's 2026-07-16 browser finding against the header as it ships today.

RESULT 1 — THE TECHNIQUE IS NOT BLOCKED. The whole DOM to foreignObject to data-URL SVG to canvas to PNG pipeline runs clean. `img-src 'self' data:` admits the SVG data URL; the parent document's `style-src` does NOT reach inside an SVG rendered as an image, so the serialised inline styles in the foreignObject are applied normally; `getImageData` did not throw, so the canvas is not tainted. Ten captures, five card kinds by two locales, PNG dimensions matching the card's getBoundingClientRect times the pixel ratio, 25-130 ms each. Pixel assertions were derived LIVE from the rendered card rather than hardcoded: the exact zone-fill colour read off the element via getComputedStyle was found in the PNG in quantity (17793 px of rgb(214, 69, 63) in the bars card, 130188 px of rgb(251, 240, 214) in the matrix), and a colour that cannot be in the card returned zero every time, so the pixel searcher was proven able to say no. Dominant-colour share 0.51-0.86, nowhere near a blank image.

RESULT 2 — THE PRE-SELECTED LIBRARY FAILS, AND ITS ROW'S PREMISE WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. `modern-screenshot` 4.7.0 threw on EVERY card in BOTH locales: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'cssRules'). Root cause read in the source, not guessed: `embedWebFont` builds a scratch document with `ownerDocument.implementation.createHTMLDocument('')` and appends a `<style>` to it (dist/index.mjs:1347-1350). That scratch document INHERITS the page's CSP, so the style element is refused, `tempStyleEl.sheet` is null, and line 1381 dereferences it unconditionally. The five style-src-elem violations attributed to modern-screenshot.js in the report are exactly this. Note what this is NOT: it is not the inline-style-in-foreignObject problem DW-038's brief predicted, and it is not fixable by widening the header for foreignObject — it is an unguarded `.sheet` on a code path that, for this app, has nothing to do. Passing `font: false` skips that path and all ten captures then succeed — but the ARABIC OUTPUT IS VISIBLY BROKEN: with the webfont gone the title reflows from one line to two and collides with the subtitle, because modern-screenshot deliberately omits width/height from the styles it copies (its `ignoredStyles`), so the clone re-lays-out under the substituted font. So `font: false` is not an escape; it trades a crash for a silent layout defect in one locale only.

RESULT 3 — `html-to-image` 1.11.13 WORKS, WITH FONTS, ZERO VIOLATIONS. All ten captures succeed in both locales and it contributes NOT ONE CSP violation; every violation in the report is either one of my three deliberate controls or modern-screenshot. It avoids the fatal construct: it inserts @import rules into the real stylesheet rather than a scratch document, and the `<style>` element carrying the font CSS is appended to the DETACHED clone, so no CSP check ever fires on it. Fonts are genuinely embedded, proved directly rather than inferred from pixels — `getFontEmbedCSS` returns 48 @font-face rules / 854 KB for en (IBM Plex Sans) and 80 rules / 1.63 MB for ar (IBM Plex Sans + IBM Plex Sans Arabic), and every one of the 48/80 `url(...)` is a `data:` URL beginning with the WOFF2 magic. ⚠ The first cut of that instrument reported `dataUrlCount: 0` beside a 874619-character string — incoherent on its face; the regex missed that the URLs are quoted. Corrected, and cross-checked against a 160-character sample of the actual CSS. The Arabic renders correctly with fonts embedded: title on one line, no collision, matching the live reference. A pixel diff quantifies the difference embedding makes — 1.60% of pixels in en, 1.26% in ar — with a self-diff control at exactly 0.0000%, so the diff can distinguish.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND IS THE OPERATOR'S: the dependency to install has CHANGED from the one they were shown. The evaluation carried into this session ranked candidates on registry metadata and picked `modern-screenshot` (186 KB, zero deps, published 2026-04-16) over `html-to-image` (315 KB, last published 2025-04-19, called stale). Measured against this app's actual CSP, the ranking inverts: the winner on every metadata axis is the one that cannot run here, and the one rejected as stale is the one that works. Nothing has been installed and no header has been touched. ⚠ Note also that DEC-068 d1's rationale carries the same wrong sizing verbatim — 'PNG export is a canvas draw and a download, blocked on nothing'. There is no canvas (OQ-022 Approved, ADR-0022: no chart library, charts are CSS primitives) and it was blocked on a real thing. The decision's OUTCOME — one slice holding these four rows — is unaffected; only that clause of its rationale is wrong, and it is recorded here rather than edited into an Approved decision.

⚠ Explicitly NOT claimed by this spike: no measurement on Firefox or WebKit (Chromium only, named above); no measurement of a full multi-card page export; no measurement of the memory cost of a 1.63 MB font payload per capture on the on-prem hardware; and no acceptance criterion written — per the standing rule an AC is written in the session that produces the build evidence, and this session produced only feasibility evidence.

WHAT SHIPPED. A Secretary or Chairman corrects a topic's type before Acceptance, from the topic detail page. Before this the only remedy for a topic submitted under the wrong type was reject-and-resubmit, which discards the record and its comments. A dedicated triage endpoint, role-gated on the command as well as the endpoint; the status guard left in the aggregate; a no-op writes no audit row and is checked BEFORE the domain call so that re-sending a past-Triage topic's own classification is not a 409.

THE ROW'S SIZING WAS RIGHT FOR THE FIRST TIME IN THIS SLICE, AND THE REGISTER'S WAS NOT. DW-032 claimed the domain method exists, is correct, is deliberately unreachable, and is not part of FR-030 because the guards are disjoint - every clause held when the code was read. DW-061, DW-040 and DW-038 had all said 'blocked on nothing' and all three were wrong, so reading the code first is what confirmed this one as much as it caught those. What the row could NOT tell me is what actually shaped the work: there was NO REQUIREMENT anywhere covering reclassification. FR-040 excludes it - the SPA's own edit screen header says it omits a type picker because 'type is reclassification, not an edit' - and FR-029 covers triage but is silent on type and source. DEC-070 chose a new requirement over binding to FR-029 or shipping an unbound criterion, and SC-031 created FR-164 before the build could be recorded at all.

THE DESIGN DECISION THAT MATTERED MOST, recorded because it is invisible from the row. Reclassification is NOT part of PUT /api/topics/{id}. That path admits the SUBMITTER on their own pre-Accept topic with NO policy check, so folding Type into UpdateTopicCommand would have turned classification into self-service - and classification drives the required template, the triage workflow and the SLA thresholds. The SPA had already drawn this line in a component header; reading it is what surfaced the decision rather than re-deriving it.

(1) AN ASSERTION OF MINE FAILED ITS MUTATION TEST. The SPA test asserting the topic's existing source is carried unchanged used the fixture's default, CommitteeMember - exactly the literal a 'hardcode the source' mutant would write - so the mutant PASSED and the assertion proved nothing. Fixed by choosing a value nothing else in the file produces. A fixture value that coincides with the obvious wrong implementation is a hollow assertion, and only mutation testing can tell the two apart.
(2) A VISUAL DEFECT WAS SETTLED BY A CONTROL RATHER THAN BY JUDGEMENT. The new dialog's first field label sits flush against the dialog description. Instead of fixing it locally or changing shared CSS on a hunch, the SHIPPED convert dialog was rendered in the same harness: identical spacing. So the new dialog MATCHES the application and changing it alone would have made it the inconsistent one. DW-077 carries the shared gap - roughly twenty dialogs, since the Field component renders .field and .field only gets top spacing from .field + .field, which cannot apply to the first one.

DEC-070 + SC-031 created FR-164 first, because the pre-build keyword sweep found no requirement covering the capability.

CORRECTION - SL-032's OWN ROW CARRIED A FALSE STATEMENT ABOUT ITSELF FOR ONE COMMIT, AND THE SAME FALSE STATEMENT REACHED AN UNAMENDABLE COMMIT MESSAGE.

WHAT WAS WRONG. The row's rewritten objective said "THE SLICE OBJECTIVE BELOW REPEATED THEM VERBATIM" and "The wrong text is left in place rather than edited away". Neither was true OF THE ROW THEY APPEARED IN. Slices require a FULL row on update, so that upsert REPLACED the objective wholesale: there was no text "below", and the original planning objective was not left in place - it was deleted from the live row and survives only in git. Commit 0e75755's message repeats the claim ("Left in place and corrected in the row's own text rather than edited away") and is pushed, so it cannot be amended.

WHY IT HAPPENED, because the mechanism matters more than the instance. The intent was genuine: leave a wrong planning statement standing rather than tidy it away, which is this project's rule. What was not checked is whether the WRITE MECHANISM could deliver that intent. `entity_upsert` replaces full rows - trap 13, known, recorded, and applied correctly twice earlier the same day when composing DEF-105 - and I still wrote a sentence describing a preservation the tool had already made impossible. THE SHAPE: an intention stated in the same breath as an operation that contradicts it, where the operation is the one that takes effect. It is not caught by any gate, because both halves are well-formed prose in a valid row.

WHAT WAS DONE. The objective is corrected to state plainly that the original was REPLACED, and to point at 0e75755^:tamheed-package/data/slices.jsonl where its 2677 characters survive verbatim - verified by reading that git object rather than asserted. The original is NOT re-typed into the row: hand-transcribing 2677 characters through the agent's own output is exactly the untrusted-transport failure LL-001 records, and the same reasoning was applied to DEF-105 earlier today. The two wrong sizing phrases the row needed to quote are quoted directly, so the point survives without the whole objective.

THE ESCAPE INTO A COMMIT MESSAGE IS THE PART TO CARRY. This is the same family as the eleventh stale statement recorded in prm-next's preamble - a wrong assertion that reached a commit message and cannot be taken back. That preamble counts TWO such escapes; this is a THIRD, and the count there is bumped in the same pass, because a counter nobody increments is the sort of dead control this project keeps finding.

⚠ NOTHING ELSE IN THE CLOSE-OUT IS AFFECTED. AC-143's verdict, the WBS transitions, the work_bind and the gate result were all measured independently and re-verified after this correction: gate 7/7, package ready:TRUE, slice ready:TRUE.

SLICE-REVIEW CEREMONY RUN FOR SL-032 at the operator's instruction, 2026-08-22. VERDICT: all four acceptance criteria hold at HEAD. Nothing was falsified. ⚠ The transition to Implemented is NOT applied here - it was offered to the operator with the finding below, because I wrote two of the four criteria I am reviewing and told them the status change stays theirs.

HOW IT WAS RUN, adversarially rather than confirmingly, since independence is the one thing this review structurally lacks.

(1) REFERENCE-GRAPH CLOSURE over all four criteria: every path named in every source_span resolves at HEAD, and every against_commit is an ancestor of HEAD. ZERO broken references across AC-140, AC-141, AC-142 and AC-143. This is the instrument that found DEF-101 (a defect id cited by three records that never existed); it is cheap and no gate provides it.

(2) THE REAL RISK THIS REVIEW EXISTED TO CATCH: AV-218 and AV-219 were recorded against 78b5ca2 and 145d9bf, and THREE merges have landed since. A verdict is only true of the tree it was measured on. Each criterion's load-bearing guard was re-checked as present at HEAD - the mobile notice's live region, MoveTopicPriority's target-identity addressing, the report card's rpt-card-tools raster filter, and the ABSENCE of the Topic::Reclassify/2 allowlist entry - and then the suites carrying them were RE-RUN at HEAD: 3 vitest files green, 75 backend cases green.

(3) HEAD'S CODE IS THE TREE CI ACTUALLY TESTED, proven rather than assumed: `git diff --stat 02101d6 HEAD -- src tests` is EMPTY, so every change since the merge is package, prompt or memory. That closes the gap between 'CI was green on the PR' and 'the thing sitting on main is what CI saw'.

⚠⚠ THE REVIEW'S OWN FINDING, AND IT IS THE THIRD INSTANCE TODAY OF ONE SHAPE. Checking AC-141's claim that a test exists to fail if anyone simplifies drag-reorder back to a delta, I grepped `tests/ --include=*.cs` for the target identifier and got ZERO - which reads exactly like the claim being false. The tests are real; they live in the SPA (api/topics.test.ts, Kanban.test.tsx) and in TopicHandlerTests under different naming (Move_by_more_than_one_MOVES_rather_than_swapping). MY SCOPING excluded where the answer was. Today that same shape produced DEF-104's first sweep returning ten of twelve because it keyed on `PageSize` while two endpoints page with `size` and `n`, and a font-embed probe reporting `dataUrlCount: 0` beside an 874,619-character string because the regex missed that the URLs were quoted. ⚠ LL-013 does NOT catch this: injecting a known fault into `tests/*.cs` would have been found, because the scanner ran, had a subject, and returned a true number about the wrong SET. The defect is the DENOMINATOR, not the instrument. Proposed as LL-015.

NO SCOPE DEVIATIONS were found during the review; no new defects; no waiver needed. Package ready:TRUE, slice ready:TRUE, gate 7/7.

entry:
DEF-104 FIXED - PR #306, squashed to bdbd8b6, CI 10/10 completed with none non-passing. Verified on origin/main BY CONTENT: 11 PageSize.Clamp call sites, ZERO lower-bound-only guards remaining. No acceptance criterion was written: this is a defect fix restoring intended behaviour, not a new capability, so it answers to the defect row rather than to a requirement.

⚠ I ALSO REMOVED A DANGLING REFERENCE I HAD CREATED. The first draft of the shared guard and both test files cited `FR-165` in their headers - a requirement that does not exist and that I had invented in passing while writing the comment. Stripped before the commit. That is the DEF-101 shape in miniature (a defect id cited by three records that never existed), caught here only because the reference-graph habit from the SL-032 review was still fresh. A capping fix does not need a requirement, and inventing one in a code comment would have created the very kind of unresolvable pointer G-IDS cannot see.

THE COUNT WAS WRONG IN THE ROW AND I RE-DERIVED IT. DEF-104's headline said TWELVE while its own enumeration listed ELEVEN; the two never agreed and nothing had compared them. Two sweeps keyed on different things - every `.Take(` call site under src (20), and every request type declaring a caller-supplied page/limit (13 files) - both return ELEVEN. ⚠ NEITHER WAS COMPLETE ALONE: the first is what sees the audit endpoint, which pages with a local named `size`; the second is what confirms no record-declared paged read was missed. This is LL-015's first application, hours after it was pinned.

THE FIX'S ONE JUDGEMENT CALL, stated because it could have been wrong quietly. Max = 500, not 50. Fifty is what GetNotifications uses and copying it would have looked like consistency - and would have broken the reports page, the dashboard, the kanban and the wiki, every one of which asks for 500. The number is grounded in ADR-0022, which records pageSize=500 as VERIFIED to cover every register at CON-001's 20-user ceiling. Measured from the SPA rather than assumed: the largest page it ever requests is 500.

ONE DELIBERATE NON-CHANGE. GetDecisions with a null limit still performs no Take. It is not caller-amplifiable, so capping where no cap existed would be a silent truncation - DEF-103's own shape, which this project fixed weeks ago by capping AND surfacing an actionable notice. Bounding only the caller-supplied value keeps the fix a fix.

⚠⚠ THE GUARD I WROTE WAS ITSELF TOO NARROW ON FIRST WRITE, AND ITS OWN DISCOVERY GUARD CAUGHT IT. PagedReadCapTests keyed discovery on the OUTPUT shape - request types returning PagedResult<T> - which structurally excluded GetNotificationsQuery, the one read that was ALREADY CORRECT, because it returns a bespoke DTO. The assertion 'discovery must find at least 10' turned red instead of the real assertion passing over nine. A discovery that cannot see a correctly-shaped read cannot see a future BROKEN one shaped the same way, so the narrowing was the entire failure. Re-keyed on the INPUT shape. LL-015 firing inside the fix that produced LL-015 is worth more than the fix.

TWO READS ARE OUTSIDE THE REFLECTION GUARD AND ARE NAMED IN THE TEST rather than silently missed: the audit endpoint has no request type to discover (a local inside a minimal-API delegate), and GetDecisionsQuery carries `int? Limit` rather than `int PageSize`. Widening the predicate to catch them would sweep in unrelated commands. Both are clamped at the call site.

GATES: Application 1167, Architecture 54, Api 368, Domain 269; `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` (which caught a real import-order break from the new usings); coverage gate 459 files at 99.59%; check-vulns clean.
